CutVisor · joinery catalog · version 0.2 · 5 November 2026

Joinery catalog

89 joints in two categories: 26 for timber construction and 63 for furniture. Every sheet has 3D views (exploded and assembled) and 2D views (with hidden edges and dimensions), parameters with the status of their source, and fabrication steps. Nothing is validated yet; metal hardware (screws, hinges, plates) has moved to the hardware module.

Rule status

  • §StandardFrom a standard or national annex; to be re-checked against the official text.7
  • ¶SourceFrom the supplied documentation (book, lecture, catalogue), page cited.486
  • ≈Trade practiceTrade rule not found in the documentation; to be confirmed by the architect or a carpenter.98
  • ?To be decidedNo good source yet; the value is decided at validation.15
  • =GeometryFollows from the definition of the joint.30

Birdsmouth (rafter notch on plate / purlin)

also: bird's mouth cut, rafter seat cut, rafter notch

Source
EN 1995-1-1:2004 (SR EN 1995-1-1), §6.5.2, eq. (6.60)–(6.63), fig. 6.11
All sources (5)Hide list
  1. EN 1995-1-1:2004 (SR EN 1995-1-1), §6.5.2, eq. (6.60)–(6.63), fig. 6.11
  2. FRILO, Dach+: Anschlüsse nach EN 1995 (2025), p. 2–3 — frilo.eu
  3. ICC, CodeNotes: Cutting, Drilling and Notching — IRC 2021 (2024), R802.7.1 → R502.8.1 — iccsafe.org

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Seating rafters on a wall plate or purlin.
Strength
Transmits the reaction by contact on the horizontal face (bearing perpendicular to grain) and on the vertical face. Load-bearing member: the notch weakens the rafter at the support → structural calculation (EC5 §6.5 check).
Fixing / glue
Nails, timber screws or angle brackets (→ metal fittings module).
Effect on the cut list
Length does not change; small volume removed (triangular prism of the notch).

Fabrication

  1. Mark on the rafter the bearing line (horizontal) and the vertical line (face of the plate), from the roof geometry.
  2. Cut the horizontal face (seat) and the vertical face (heel) until they meet.
  3. Test fit on the plate; adjust so it bears over the whole face.
  4. Fix (nails / timber screw / angle bracket).

Parameters

ParameterValueStatus
notch depth in the rafterby structural calculation: shear check of the beam notched at the support (factor k_v)EN 1995-1-1:2004 §6.5.2?To be decided
constructive depth limitremaining depth h_ef ≥ 0.5 h (DIN 1052:2008 §11.2; ÖNORM B 1995-1-1, at 6.5.2); US IRC: at most h/4 at the endFRILO Dach+ (2025) p. 2–3; ICC CodeNotes IRC 2021§Standard
horizontal bearing surfacewidth of the plate/purlin, full or partial — to be determinedno source found yet?To be decided

Notes. ⚠️ Load-bearing member: structural disclaimer required. EN 1995-1-1 sets no geometric limits for notches (FRILO Dach+ p.2); the limits above come from DIN 1052, ÖNORM and the US IRC. Notches in service class 3 are always reinforced (FRILO Dach+ p.2). The Australian rule 'at most 1/3 of the rafter depth' (AS 1684.2, cited by RMIT) has not been checked against the standard. Screw reinforcement is in feronerie_constructii.json. Correspondence: compas_timber TBirdsmouthJoint; BTLx BirdsMouth.

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Transmitting compression from an inclined strut or brace into a beam / sill.
Strength
Compression by contact on the step face; the main risk is shear of the wood in front of the step. Structural calculation.
Fixing / glue
Locating bolt or timber screw (→ metal fittings module).
Effect on the cut list
Strut length = length to the bottom of the step (from the geometry). The beam loses the notch volume.

Fabrication

  1. Determine the strut angle and the allowed h_c (h/4 … h/6).
  2. Mark on the beam the step face (normally on the bisector of the outer angle for a front notch) and the length of wood in front of the step.
  3. Cut the notch in the beam to depth h_c.
  4. Cut the end of the strut to the mating shape.
  5. Assemble; secure the position with a locating bolt / timber screw.

Parameters

ParameterValueStatus
step depth h_c (angle ≤ 50°)≤ h/4DIN EN 1995-1-1/NA, NA.12.1, eq. (NA.160) — after FRILO HO2+ p. 3; same in DIN 1052:2008 §15.1§Standard
step depth h_c (angle ≥ 60°)≤ h/6DIN EN 1995-1-1/NA, NA.12.1, eq. (NA.160) — after FRILO HO2+ p. 3; same in DIN 1052:2008 §15.1§Standard
step depth h_c (50°–60°)linear interpolation between h/4 and h/6DIN EN 1995-1-1/NA — after FRILO HO2+ p. 3; Colling (2004) p. 21§Standard
hheight of the member in which the step is cutfrom the joint definition=Geometry
front-wood length l_p (in the calculation)taken as at most 8·h_cDIN EN 1995-1-1/NA, NA.12.1 — after FRILO HO2+ p. 3§Standard
front-wood length l_p (constructive)≥ 200 mmColling (2004) p. 22 — constructive recommendation, not a code requirement≈Trade practice
h_c max50 mmh/4

Maximum notch depth h_c: detailing limit from the German National Annex (h/4 up to 50°, h/6 from 60°); not a strength check.

Notes. The limits come from the German national annex (NA.160) and from DIN 1052:2008; the NA text was seen only through the DIN table of contents and through FRILO, BW and Colling, so it must be checked against the official text. The Romanian annex SR EN 1995-1-1/NB is not public online and no source attributes step-joint rules to it. Also to be compared with EN 1995-1-1:2025. Correspondence: compas_timber TStepJoint; BTLx StepJoint + StepJointNotch.

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Struts with high compressive force, when a single step is not enough.
Strength
Two contact faces in compression; shear of the wood in front of the step on two levels. Structural calculation.
Fixing / glue
Locating bolt / timber screw.
Effect on the cut list
As for the single step: strut length from the geometry; the beam loses the volume of the two notches.

Fabrication

  1. Set h_c1 (front notch) and h_c2 (heel notch, deeper by ≥ 10–15 mm).
  2. Mark both contact faces on the beam.
  3. Cut the stepped notch.
  4. Cut the strut end to mate (two faces).
  5. Assemble with a locating bolt.

Parameters

ParameterValueStatus
each steplimits of the single step (h/4 … h/6)DIN EN 1995-1-1/NA, eq. (NA.160) — after FRILO HO2+ p. 3; BW sheet 1-H3-5, p. 20§Standard
cuts on both faces1/6 of the depth per cutBW sheet 1-H3-5, p. 20; Colling (2004) p. 22¶Source
difference between the depths of the two steps≥ 1 cm (DIN 1052); ≥ 1.5 cm (ÖNORM B 1995:2015)FRILO HO2+ p. 7§Standard
depth ratioh_c1 ≈ 0.8 · h_c2 (calculation assumption)FRILO HO2+ p. 7; BW sheet 1-H3-5, p. 20≈Trade practice

Notes. The 1 cm / 1.5 cm difference is cited by FRILO without a clause number; it must be checked against the DIN 1052 and ÖNORM texts and confirmed in the Eurocode context. Correspondence: BTLx StepJoint (twice); compas_timber TStepJoint (DOUBLE variant).

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Two opposite rafters meeting at the ridge (roofs with or without a ridge purlin).
Strength
Transmits the horizontal force between rafters by contact and fixing; the bridle variant is stiffer laterally.
Fixing / glue
Wooden peg, nails or bolt.
Effect on the cut list
Rafters extend past the ridge line over the overlap zone (from the geometry); volume removed by the notches.

Fabrication

  1. Mark the ridge line (vertical) on both rafters from the roof pitch.
  2. Half-lap variant: remove half the thickness on opposite faces over the overlap zone.
  3. Bridle variant: cut the fork (b/3) in one rafter and the tongue in the other.
  4. Assemble and fix with wooden peg / bolt.

Parameters

ParameterValueStatus
variantshalf-lap at the ridge, pegged; bridle (tongue and fork); French ridge lapSobon (2004) p. 38, fig. 14; BTLx 2.3 p. 37–38=Geometry
lap length (French ridge lap)= width of the rafter's reference sideBTLx 2.3, FrenchRidgeLap p. 37¶Source
other proportionsto be determined; the sources give examples, not rulesSobon (2004) p. 38; Timber Frame HQ?To be decided

Notes. Sobon: the mortised versions (open or blind) perform best at the peak. Timber Frame HQ shows a tongue-and-fork example: 4×6 in rafters, 1½ in tongue, ¾ in oak peg. The French ridge lap appears only in software specifications (BTLx, compas_timber), not in the historical manuals. Correspondence: compas_timber LFrenchRidgeLapJoint; BTLx FrenchRidgeLap, RidgeValleyCut.

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Post-to-sill, post-to-beam, struts; also in furniture.
When not to use
Mortise too close to the end of the piece: the wood in front of it may split.
Strength
Resists shear through tenon contact in the mortise; in tension it holds only by peg (wooden nail) or wedges. Load-bearing members → structural calculation.
Fixing / glue
Wooden peg (wooden nail); optional wedges; in carpentry usually no adhesive.
Effect on the cut list
The length of the tenoned piece INCREASES by the tenon length (taken from the geometry). The mortised piece loses the mortise volume. The wooden peg = additional part.

Fabrication

  1. Mark the tenon on the end of piece B (thickness ≈ b/3, centered) and the mortise on piece A.
  2. Cut the tenon cheeks and shoulders.
  3. Cut the mortise (drill + chisel or router) 5–10 mm deeper than the tenon length.
  4. Test fit; if pegged, drill through the mortise and tenon (optionally offset for drawbore tightening).
  5. Assemble and drive the peg.

Parameters

ParameterValueStatus
tenon thickness≈ b/3 (b = member width); Rivington: not necessarily 1/3, sized to the stressRivington (1891) p. 67; Joinery Handbook (2020) p. 76¶Source
tenon lengthto be determined; no general rule in carpentry (furniture: ≤ 4 × tenon thickness)Joinery Handbook (2020) p. 76 — furniture only?To be decided
clearance at mortise bottommortise deeper than the tenon so the shoulders bear; default 5–10 mmRivington (1891) p. 67; TFEC Tech. Bulletin 2011-03, rule 3; TFEC 2-2018 §6.02 tolerances give 0–16 mm≈Trade practice
peg-to-end distance (relish)≥ 2.5 D in compression; in tension along the grain ≥ 4 D (softwood) / 3 D (hardwood); D = peg diameterTFEC 1-2019, table 3C, p. 21¶Source
wooden pegØ 19–32 mm and ≤ 2/3 of the tenon thickness; placed ~1/3 of the tenon length from the shoulderTFEC 1-2019 §3.4.1(g), §3.4.6.3; Rivington (1891) p. 67¶Source
variantsstraight, stub, through tenon; with or without wooden pegRivington (1891) p. 69–70; Sobon (2004) p. 38; BTLx 2.3, Tenon / Mortise p. 50–52=Geometry

Notes. Napier p.17 (dowels ≥ 6 mm, drilled through all pieces in one operation) refers to EC5 structural dowels, not directly to the traditional peg; mentioned only as a reference. Tredgold (1820) p.143–144 gives thinner tenons on sills and rafters (≈ 1/4–1/5 of the thickness). Correspondence: compas_timber TTenonMortiseJoint, LTenonMortiseJoint; BTLx Tenon + Mortise.

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Frame corners, rafter ridge.
Strength
Large contact surfaces on the cheeks; laterally stable; fixed with a peg.
Fixing / glue
Wooden peg or bolt.
Effect on the cut list
For L both pieces reach the outer face of the other (length from the geometry); volume removed by the slot and by the tongue cheeks.

Fabrication

  1. Mark the tongue (≤ b/5, centered) on piece B and the slot on the end of piece A.
  2. Cut the tongue cheeks and shoulders.
  3. Saw the slot and remove the core (drill at the bottom + chisel).
  4. Assemble, drill and drive the peg.

Parameters

ParameterValueStatus
tongue thickness≤ b/5 (20 mm in the model for b = 100); wider, the cheeks of the slot become weak and can be wrenched offRivington (1891) p. 74¶Source
slot depthto be determined; in the model = width of the mating pieceno rule found; Treatise vol. 2, art. 84 shows the housing as deep as the strut?To be decided

Notes. The tongue follows Rivington's rule (≤ b/5), thinner than a tenon (≈ b/3); for small b, check there is room for the peg (Ø16 in a 20 mm tongue). Correspondence: BTLx Slot + Tenon.

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Beams crossing in the same plane, frames, corner wall plates.
When not to use
When one of the pieces is heavily loaded in bending at the joint (the section is halved).
Strength
Wood-to-wood contact in the notch; works in shear/bearing only together with fixing (nails, timber screws, wooden peg). No strength calculation in CutVisor.
Fixing / glue
Nails, timber screws or wooden peg (→ hardware list / metal fittings module).
Effect on the cut list
Length does not change; volume and mass decrease by the notch volume (W_mate × W × h/2 on each piece).

Fabrication

  1. Mark the width of the mating piece on both pieces, on the reference face.
  2. Mark the depth h/2 on the side faces.
  3. Saw the shoulders down to the depth line; make intermediate cuts every 20–30 mm.
  4. Remove the waste with a chisel, pare the notch floor flat.
  5. Test fit, assemble, fix with nails / timber screws / wooden peg.

Parameters

ParameterValueStatus
notch depth (equal sections)h/2 on each pieceRivington (1891) p. 64–65; Joinery Handbook (2020) p. 75¶Source
depth for different sectionssum of depths = joint height; split to be determined (compas_timber: cut_plane_bias, default 0.5)compas_timber 2.1.2, TLapJoint / XLapJoint?To be decided
notch widthwidth of the mating piece + clearance (default 0)from the joint definition; BTLx 2.3, Lap p. 31=Geometry

Notes. Napier p.5: forces are usually transmitted through lap joints, with adhesive or with dowel-type fasteners — general context, not a rule. Rivington p.64 describes the wall-plate corner (half the thickness taken from each piece, faces flush) and p.65 the double notching of crossing timbers. Correspondence: compas_timber LLapJoint/TLapJoint/XLapJoint; BTLx Lap.

Dovetail

SheetC08

Dovetail (lap / tenon)

also: carpentry dovetail joint

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Connections that must not pull apart: tie beams, collar ties.
Strength
Mechanical lock against pull-out through the trapezoidal shape; in compression it works by contact.
Fixing / glue
Nails or a safety wooden peg.
Effect on the cut list
The dovetail tenon variant adds length to piece B (as for a tenon); the half-lap variant does not change the length. A loses the housing volume.

Fabrication

  1. Mark the dovetail on the end of piece B (trapezoid, wide toward the end).
  2. Cut the dovetail (half-lap or full height, depending on the variant).
  3. Transfer the outline to piece A and mark the housing.
  4. Cut the sloped flanks of the housing and remove the waste with a chisel.
  5. Drive B into the housing from above; fix with nail / peg.

Parameters

ParameterValueStatus
dovetail angleto be determined; carpentry manuals give no slope; BTLx: flank angle default 15° (5–35°)BTLx 2.3, DovetailTenon p. 59?To be decided

variantshalf-lap dovetail or dovetail tenonRivington (1891) p. 65, 70; BTLx 2.3 p. 58–60=Geometry

Notes. The dovetail slope in carpentry remains to be determined. The old manuals consider it a weak carpentry joint, because the timber shrinks across the grain and the dovetail loosens (Rivington p.64; Tredgold p.146 on collar beams). Correspondence: compas_timber TDovetailJoint; BTLx DovetailTenon + DovetailMortise, Dovetail.

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Extending beams / sills longer than the available lumber; connects directly to Multi-Board Splicing.
When not to use
Splicing in the zone of maximum moment of a bent member; glued splice when there is load perpendicular to the glue plane or variable moisture (Napier p.20).
Strength
Traditional variants (with tooth, Jupiter) have a mechanical lock and are tightened with wedges/bolts; the simple glued scarf works through adhesive on the sloped surface.
Fixing / glue
Hardwood wedges, wooden pegs, bolts; or structural adhesive for the glued variant.
Effect on the cut list
Each segment is lengthened by L_s (or L_s/2 per end, depending on the variant) — the splicing must add this length. Wedges / pegs = additional parts.

Fabrication

  1. Choose the variant and the overlap length L_s.
  2. Mark the same shape (mirrored) on the ends of both segments.
  3. Cut the sloped plane / steps / teeth (saw + chisel or CNC).
  4. For the Jupiter / tooth variant: prepare the double wedges.
  5. Assemble (gluing or wedges + bolts), clamp, check alignment.

Parameters

ParameterValueStatus

Notes. Napier p.10 shows a traditional hooked scarf with a wedge (photo) and the glued splayed scarf (TRADA diagram). Tredgold gives the bolted length as a multiple of the beam breadth; Rivington tabulates it as a multiple of the depth. Current practice uses shorter lengths (see the splice cards). The finger joint has its own card. Correspondence: BTLx SimpleScarf, ScarfJoint (compas_timber has no scarf class yet).

SheetC10

Finger joint (horizontal / vertical)

also: glued finger joint, end finger joint, Keilzinken

Îmbinare încleiată în dinți panăKeilzinkenverbindung

Used in: Lengthening long membersVisibility: exposed

TopologyI
Source
Timber connections (Napier, Livingstone), p. 10, 20-21

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
End-to-end jointing of laminations for glulam, finger-jointed structural solid timber (KVH) and short lumber; done in the factory on automatic lines.
When not to use
Load perpendicular to the glue plane; fluctuating moisture conditions with different materials (Napier p.20). Not made by hand for load-bearing members.
Strength
Strength through adhesive over the large area of the finger flanks; rigid joint, no slip (the stiffest in the load-slip curves, Napier p.65).
Fixing / glue
Structural adhesive only; no metal fittings.
Effect on the cut list
Each jointed end loses ≈ the finger length (10–20 mm) plus the cross-cut; in the list it appears as extra length per splice. No additional parts.

Fabrication

  1. Remove defects (large knots) by cross-cutting.
  2. Mill the finger profile on both ends (profile cutter).
  3. Apply adhesive to the fingers.
  4. Press the ends together lengthwise until the fingers close.
  5. Leave to cure, then plane to size.

Parameters

ParameterValueStatus
finger orientationhorizontal (fingers visible on the side face) or vertical (visible on the wide face)Timber connections (Napier) p.10¶Source
adhesiveRF, MUF (lamination, finger jointing) or PRF; PVA is not structuralTimber connections (Napier) p.21¶Source
finger length≈ 10–20 mm (structural fingers ≈ 15–20 mm)factory rule of thumb, not in the documents≈Trade practice
finger pitch≈ 4–6 mmfactory rule of thumb, not in the documents≈Trade practice
quality controlstrict (pressing, moisture, curing time)Timber connections (Napier) p.20¶Source

Notes. Finger dimensions do not appear in the documents (practice / product standards EN 14080, EN 15497 — to be verified). Napier p.10 gives no dimensions. The Romanian term 'îmbinare în dinți' to be confirmed.

Splayed scarf with square-cut stops, pegged

  3. Notes on Building Construction, Vol. 1 (Rivingtons; ed. H. Fidler) — Tredgold's rules — chestofbooks.com

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Extending beams, purlins and wall plates loaded mainly in moderate bending, with the splice placed in a zone of low moment.
When not to use
Members in tension without a key or wedges (tensile resistance comes only from the treenails); a splice at midspan or directly above a post.
Strength
The inclined faces carry compression and shear over a large area of longitudinal grain; the stops (square-cut ends) prevent sliding on the slope and splitting of the tips; the treenails hold the faces in contact. No glue; weak in tension.
Fixing / glue
Treenails (oak/locust); no glue. Metal alternatives only in the hardware module.
Effect on the cut list
Each piece is cut L/2 longer relative to the splice axis (total +L = +800 mm at h = 200). Extra parts: 3 treenails Ø24 × 220.

Fabrication

  1. Fix the splice position in a low-moment zone and the length L.
  2. Mark the inclined line and the 20 mm stops on both side faces (same shape, rotated 180°, on the two pieces).
  3. Saw the inclined face and smooth it with plane/chisel; cut the stops square to the axis.
  4. Trial-fit the pieces dry; adjust until both stops and the inclined face bear at the same time.
  5. Drill the Ø24 treenail holes through both pieces (2 mm offset) and drive slightly tapered treenails.

Parameters

ParameterValueStatus
recommended usethe splayed scarf is used for members loaded in bendingAdvisory Leaflet 2 (Surrey), p.1, repair figure¶Source
splice length L (classic rule, no bolts)6 × h for oak, ash, elm; 12 × h for fir and other straight-grained softwoods (3 × h / 6 × h with bolts; 2 × h / 4 × h with bolts and indents)Notes on Building Construction Vol.1 — Tredgold's Rules (chestofbooks)¶Source

treenails3 pcs Ø24 (≈ b/6) of dry oak or locust, vertical, at L/4, L/2, 3L/4, on the width centerline; holes offset 2 mm for drawboringtrade rule≈Trade practice
treenail distance to piece end≥ 2.5 × d (≥ 60 mm for Ø24)trade rule≈Trade practice
locationin the least stressed section; not above a post (maximum shear) and not at midspan (maximum moment)Karolak & Jasieńko, SAHC 2020, p.1; Hamill Creek (blog)¶Source

Notes. The general “scarf-joint” card (constructii.json) covers the straight halved scarf with treenails; this is the splayed variant. Tredgold's rules (6h/12h) apply to joints without bolts and give very long lengths; current practice with treenails uses 3–4h, so the capacity must be checked. The Joint Book p.34–35 gives a 1:8 slope for the glued-only splayed scarf (board), and p.36 recommends reinforcing with pegs, screws or metal plates when extending structural members. Metal alternatives (bolts, plates, resin with rods) — separate module. The term “wedge-type scarf” is used here descriptively.

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Extending wall plates, sills and supported purlins, where the splice must not open vertically; an improved version of the straight halved scarf.
When not to use
Members in high tension (the inclined ends stop lifting, not pulling apart); long spans without a nearby support.
Strength
The ends cut at an angle (undersquinted) hook under each other and prevent the joint from opening vertically; large area of longitudinal contact. Treenails or a transverse key hold the pieces together.
Fixing / glue
Treenails Ø24 or a hardwood transverse key; no glue.
Effect on the cut list
Each piece +L/2 relative to the splice axis (total +L = +800 mm). Extra parts: 4 treenails Ø24 × 220 (or one key 40 × 40 × 160).

Fabrication

  1. Mark the centerline (h/2) on the side faces over the length L = 4h.
  2. Mark the ends at 70° to the faces, mirrored on the two pieces.
  3. Cut the inclined ends (saw tilted at 70°), then remove the half thickness with saw and chisel down to the centerline.
  4. Clean the inclined shoulders with the chisel guided on the layout line; trial-fit by sliding sideways.
  5. Drill and drive the treenails (or cut the mortise for the transverse key).

Parameters

ParameterValueStatus

Notes. The straight halved scarf with treenails is the “scarf-joint” card (constructii.json) — not repeated here. The 4 × thickness rule in The Joint Book is stated for boards; applying it to beams is an extrapolation (the order of magnitude matches carpentry practice of 3–4h). Alternatively, the shoulders can have wedges (Hamill Creek: undersquinted variant with wedge). Bolts/metal plates — separate module.

When to use
Extending wall plates and sills in timber-frame construction; traditional for roof plates and sills.
When not to use
Timber with sloping grain or knots in the blade zone; high sustained tension without wedges.
Strength
A halved lap in which each end finishes in a thin blade housed in the shoulder of the other piece; the blades stop the ends from opening sideways and vertically. Treenails take light tension.
Fixing / glue
Treenails Ø24; optional wedges in the cogged variant.
Effect on the cut list
Each piece +L/2 relative to the splice axis, plus the blade length (60) included in the length of the piece that carries it: total +L + 120 = +720 mm. Extra parts: 4 treenails Ø24 × 220.

Fabrication

  1. Mark the halved lap (h/2) over L = 3h and the blades at the ends.
  2. Cut away the half thicknesses; leave a 50 × 100 × 60 blade at the end of each piece.
  3. Chop the blade housing (52 × 100 × 62) in the shoulder of the opposite piece.
  4. Assemble by lowering vertically; check that the faces are flat.
  5. Drill and drive the treenails.

  4. Preservation & Repair of Timber Framed Buildings, Advisory Leaflet 2 (Surrey County Council and district councils), p.1, repair figure (“wedged scarf in members subject to tensile, bending or compression stress”)
  5. Hamill Creek Timber Homes, What is a scarf joint used for? (blog) — hamillcreek.com

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Extending members in tension or bending: truss bottom chords (tie beams), wall plates, purlins; the table and the key take the tension.
When not to use
Green timber, where shrinkage loosens the key with no possibility of re-driving it; small-section pieces (the table weakens the section a lot).
Strength
The table at the middle of the lap works in compression on the grain; the key or the pair of opposing wedges tightens the pieces and makes them work in tension without metal. Longitudinal shear in the grain behind the table is the failure mode to check.
Fixing / glue
Key or opposing wedges of oak/locust; 2 treenails Ø24.
Effect on the cut list
Each piece +L/2 (total +600 mm). Extra parts: 2 wedges 40 × 160 × (12→28) or one key 40 × 40 × 160; 2 treenails Ø24 × 220.

Fabrication

  1. Mark the lap L, the centerline and the 40 mm table at L/2.
  2. Cut each piece in steps: the thick half (h/2 + t/2) toward the shoulder, the thin half (h/2 − t/2) toward the end.
  3. Leave a 40 mm gap between the table faces for the key (40 × 40 slot across the full width).
  4. Assemble and drive the pair of opposing wedges from both sides until the ends seat on the shoulders.
  5. Drill and drive the treenails; trim the wedge surplus flush with the face of the piece.

Parameters

ParameterValueStatus

Notes. The difference between the classic rule (6h/12h) and current practice (3–4h) is large; the final value must be verified by calculation (EN 1995-1-1 has no rules for carpentry joints; check compression on the grain at the table and longitudinal shear). In the historic version many authors add bolts or iron straps — these belong to the metal module.

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Extending members in tension and bending (sills, wall plates, purlins, tie beams); used historically and for repairing members in old structures.
When not to use
High-moment zone: even with bolts, bending capacity in laboratory tests was about 1/3 of the continuous beam.
Strength
Two parallel inclined faces, offset by a perpendicular table at the middle; the pair of opposing wedges driven into the gap at the table pushes the ends onto the stops and puts the joint in tension. Works well in tension, poorly in bending.
Fixing / glue
Pair of opposing wedges of oak/locust; optional 2 treenails Ø20.
Effect on the cut list
Each piece +L/2 = +270 (total +540 mm). Extra parts: 2 wedges 30 × 180 × (12→28).

Fabrication

  1. Mark the profile in the vertical plane on both side faces: stop 40 – inclined face – table 30 – inclined face – stop 40.
  2. Cut the inclined faces and the stops; chop the 40 × 30 wedge gap at the table.
  3. Trial-fit the pieces: they must slide in sideways with small clearance at the table (the wedge gap).
  4. Drive the pair of opposing wedges from both sides until the stops close.
  5. Optional: Ø20 treenails through the inclined faces to hold the pieces in plane.

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Extending posts loaded only in axial compression and braced laterally (by beams, braces, walls).
When not to use
Posts in bending, tension or without close lateral restraint; exterior use with the recess in the lower piece (it collects water).
Strength
Compression passes through the ends cut exactly square to the axis (wood-to-wood contact on the grain); the tenon only centers the pieces and stops lateral movement. The cross version stops movement in both directions and rotation.
Fixing / glue
No fasteners; optional transverse Ø20 treenail through the tenon.
Effect on the cut list
Piece with the tenon +70 mm; piece with the recess no addition. No extra parts (optional one treenail Ø20 × 160).

Fabrication

  1. Cut both ends exactly square (check with a square on two faces).
  2. Mark the tenon centered on the end of the lower piece (54 × 54 × 70).
  3. Chop the 56 × 56 × 75 recess in the upper piece (or the cross shape for the cross variant).
  4. Assemble vertically and check plumb; restrain laterally with the members that tie the post.

SheetC17

Seated gooseneck / seated dovetail splice (koshikake kama tsugi / koshikake ari tsugi)

also: seated dovetail splice, gooseneck splice, koshikake kama tsugi

Înnădire pe reazem, cu cap în cârlig sau în coadă de rândunică (koshikake kama / koshikake ari)

Used in: Lengthening long membersVisibility: exposed

TopologyI
Source
M. Toda, Performance of wooden joints in the Japanese traditional wooden house, Part 1: Tensile strengths of straight joints, Hokkaido Forest Products Research Institute Report No.541 (2012), p.10–14 (fig. 1, tab. 1–2) — hro.or.jp

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Extending sills resting on a foundation and purlins/beams right next to a support; the head holds the pieces in light tension, the seat transfers the shear force.
When not to use
Within the span, away from a support; members in high tension (capacity 2–3 times lower than kanawa or okkake daisen at the same section).
Strength
The head (gooseneck or dovetail) hooks into a recess of the same shape; the head flanks with a 1:10 slope tighten the joint as it is lowered. Tension is carried by compression on the head jaws and shear of the neck — modest strength.
Fixing / glue
No metal; optional hardwood square peg 18 × 18.
Effect on the cut list
Male piece +L = +120 mm (the head); female piece +30 (the seat). Extra parts: optional peg 18 × 18 × 140.

Fabrication

  1. Mark on the male piece the head (neck 30 × 60, head 45 × 60) in the upper half and the bearing rabbet below.
  2. Cut the head with slightly inclined flanks (1/10 over the height).
  3. On the female piece chop the head recess in the upper half and leave the 30 seat in the lower half.
  4. Assemble by lowering the male piece: the head tightens on the flanks, the end bears on the seat.
  5. Optionally drive the 18 × 18 square peg.

also: timber fish-plate splice, fished butt splice with side cheeks

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Simple, inexpensive extension of posts and of members in compression or with occasional light tension; useful when a long scarf cannot be cut.
When not to use
Significant bending and permanent tension (treenails fail in bearing); exposed members where fish plates are not aesthetically acceptable.
Strength
The butted ends transmit compression; the side fish plates, indented into the pieces, take tension and prevent lateral movement; the treenails hold the plates in the indents.
Fixing / glue
Hardwood treenails Ø24; the historic version uses bolts (metal module).
Effect on the cut list
No added length on the main pieces (butt joint). Extra parts: 2 fish plates 50 × 200 × 600; 4 treenails Ø24 × 260.

Fabrication

  1. Cut the piece ends square and butt them together.
  2. Make the two fish plates 50 × 200 × 600 and cut on the inner face two 15 × 150 indents at each end.
  3. Chop the indent housings (15 deep) in the side faces of the pieces.
  4. Clamp the plates, drill through plate–piece–plate and drive the treenails.

SheetC19

Kanawa tsugi (stepped rabbeted splice with central key)

also: kanawa tsugi, splice with central key and guide tongues

Înnădire japoneză kanawa (în trepte, cu pană conică centrală)

Used in: Lengthening long membersRestoration repairsVisibility: exposed

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Extending posts and beams; in restoration, replacing the decayed part of a post (the base) without metal, since the pieces can be inserted from the side.
When not to use
Timber with checks in the tongue zone (mechigai) — splitting starts there.
Strength
Stepped lap with perpendicular jaws at both ends; the tapered key driven into the central gap pushes the pieces in opposite directions and tightens the jaws. The small tongues at the ends prevent lateral opening. Good tensile and bending strength for a joint without metal.
Fixing / glue
Tapered hardwood key (square peg); no metal.
Effect on the cut list
Each piece +L/2 relative to the splice axis, plus 15 for the tongue (total +L + 30 = +330 at h = 150). Extra parts: key 24→18 × 15 × 170.

Fabrication

  1. Mark the same profile on both pieces (the pieces are identical, rotated 180°).
  2. Cut the lap over half the width in two steps offset by 15, with perpendicular jaws at the ends.
  3. Cut the 15 tongues at the ends and the matching grooves in the shoulders.
  4. Insert the pieces from the side and check alignment.
  5. Drive the tapered key into the central gap until the jaws tighten.

Parameters

The tests are on Japanese cedar (sugi) and Todomatsu fir — values for oak/spruce from Romania are still to be established. Used in Japanese restoration for the base of posts (netsugi) — see card “repair-post-base-splice”.

SheetC20

Okkake daisen tsugi (sliding stepped splice with two square pegs)

also: okkake daisen tsugi, sliding splice with square pegs

Înnădire japoneză okkake daisen (cu fețe glisante și cuie de lemn pătrate)

Used in: Lengthening long membersVisibility: exposed

TopologyI
Source
M. Toda, Performance of wooden joints in the Japanese traditional wooden house, Part 1, Hokkaido Forest Products Research Institute Report No.541 (2012), p.10–14 (fig. 3, tab. 1, 4) — hro.or.jp
All sources (2)Hide list

  2. Chapter on Japanese joints, De Gruyter / Birkhäuser, doi:10.1515/9783035624373-011

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Extending beams and purlins (including eave beams) in traditional Japanese construction; the strongest of the traditional straight splices tested in tension.
When not to use
Situations where the pieces cannot be brought toward each other along the axis (assembly from one direction only); shallow beams (shear failure).
Strength
Stepped lap with slightly inclined faces, perpendicular jaws and tongues at the ends; the pieces are pushed over each other (sliding), then two transverse square pegs lock them. At small depths it fails in shear, at large depths by compression on the jaws.
Fixing / glue
2 hardwood square pegs; no metal.
Effect on the cut list
Each piece +L/2, plus 15 for the tongue (total +L + 30 = +510 at h = 240). Extra parts: 2 pegs 15 × 15 × 140.

Fabrication

  1. Mark the profile on the side faces: jaws at the ends, 15 step in the middle, faces with a small slope.
  2. Cut the lap over half the depth, the 15 tongues at the ends and their grooves.
  3. Drill 15 × 15 square holes transversely at L/4 and 3L/4 (with 1–2 mm offset for drawboring).
  4. Place the pieces offset and push them along the axis until the jaws close.
  5. Drive the two square pegs.

Parameters

ParameterValueStatus
splice length L≈ 2 × h (300 at h = 150, 480 at h = 240, 600 at h = 300)Toda 2012, p.11, tab. 1¶Source
central step and tongues15 mmToda 2012, p.11, fig. 3¶Source
square pegs (daisen / komisen)2 pcs 15 × 15, transverse, at L/4 from each end of the lap; of oakToda 2012, p.11, fig. 3¶Source
tensile capacity (Japanese cedar, width 120)Pmax ≈ 38.5–78.6 kN for h = 150…300 (higher than kanawa)Toda 2012, p.12, tab. 4¶Source
failure modesshear (small h), compression on the jaws (large h), splitting from the tongue (eccentricity)Toda 2012, p.14¶Source

The 15 × 15 pegs in the test are smaller than the traditional “daisen” (large pegs, usually 18–24 mm) — to be established for oak. The capacity values are for Japanese cedar.

  5. Preservation & Repair of Timber Framed Buildings, Advisory Leaflet 2 (Surrey County Council and district councils), p.1 (repairs: “patch incorporating tenon”, “slip tenon”), p.2 (rules 3–4; rot treatment, items 2–3)
  6. ICOMOS, Principles for the Preservation of Historic Timber Structures (1999), art. 5, 6, 9, 10, 11, 13 — alanbaskanligi.bursa.bel.tr (full text)

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Replacing the rotten end of a beam built into damp masonry (bearing), keeping the rest of the original beam; same logic for tie beams and floor beams.
When not to use
Before the cause of the dampness is removed; when the decay exceeds the length over which the splice can be made in a low-moment zone (then evaluate full replacement or sistering).
Strength
Lap over half the width (vertical plane), with inclined ends that work as an oblique bearing, the treenails transferring forces between the halves. Being near the support, the splice works mainly in shear, with low moment.
Fixing / glue
3 treenails Ø24–30 (oak/locust); no glue.
Effect on the cut list
The old beam loses d + c (decay + extra cut) and receives the lap cut. New replacement piece: length = d + c + L (e.g. 500 + 900 = 1400), section as the beam. Extra parts: 3 treenails Ø24 × 180; lead membrane (outside the cut list).

Fabrication

  1. Temporarily shore the beam near the support; remove the cause of the dampness; document (photos, survey).
  2. Cut the decayed end back to sound wood (+500 for dry rot); verify by probing.
  3. On the old beam cut the half width over the length L, with the end inclined at 60°.
  4. Make the replacement piece of the same species with similar moisture content; cut the complementary half and re-form the bearing end.
  5. Fit the piece on a lead membrane in the wall pocket, clamp, drill and drive the 3 treenails.
  6. Discreetly mark the new piece and document the intervention.

For rotten tenons, the Surrey leaflet also shows patches with an incorporated tenon and an applied tenon (slip tenon). Alternatives: bolts, plates, epoxy-resin prostheses with rods (ICOMOS 1999 art. 13: modern materials only with great caution) — metal module.

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Replacing the rotten base of a post (rising damp, ground contact), keeping the original upper part and its joints.
When not to use
Joints that collect water (recesses or V shapes open upward in the lower piece); without temporary support of the structure.
Strength
The post works in compression; the scissor (V) splice transmits compression through inclined faces and, being housed, stops lateral movement. The inverted-V variant (apex up on the new piece) does not channel water into the joint.
Fixing / glue
2 treenails Ø24; no metal.
Effect on the cut list
The old post loses d + c (decay + cut). New base: length = d + c + 320 (e.g. 400 + 320 = 720), section 160 × 160. Extra parts: 2 treenails Ø24 × 180.

Fabrication

  1. Temporarily support the structure around the post (beams, props, jacks).
  2. Cut the decayed base back to sound wood; document.
  3. Cut in the old post the inverted-V housing (open downward) over the central third of the thickness.
  4. Make the new base of the same species; cut the V tongue with the apex up and the shoulders inclined outward.
  5. Fit from below, lower the load onto the post, drill and drive 2 transverse treenails.

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Replacing the rotten portion of the sill at the base of a timber-frame wall (or of a base log), with two splices at the ends of the new portion.
When not to use
Splices under studs or posts (the tenon mortises weaken the zone); splices with the lap in the vertical plane where the longitudinal joint on the top face collects water.
Strength
The sill bears continuously on the plinth, so moments are small; the splices must resist mainly tension (wall thrust) and must not lift — the halved scarf with undersquinted ends or with blades is suitable.
Fixing / glue
Treenails Ø20 (3 per splice); the stud tenon pegs are re-made.
Effect on the cut list
New piece = removed portion (d + 2c) + 2 × L (e.g. 1400 + 2 × 480 = 2360), section as the sill. Extra parts: 6 treenails Ø20 × 140; new pegs for the stud tenons.

Fabrication

  1. Temporarily shore the wall (props under the beam at the upper level or under the studs).
  2. Cut out the decayed portion + sound timber on each side; mark the stud positions.
  3. Cut the halved laps with 70° ends on the ends of the old sill (upper half retained).
  4. Make the new piece, cut the complementary laps and re-form the tenon mortises at the original positions.
  5. Set the new piece on lead, lower the studs onto the tenons, drive the treenails.

ParameterValueStatus

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Replacing the rotten foot of the rafter (bearing zone on the wall plate and the eaves), keeping the original rafter.
When not to use
When the foot is concealed and has no appearance value — there, sistering with new timber alongside is simpler; when all rafters have the same decay and the wall plate is also decayed (fix the wall plate first).
Strength
Splayed scarf in the depth plane, near the support: the moment is small, shear and axial compression are carried by the inclined faces and stops; the treenails hold the pieces together.
Fixing / glue
3 treenails Ø20 (oak/locust).
Effect on the cut list
The old rafter loses d + c. New foot = d + c + 640 (e.g. 500 + 640 = 1140), section 80 × 160. Extra parts: 3 treenails Ø20 × 180.

Fabrication

  1. Temporarily support the rafter (prop or support beam) and unload the foot.
  2. Cut the decayed foot back to sound wood.
  3. Cut the splayed face with stops on the old rafter (in the depth plane), over the length 640.
  4. Make the new foot of the same species; cut the complementary splayed face, the bearing notch (birdsmouth) and the eaves end to pattern.
  5. Fit, drill and drive the treenails; re-make the connection to the wall plate.

Parameters

For thin rafters (b = 80) the Ø20 treenails are at the limit — to be verified; Hoath also mentions fixing with stainless bolts/screws or adhesives, which belong to the metal module. “Birdsmouth” = the bearing notch of the rafter (card “birdsmouth”).

Wall-plate repair splice

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Replacing the decayed portion of the wall plate (on a wall or on posts) under eaves with leaks, keeping the rest of the piece and the rafter bearings.
When not to use
A splice directly above a post (maximum shear, tenon housing) or midway between supports; before the water leaks are repaired.
Strength
On a wall, the wall plate bears continuously, and the splice must resist mainly the tension from the rafter thrust; on posts, the splice also works in bending and is placed close to the post.
Fixing / glue
Treenails Ø24 (4 per splice).
Effect on the cut list
New piece = removed portion + L at each spliced end (e.g. 1000 + 2 × 640 = 2280), section 160 × 160. Extra parts: 8 treenails Ø24 × 200.

Fabrication

  1. Fix the cause first (gutters, downpipes, roof covering); temporarily support the affected rafters.
  2. Cut out the decayed portion + sound timber; survey the rafter bearings and the tenons.
  3. Cut the halved laps with undersquinted ends on the old ends (lower half kept on the old wall plate if on a wall, so the new piece can be set from above).
  4. Make the new piece, cut the complementary laps, the housings for the post tenons and the rafter notches.
  5. Fit on lead (on a wall), drive the treenails, lower the rafters back.

Dutchman (inlaid timber patch)

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Repairing local damage (surface rot, knot hole, split) on the face of a member without replacing it; keeps the maximum of original material.
When not to use
Damage across the full section or in high-stress zones, where a splice is needed; timber that is still wet (fix the cause first).
Strength
The patch restores volume and appearance; it has little structural role unless glued and clamped. With slightly undercut edges (dovetailed in depth) it stays mechanically locked.
Fixing / glue
Water-resistant adhesive or a tight fit with undercut edges; optional 2 wooden pegs Ø8.
Effect on the cut list
The main member is not shortened. Extra part: patch of the same timber, e.g. 225 × 95 × 40 (with 5 allowance on the perimeter and 5 on the thickness for planing).

Fabrication

  1. Clean the finish around the damage and chisel out the decayed timber down to sound wood.
  2. Make the patch from the same dry timber, grain in the same direction, slightly larger than the void, with ends at 65°.
  3. Lay the patch over the void and scribe its outline on the old timber.
  4. Chop out to the line (chisel/router) to the patch depth, with slightly undercut edges.
  5. Fit the patch (glued or driven tight), plane flush with the face, and finish.

Parameters

Notes. Preservation Brief 45 mentions epoxy adhesive for wood as an example; here it is treated as an adhesive, while resin-and-rod consolidation or epoxy fills belong to the metal/resin module. It also recommends treating the surrounding timber with fungicide (chemical product, outside the cut list). The term “dutchman” is used in timber restoration; to be confirmed as the preferred term. The Surrey leaflet also shows the variant with a tenon incorporated in the patch (for ends of pieces with a rotten tenon).

Joinery for furniture and cabinetmaking: edge joints, laps, housings, mortise and tenon, miters, dovetails, dowels and biscuits.

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
The basic joint for frames (doors, windows, panels), legs with aprons/rails, and chair and table stretchers; the tenon at the end of one piece enters a blind mortise in the other, at 90°.
When not to use
Tensile load is the weak case: unless it is glued, the tenon has little hold against being pulled out, so joints loaded in tension get a peg, wedges or a drawbore (p.72). Tenon thickness is a compromise between two failure points: oversize thins the mortise walls, undersize leaves the tenon itself fragile (p.72, p.76). The wood must be at its equilibrium moisture content: otherwise the joint loosens as it dries, or the piece splits on assembly (Joinery Handbook 2020, p.76).
Strength
Very resistant to bending and racking thanks to the glue on the tenon faces (long grain on long grain) and the shoulders that take up rotation; in tension it depends on the glue. The shoulders (p.68) fix how deep the tenon goes, hide the outline of the mortise, add stiffness against racking and let the tenon sit away from the ends and edges where the wood is weak.
Fixing / glue
Glue; optionally a transverse wood peg near the shoulder (pinned tenon, p.90), wedge or drawbore for tension.
Effect on the cut list
The rail (tenoned piece) is lengthened by 2×L (tenon at both ends), e.g. +2×30 mm. The stile gets +15–25 mm horn at each end if the mortise is at the corner (cut off after gluing). Volume removed: mortise t × tenon width × depth.

Fabrication

  1. Plane the reference face and edge true. Lay the rail on the stile and mark its width; at a corner, leave the stile long (horn) so its end does not split while the mortise is chopped.
  2. Mortise ends: inset from the rail width by the size of the edge shoulders. Mortise sides: mortise gauge set to the chisel nearest T/3, leaving walls of at least T/4.
  3. Chop with the chisel (from the middle toward the ends) or drill with a Forstner bit/rout, then clean the walls and bottom.
  4. Tenon layout: the shoulder line runs all round the rail at a distance equal to the mortise depth; the cheeks are scribed with the gauge setting used for the mortise.
  5. Cut the shoulders, then the cheeks (saw, tenoning machine, circular saw with jig or router); fit the tenon to the mortise.
  6. Glue, clamp, cut off the horn and smooth.

Parameters

ParameterValueStatus
mortise width = tenon thickness t≈ T/3 (T = piece thickness); rounded to the available chisel (6/8/10 mm); Rivington (1891) allows 1/4…1/3The Joint Book p.76; Wood Joinery p.17; Constantinescu & Cârstea (1959) p.109, p.117; Fairham (1921) p.67; Ellis (1902) p.78; Hayward (2016) p.914; Joinery Handbook (2020) p.76; Rivington (1891) p.241 (1/4…1/3)¶Source

Notes. The book compares the blind (stub) mortise and tenon with the through one; for variants see the separate entries. The T/3 proportion is a general rule (p.76), adjusted to the chisel. The Joint Book gives no tenon length; the values here come from Constantinescu & Cârstea (1959), Fairham (1921), Bellu (1939) and the Joinery Handbook (2020). Hinescu (1989, p.43–44) classifies the joints by how much shows (hidden, half-hidden, open) and by depth (through or stopped) and gives a thicker tenon for furniture production (0.4–0.5 of the thickness) than the T/3 rule.

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Corners of frames (doors, mirrors, furniture frames), legs and chair/table frames; the end of one piece is split into a fork (slot), and the other has a full-width tenon.
When not to use
Without glue or pegs it opens easily (the slot is open at the end); not suitable where the end stays visible and the end-grain look is not wanted.
Strength
Large glue area (double that of a half-lap) and good racking resistance; durable (Wood Joinery p.9). Cross pegs through the assembled joint add mechanical hold where the corner is loaded or pulled apart (p.72).
Fixing / glue
Glue; optionally 1–2 transverse wood pegs.
Effect on the cut list
Each piece is lengthened by the width of the other (the corner overlaps fully): A +W_B, B +W_A relative to the inside length of the frame. Volume removed: the T/3 core from A and the 2 T/3 cheeks from B.

Fabrication

  1. With the mortise gauge, split the thickness of the slotted piece into thirds; the lines go over the end and continue along both edges.
  2. Mark the slot bottom line at a distance = width of the other piece; optionally drill at the bottom.
  3. Slot: cut on the waste side (saw, radial arm saw with dado head and jig, or circular saw with tenoning jig) and remove the core. With the chisel, work in from both edges, each a little past halfway, so the fibres do not break out at the exit.
  4. Tenon: on the other piece cut the shoulders on both faces at a distance = width of the slotted piece, then the cheeks.
  5. Fit, glue, optionally peg.

Parameters

ParameterValueStatus
thickness division3 equal parts: 2 fork arms + central tenon (≈T/3 each)The Joint Book p.80; Constantinescu & Cârstea (1959) p.109; Fairham (1921) p.30¶Source
open slot width≈ T/3, marked on the end and on both edgesThe Joint Book p.80; Constantinescu & Cârstea (1959) p.109 (mortise chisel ≈ 1/3 of the thickness)¶Source

Notes. Wood Joinery describes it as a relative of the mortise and tenon with more open slots; uses: frames, doors, chairs, tables. Geometrically it is a lap joint whose thickness is split into three equal parts instead of two (p.80). In English it is usually called a corner bridle joint. Romanian manuals call it 'cep drept deschis' (Hinescu 1989, fig. 3.8 a) and the 'slot and flat tenon joint at 1/3 of the thickness' (Constantinescu & Cârstea 1959, p.109), used on most objects and held by glue. Ellis (1902, p.80) ranks it as a joint for plainer work, secured with a peg.

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Where the tenon end may be seen on the opposite face (rustic/arts & crafts furniture, leg stretchers, shelves in side panels) and as the basis for the wedged tenon or the tenon with a transverse key.
When not to use
Tear-out is the main hazard: the face where the chisel or bit breaks through is not hidden by any shoulder. Cutting in from both faces so the two halves meet inside avoids it (p.82).
Strength
Like the blind tenon, but with maximum glue area (tenon across the full width of the piece) and the end accessible for wedges/pegs.
Fixing / glue
Glue; optionally wedges in the tenon end (see through wedged tenon) or a peg.
Effect on the cut list
The tenoned piece is lengthened by the thickness of the pierced piece + 1–2 mm at each joined end (e.g. +47 mm on a 45 leg). Volume removed: through mortise t × tenon width × T_A.

Fabrication

  1. Lay out as for the blind tenon, then continue the end lines to the far face and gauge the width on both faces, always registering the gauge on the same reference face.
  2. Deeply score the outline on both faces (against tear-out).
  3. Remove the waste half from each side (brad-point bit, then chisel), meeting in the middle.
  4. Cut the tenon to length = thickness of the piece + 1–2 mm.
  5. Glue, then plane the tenon end flush with the face.

Notes. The Joint Book gives no other proportions for the through variant. Constantinescu & Cârstea (1959, p.116–117) give a mortise 1/3 of the thickness, chopped from both faces to halfway; Hinescu (1989, fig. 3.8 e–f) calls it 'cep drept străpuns' (straight through tenon), paired with 'cep drept nestrăpuns' (stopped).

  2. The Joint Book, p. 75, 84-86
  3. W. Fairham, Woodwork Joints (Lippincott, 1921), p. 64–66 — archive.org
  4. Hinescu, A., Cartea tâmplarului universal (Ed. Tehnică, 1989), p. 44, 97 — archive.org
  5. C. H. Hayward, The Woodworker: The Charles H. Hayward Years, Vol. III — Joinery (Lost Art Press, 2016), p. 910 — blog.lostartpress.com

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Frames where the rail meets the stile at an angle other than 90° (chairs with a trapezoidal seat frame, raked frames); the mortise is inclined relative to the stile, and the tenon shoulders are cut to the angle.
When not to use
The first choice is to angle the tenon; an angled mortise is used only when an angled tenon would be left without continuous long grain (p.75, see 'angled tenon and shoulder'). At very acute angles, where the grain of the rail would be cut across too much, Fairham (1921, p.66) and Ellis (1902, p.80) switch to inserted hardwood tenons set square to the shoulder.
Strength
Like the basic joint, if the tenon stays parallel to the grain of the rail; angle accuracy is critical.
Fixing / glue
Glue; optionally a peg.
Effect on the cut list
The rail is lengthened by the tenon length measured along its axis (L, e.g. 25–30 mm) plus the shoulder difference due to the angle (W·cot α on the long side); cut from longer stock and trimmed to the drawing.

Fabrication

  1. Draw the joint at full size; the sliding bevel carries its angle to the outer face of the stile.
  2. Tilt the stile on a stepped support block until the mortise axis is vertical under the drill press (or square to the base of the routing box).
  3. Drill/chop to the marked depth and clean with the chisel.
  4. On the overlong rail, take from the drawing the angle of the edge shoulders, the position of the mortise and the tenon thickness; the face shoulders stay square.
  5. Cut the shoulders and cheeks; if two tenons meet in the leg, miter the ends at 45°.
  6. Fit and glue.

Parameters

ParameterValueStatus
joint angle αtaken with a sliding bevel from the 1:1 drawing; typically 75–85° on chairsThe Joint Book p.84-86; typical values = trade practice¶Source
mortise width / tenon thickness≈ T/3; width and ends are laid out on the working edge, as for a square mortiseThe Joint Book p.76, p.84¶Source
mortise endsinclined at α (the mortise follows the direction of the tenon)=Geometry
shouldersedge shoulders at α, taken from the drawing; face shoulders square across both faces, meeting the angled lines on the edgesThe Joint Book p.86 (steps 1-4); Hinescu (1989) p.97 (angled or profiled shoulders cut on the tenoning machine)¶Source
tenons meeting in the legends cut at 45° to the shoulder (tenons mitered)The Joint Book p.86 (step 5); Fairham (1921) p.64–65; Hayward (2016) p.910; Hinescu (1989) p.97 (tenon end cut at 45° on the tenoning machine)¶Source

Notes. The book covers the angled mortise here (p.84-85) and the marking of the angled tenon (p.86); the variant with an angled shoulder on raked legs is the separate entry 'mortise-tenon-angled-shoulder'. Hinescu (1989, p.44) lists tenon joints 'at 90° and at 45°'; in production, angled shoulders and tenon ends at 45° are cut on the tenoning machine (p.97).

SheetF05

Draw-bored tenon

also: drawbore pegged tenon, offset-peg tenon, draw-pinned tenon

Cep fixat cu cui de lemn în găuri decalate

Used in: Frames (doors, windows, pictures)Tables, chairs and bedsVisibility: half-hidden

Source
W. Fairham, Woodwork Joints (Lippincott, 1921), p. 64 — archive.org
All sources (5)Hide list
  1. W. Fairham, Woodwork Joints (Lippincott, 1921), p. 64 — archive.org
  2. The Joint Book, p. 72, 88-90
  3. G. Ellis, Modern Practical Joinery (Batsford, 1902), p. 61 — archive.org
  4. Bellu, P., Manualul tâmplarului, vol. I (Ed. Uniunea Camerelor de Muncă, 1939), p. 71–72 — archive.org
  5. Constantinescu, V., Cârstea, I., Lucrări practice de tâmplărie (1959), p. 107 — archive.org

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Country furniture, green-wood work and timber framing: a tapered wood peg through deliberately misaligned holes pulls the shoulders home with no clamps, and the joint can even go without glue.
When not to use
Rare in fine cabinetwork (p.89). In species that move a lot, a thick peg fights the seasonal movement and may split the mortised part, so it is kept slim and close to the shoulder (p.88). Ellis (1902, p.61) rates it less effective and less neat than a glued and wedged joint; on painted work the peg ends show once the wood shrinks.
Strength
Permanent mechanical lock in tension; the shoulders stay tight even after the wood shrinks.
Fixing / glue
Tapered wood peg (riven, straight grain), with or without glue.
Effect on the cut list
As for the basic tenon (rail +L at each end). Extra parts: 1 wood peg per joint, Ø8 × (T_A + 10 mm) with a tapered point.

Fabrication

  1. After cutting the mortise, bore the peg hole through one wall, centred on the mortise length and about a quarter of the stile width in from the edge; a scrap block underneath prevents breakout.
  2. Cut the tenon and clamp the joint dry; push the bit back into the hole to prick the hole centre onto the tenon.
  3. Take the joint apart and bore the tenon with the centre moved a little toward the shoulder (the offset).
  4. Assemble and drive the tapered peg, which draws the tenon to the shoulder; cut flush.

Parameters

ParameterValueStatus
hole position in the mortised pieceat the middle of the mortise length, at ≈ 1/4 of the piece width from the entry edgeThe Joint Book p.90 (step 1)¶Source
hole offset in the tenonthe tenon hole is moved toward the shoulder relative to the pricked mark: ≈ 1.6 mm (1/16 in, Ellis 1902) … ≈ 3 mm (1/8 in, Fairham 1921)The Joint Book p.90 (step 3); Ellis (1902) p.61; Fairham (1921) p.64¶Source
the peg (pin)tapered, driven through the offset holes; in the open-mortise version the hole in the fork cheeks is positioned accordingly; a square-section peg may be used, driven so that it locks; best cleft and left with sharp arrises rather than rounded (Ellis 1902)The Joint Book p.72, p.89; Ellis (1902) p.61¶Source
peg diametersmall: 6–10 mm (≈ T/3 on a 22–30 piece); Fairham (1921) bores ≈ 10 mm (3/8 in)The Joint Book p.88 (small diameter); Fairham (1921) p.64 (≈ 10 mm); 6–10 mm = trade practice¶Source
variant — bored after glue-up, no offseton window sashes, after gluing and cramping, frame and tenon are bored together and the peg is driven; the pegs go in from the glass side, so rain does not swell them and push them outBellu (1939) p.71–72¶Source

Notes. The Joint Book does not give the offset; Ellis (1902) gives ≈ 1.6 mm, Fairham (1921) ≈ 3 mm. The Romanian manuals consulted do not mention offset holes: Constantinescu & Cârstea (1959, p.107) and Bellu (1939, p.71) only describe pinning the tenon with a wood peg through holes bored together. Related variant: the plain pinned tenon, where a glued peg is fitted after glue-up, near the shoulder, and trimmed flush (p.90).

Haunched tenon

  3. W. Fairham, Woodwork Joints (Lippincott, 1921), p. 54–56, 65, 69–70 — archive.org
  4. G. Ellis, Modern Practical Joinery (Batsford, 1902), p. 78 — archive.org
  5. P. N. Hasluck (ed.), Cassell's Carpentry and Joinery (D. McKay, 1907), p. 67 — archive.org

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Corners of frames (doors, windows, panels) where the tenon is at the end of the stile: a short haunch the full thickness of the tenon fills the area between the mortise and the end, keeping the rail width resistant to twisting.
When not to use
A narrow tenon with deep edge shoulders and no haunch is the weak option: less long-grain glue area, and a wide rail is poorly held against twist (p.96). Conversely, a tenon wider than half the rail width weakens the stile end, which can be driven out when wedging (Hasluck 1907, p.67).
Strength
The haunch adds glue area and resistance to twisting and racking, without weakening the end of the stile (p.72, p.96). The English manuals explain the haunch the same way: it keeps the faces of rail and stile level and stops twisting (Fairham 1921, p.54–55; Hasluck 1907, p.67; Joinery Handbook 2020, p.75).
Fixing / glue
Glue; optionally a peg/drawbore.
Effect on the cut list
Rail +L at each end (the tenon) – the haunch adds no length beyond L. Stile +15–25 mm horn at each end, cut off after gluing. Volume removed in the stile: the mortise + the haunch housing t × t × t.

Fabrication

  1. Lay out the mortise on the stile so that it starts one tenon thickness (t) inside the horn cut line. Between the mortise and that line, mark the haunch housing on the edge and on the horn end: width = mortise width, depth = t.
  2. Chop the mortise. Saw down the two sides of the haunch housing through the horn, to the marked depth.
  3. Chisel out the waste between the kerfs; the housing bottom ends flat and parallel to the face.
  4. Lay out the tenon from the finished mortise. On the outer edge, the haunch line lies t beyond the face shoulder line, toward the end.
  5. Sawing order: haunch, face shoulders, edge shoulder, cheeks.
  6. Dry-fit: the shoulders must close fully, with neither the haunch nor the tenon end bottoming out. Glue up, then cut the horn off.

Parameters

ParameterValueStatus
haunch thickness= tenon thickness t (≈ T/3)The Joint Book p.97=Geometry
haunch projection (depth of the housing)= mortise width t; other values: ≈ 13–25 mm (1/2–1 in, Rivington 1891); 6–10 mm (1/4–3/8 in) on 38–75 mm rails without a groove (Hayward 2016)The Joint Book p.97 (step 1, step 4); Rivington (1891) p.241; Hayward (2016) p.915¶Source
haunch length (across the rail width)= t; the mortise starts at distance t from the horn cutting line; Hayward (2016): the haunch zone takes at least 1/3 of the rail width, the mortise ≈ 2/3The Joint Book p.97 (step 1); Hayward (2016) p.912, p.915¶Source
tenon lengthas for the basic tenon (≈ 2/3 W_A)≈Trade practice
horn on the stilekept until after gluingThe Joint Book p.97 (step 6); Fairham (1921) p.56¶Source
twin tenonsvariant for wide or near-square pieces; the tenons stand edgewise to the load; on a wide (≈ 30 cm) bottom rail of a door: two tenons in the same piece, with a haunch between themThe Joint Book p.73, p.97; Bellu (1939) p.70–71; Ellis (1902) p.78; Rivington (1891) p.241–242; Fairham (1921) p.65¶Source
tenon width≈ 1/2 of the rail width; a wider tenon leaves too little wood at the stile end, which can be driven out when wedgingHasluck (1907) p.67; Ellis (1902) p.78; Fairham (1921) p.54¶Source

Notes. The Romanian term 'pinten' is weakly attested: it does not appear in Hinescu (1989), Constantinescu & Cârstea (1959), Bellu (1939) or the woodworking course of c. 1934. Hinescu (1989, p.44) mentions 'half-hidden' (semiascuns) joints without a drawing; 'umăr de umplere' (filling shoulder) is a description, not an attested term. The Joint Book gives a square haunch equal to the tenon thickness; Rivington (1891) and Hayward (2016) give other projections (see parameters).

Sloped haunched tenon (secret haunch)

also: secret haunched tenon, sloping haunch tenon, hidden haunch

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Frame corners where the haunch must not show at the end of the stile (rabbeted frames for panel/glass, fine furniture); the sloped haunch does not come out at the end. It is also used on table rails joined to slender legs: two square haunches would leave too little wood between them, which splits, while sloped ones weaken the top of the leg less (Ellis 1902, p.84; Hayward 2016, p.915). Ellis also gives it for the top rails of dwarf doors, where a square shoulder must show.
When not to use
The sloped haunch has less gluing and gripping area than the square one; where the look of the stile end does not matter, Hayward (2016, p.915) prefers the square haunch.
Strength
Benefits (p.98): the end of the stile is not cut open, so it keeps its strength; there is more long-grain glue surface; and the haunch locks the rail against twisting. Hayward (2016) rates it differently in two articles: the secret haunch is somewhat stronger because it leaves more wood above the mortise (p.910), but the square one is stronger through its larger area (p.915).
Fixing / glue
Glue.
Effect on the cut list
As for the haunched tenon: rail +L at each end; stile +horn at the ends. Additional volume removed: triangular prism t × t × slope length.

Fabrication

  1. Mortise as for the square haunch. The haunch housing is then pared as a ramp: zero depth just inside the horn cut line, reaching depth t where it meets the mortise.
  2. Lay out the tenon. The haunch is a triangle on the outer edge: its sloping cut runs from the face shoulder line to a point t away from it.
  3. Cut the shoulders and cheeks.
  4. Pare the slope until it sits just below the top edge and seats in its ramp, so it cannot be seen once assembled.

Parameters

ParameterValueStatus
maximum slope depth (next to the mortise)= mortise width tThe Joint Book p.99 (step 1)¶Source
slope on the tenonfrom the face shoulder line on the top edge to a measure = tenon thicknessThe Joint Book p.99 (step 2)¶Source
haunch housingstarts inside the horn cutting line (depth 0 at the end) and descends toward the mortiseThe Joint Book p.99 (step 1); Hayward (2016) p.913¶Source
slope length (across the rail width)≈ t … 1.5 t?To be decided
variant multiple tenons/cutsthe tenon width is reduced by a haunch; twin tenons; saw cuts for thin tonguesThe Joint Book p.99¶Source

Notes. No source consulted gives the slope length; 10 mm is chosen for the example. The slope starts from nothing at the end of the stile (Hayward 2016, p.913). Variant used on the rabbeted frame (p.74, p.102-103).

Haunched mortise-and-tenon for a grooved panel frame

also: frame-and-panel joint, haunched tenon in groove, grooved frame with tenon

  3. W. Fairham, Woodwork Joints (Lippincott, 1921), p. 54–55, 74–75 — archive.org
  4. P. N. Hasluck (ed.), Cassell's Carpentry and Joinery (D. McKay, 1907), p. 330 — archive.org
  5. C. H. Hayward, The Woodworker: The Charles H. Hayward Years, Vol. III — Joinery (Lost Art Press, 2016), p. 910, 913, 915 — blog.lostartpress.com

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Cabinet doors and frames holding a flat or raised panel that floats unglued. The panel groove is centred on the inner edges and lines up with the mortises; where it would show at the stile end, a square haunch on the rail plugs it.
When not to use
The mortise never goes past the bottom of the groove; a tenon that is too wide is eased on the edge next to the haunch, never on the inner edge, which would shift the rail and throw the frame out of square (Hayward 2016, p.913, p.915).
Strength
The haunch both closes the groove and acts as an extra shoulder against racking; the tenon itself stays clear of the stile end (p.72).
Fixing / glue
Glue at the tenon; the panel unglued (floating) in the groove.
Effect on the cut list
Rail +L at each end; stile +horn. Panel: size of the opening + 2 × (groove depth − 2 mm expansion clearance). Volume removed: groove 8 × 8 on all inner edges.

Fabrication

  1. Start from the groove: its width (≈T/3) sets the tenon thickness. Mark the groove depth in from the rail edge; the tenon begins beyond that line, which fixes its width and the mortise location.
  2. Chop the mortises, then run the groove along every inner edge; it passes over the mortises and exits at the stile ends.
  3. Size the haunch so it fills the exposed groove at the stile end.
  4. Sawing order on the rail: haunch shoulder, face shoulders, cheeks.
  5. Glue (panel floating, unglued), cut off the horn.

Parameters

ParameterValueStatus
groove width≈ T/3The Joint Book p.100¶Source
groove depth≈ equal to the groove widthThe Joint Book p.100¶Source
tenon thickness / mortise width= groove width; tenon cheeks aligned with the groove wallsThe Joint Book p.101 (step 1), p.102¶Source
tenon widthstarts below the groove bottom (inner shoulder = groove depth)The Joint Book p.101 (step 1); Fairham (1921) p.75; Hayward (2016) p.915¶Source

Notes. The panel itself is held either in a groove or in a rabbet with a bead or stop (p.100); this entry covers the grooved case. The haunch length is not numeric in the book.

Mortise-and-tenon for a rabbeted frame

also: offset-shoulder tenon, rabbeted frame joint, sash tenon

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Rabbeted frames for glass (puttied) or panel with a retaining bead, sashes; the rabbet on the inner edge requires shoulders of different lengths on the two faces of the tenon. Fairham (1921, p.58) gives it for framed office partitions, greenhouses and sheds, wherever both stiles and rails are rabbeted; it needs very careful marking out.
Strength
As the haunched tenon; the sloped haunch hidden under the rabbet keeps the end of the stile intact (p.74).
Fixing / glue
Glue; glass fixed with putty or bead.
Effect on the cut list
Rail: +L at each end, measured from the long shoulder (the rabbet side); the lip shoulder is closer to the end by the rabbet width. Stile +horn. Volume removed: rabbet 20 × 10 on the inner edges.

Fabrication

  1. Fix the rabbet size first, since the sloped haunch sits under it; this gives the size and position of the mortise. Lay out and chop the mortise.
  2. Rabbet the inner edges down to the mortise cheek on the lip side. On the rail, the lip-side shoulder is placed further from the end by the rabbet width, so that it covers the lip.
  3. Sawing order: haunch slope, the two offset shoulders, the cheeks, then the cuts along the tenon thickness.
  4. Glue up; remove the horn after the glue has cured.

Parameters

ParameterValueStatus
tenon thickness / mortise width≈ T/3, matched to the width set firstThe Joint Book p.102, p.76¶Source
rabbet depth (across the thickness)≈ 2/3 of the thickness, from the back face, to the cheek of the mortise facing the show face; remaining lip ≈ T/3The Joint Book p.102; p.103 (step 2)¶Source
rabbet width (across the piece width)≈ T/3 or moreThe Joint Book p.102¶Source
offset shoulderthe shoulder on the lip side is offset (set back) by the rabbet width, to enclose the lip of the stileThe Joint Book p.102; p.103 (step 2); Fairham (1921) p.58; Hayward (2016) p.910 (back shoulder longer by the rabbet depth); Joinery Handbook (2020) p.75¶Source
tenon width= W − rabbet width − haunch zone; mortise placed after the rabbet marked on the end of the railThe Joint Book p.102¶Source
haunchsloped, under the rabbetThe Joint Book p.74, p.103 (step 1, 3)¶Source
corner on curved railsarched rails: the short grain at the corner is avoided by giving the shoulder a small 45° return that seats in a matching cut in the stileThe Joint Book p.103 (variants)¶Source

Notes. Two statements in the book seem to differ: the text gives the rabbet as ≈ 2/3 of the thickness, while the steps take it down to the mortise cheek nearest the show face. They agree if the rabbet is cut from the back and the tenon is centred (that cheek lies T/3 from the show face). The length of the haunch slope is not given. Hayward (2016, p.910): the mortise is set in at the inside by the same amount, because the rabbet cuts away part of the tenon. On sashes Bellu (1939, p.71–72) pins the tenons with wood pegs, because glue exposed to rain and sun is not enough.

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Frames with a molding (bead) on the inner edge that must return continuously at the corner: the molding on the stile is removed over the zone of the rail and both moldings meet at 45°.
Strength
As the haunched tenon; the miter of the molding is only aesthetic. With an angled tenon/small-miter shoulder, short grain is avoided (p.105).
Fixing / glue
Glue.
Effect on the cut list
Rail +L at each end, measured from the rabbet bottom (both shoulders on the same line, rail molding mitered). Stile +horn. Volume removed: the stile molding over the rail width.

Fabrication

  1. With the molding already run on the inner edge of the face, lay out the rabbet and the haunched mortise so that both terminate at the molding line.
  2. Then cut, in this order: the mortise, the rabbet (stopping at the molding line), the tenon layout and the tenon itself.
  3. Over the rail width, cut the stile molding back flush with the mortise.
  4. Miter both moldings at 45° using a chisel guide clamped to the edge, then dry-fit and glue.

Notes. The Joint Book does not specify the molding; the quarter round is an example. Bellu (1939, p.62–63) calls the molding returned at the corner 'ciubuc unghiular'. Fairham (1921, p.59–60) gives the joint for light cabinet work and also shows the alternative where the rail shoulder is scribed to the stile molding, with no miter.

SheetF11

Slip, or loose, tenon

also: floating tenon, false tenon, spline tenon, Domino tenon

Cep aplicatFremdzapfen

Used in: Frames (doors, windows, pictures)Tables, chairs and bedsVisibility: hidden

TopologyTL

All sources (5)Hide list

  4. W. Fairham, Woodwork Joints (Lippincott, 1921), p. 66 — archive.org

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Router-made frames: each piece gets a mortise and a separate tenon bridges the two, so no shoulders have to be cut and fitting is easier; also a standard way to replace a broken tenon in restoration. Older manuals use it where an integral tenon would have its grain cut across: pieces meeting at an acute angle, or curved rails; the hardwood tenon is glued into one piece and wedged into the other (Fairham 1921, p.66; Ellis 1902, p.80).
When not to use
Watch the terminology (p.93): in English 'slip joint' usually means the open bridle joint, and 'loose tenon' is also used for an unglued through tenon locked by a key; this entry is neither.
Strength
Comparable to an integral tenon if the tenon is well fitted and glued in both mortises.
Fixing / glue
Glue; the separate tenon. Variant: round tenons / dowels (p.94).
Effect on the cut list
No lengthening of the rails (cut to the length between stiles). Extra parts: 1 tenon per joint, e.g. 8 × 50 × 48 mm, from a planed strip (hardwood).

Fabrication

  1. Work out widths, lengths and mortise positions on a full-size drawing. Stiles are cut to full length and rails to the clear distance between stiles, since they carry no tenons.
  2. Clamp each corner pair together (rail on end, stile flat) and mark both mortises in a single layout.
  3. Rout each mortise with a straight bit and edge guide (or jig) in shallow passes: in the rail end and in the stile edge.
  4. Plane a strip for the tenons: width equal to the mortise length, thickness equal to the mortise width; round its edges to suit the mortise ends.
  5. Crosscut the tenons against a stop, each a little shorter than the two mortise depths combined.
  6. Glue, clamp and check the diagonals.

Parameters

ParameterValueStatus
mortisesrouted with a straight bit of diameter = mortise width, round endsThe Joint Book p.93¶Source
mortise width≈ T/3The Joint Book p.76; Joinery Handbook (2020) p.76¶Source
tenon strip width= mortise length; thickness = mortise widthThe Joint Book p.94 (step 5)¶Source
tenon lengthslightly less than twice the mortise depth (e.g. 2×25 − 2 = 48 mm)The Joint Book p.95 (step 7)¶Source
end fittingeither square the mortise corners or round the tenon edgesThe Joint Book p.94 (step 6)¶Source
mortise depth≈ 25–30 mm in each piece (≈ 3–4 × tenon thickness)≈Trade practice

Notes. The industrial equivalent (Domino tenon) is not in the book. Integral round tenons or dowels appear as a variant (p.94-95). Hinescu (1989, p.44, fig. 3.8 c–d) calls separate pieces joining two mortises 'cepuri aplicate' (applied tenons: a triangular one at a 45° corner, a round one).
