Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Door and panel frames, with dowels in place of the rail tenon. The panel groove, rabbet, profile or shoulders are machined once the holes are bored.
Strength
Resists shear well (door frames); the flutes keep glue on the dowel all the way down the hole. Under twisting loads it is weaker than a mortise and tenon (Joint Book); Joinery Handbook (p.77) still rates it almost as strong, thanks to modern adhesives, and easier to make.
Fixing / glue
Glue + fluted dowels.
Effect on the cut list
The rail is cut to the opening between stiles (no tenon length), plus the profile depth if there is a mating profile. Extra parts: 2 dowels per corner.

Fabrication

  1. Lay a template over the joint where the mortise and tenon would be and prick the hole centres on rails and stiles.
  2. Bore with a doweling jig set on the marks; when the holes must be off the centre line, a thin shim against the face moves them over.
  3. Machine any groove, rabbet, profile or shoulders, then glue the dowels and close the frame.

Parameters

ParameterValueStatus

Hinescu (1989, p.44) lists the 'applied round tenon' (dowel) among the forms of the mortise and tenon; in the chair on p.52 the front and back rails join the side frames with dowels.

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Corners of flat frames (rail butted against a stile, faces flush); it needs one slot per part, so it is very quick to make.
Strength
Good for light frames; for thick parts, double the biscuits. Glue + biscuit.
Fixing / glue
Biscuit + glue.
Effect on the cut list
Rail = opening between stiles. One biscuit (or two) per corner.

Fabrication

  1. With the parts cut and laid out as assembled, draw one line across the joint at the biscuit centre; use the largest biscuit the rail width takes.
  2. Set the 90° fence so the blade is centred in the thickness and select the biscuit size; slot the rail end and the stile edge on the line.
  3. Glue goes in the slots and on the meeting faces, not on the biscuit. Insert the biscuit, close the joint and use the side play in the slot to bring the parts into line.

Parameters

ParameterValueStatus
biscuit sizethe largest that fits the part width; the slot is ~54 mm long at the surface for #0, ~60 mm for #10, ~66 mm for #20The Joint Book p.167; Lamello catalogue 26/27 p.114¶Source
fita dry biscuit slides into the slot with no slack across its thicknessThe Joint Book p.166¶Source
fence90°, set at mid-thicknessThe Joint Book p.167; wolfcraft (2014) p.15 (fence for 90° and 45°)¶Source
double biscuitsthick parts: two slots stacked in the thickness, each cut with the fence on a different faceThe Joint Book p.167¶Source
minimum part width for #20the slot is ~66 mm long at the surface; Lamello asks for a minimum part width of 71 mmLamello catalogue 26/27 p.114; Lamello product page¶Source
frames from narrow stripsmatch the biscuit size to the width of the cut; very slim strips are better joined with round dowelswolfcraft (2014) p.17¶Source

Notes. Joint Selector (JB p.185): listed under 'Dowels and biscuits'. The earlier figure '#20 from ~50 mm' was too small: a #20 slot breaks out of parts narrower than ~66 mm (Lamello). Joinery Handbook (p.78) also recommends biscuits for keeping parts aligned during assembly.

End lap (corner half-lap)

also: corner halving joint, half-lap corner joint, corner lap

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Corners of frames, support frames and panels, simple door frames; combined with a center joint it forms a T.
When not to use
Glue alone does not resist sideways loads; where they occur, add screws or nails driven from the back (Joinery Handbook 2020, p.75). It is less strong and stable than mortise and tenon or dovetail joints.
Strength
Cheek-to-cheek contact gives a large long-grain glue area, but nothing locks the parts mechanically; where sideways loads are expected, add screws in drilled, countersunk holes.
Fixing / glue
Glue; optional countersunk screws or through dowels.
Effect on the cut list
No length allowance (the pieces overlap at the corner); volume removed T/2 x W_mating x W at each end.

Fabrication

  1. Layout: shoulder line at the width of the mating piece; centerline on the edge and across the end.
  2. Finding half depth on the table saw: cut a scrap from both faces, raising the blade a little each time, until the two kerfs meet and no lip is left in the middle. Then cut the shoulders on the miter gauge, with a spacer block clamped to the fence ahead of the blade to set the distance.
  3. Remove the cheek with a tenoning jig or with repeated kerfs. Band-saw alternative: kerf the shoulder first, then saw the cheek with a stop setting the depth.
  4. Router-table alternative: take the waste in successive passes, then level the cheek with light sideways passes over the bit.
  5. Square the inside corner with a chisel. When gluing, put a block between clamp and cheek so the pressure spreads over the whole glue face.
  6. Variants: mitered halving or dovetail lap.

Parameters

ParameterValueStatus
Depth (halving rabbet)1/2 of thickness (e.g. 10 mm at T = 20)The Joint Book p.40-41; Constantinescu & Cârstea (1959) p.109; Fairham (1921) p.22–23¶Source
Cheek length= width of the mating piece (e.g. 45 mm)The Joint Book p.47; Constantinescu & Cârstea (1959) p.109=Geometry
Piece thicknessesequalslides p.25¶Source
Screws for lateral loadsdrilled and countersunkThe Joint Book p.45; Fairham (1921) p.12; Joinery Handbook (2020) p.75¶Source
Fitthe parts go together under a blow of the fist; a heavy mallet or hammer spoils the workFairham (1921) p.26¶Source

Notes. Slides p.25 describe the half-lap joint generically; assigned here (L) and to center-lap (T/X). Constantinescu & Cârstea (1959, p.109) call it „îmbinare de colț prin chertare la 1/2 din grosime”. For outdoor work Fairham (1921, p.12) coated the cheeks with paint instead of glue and nailed or screwed the corner.

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Frames with intermediate rails, cabinet face frames, window and screen lattices, and traditional-style doors built entirely from half-laps. Constantinescu & Cârstea (1959) use it where the divisions of simple frames cross.
Strength
Each piece bears against two shoulders, so the joint resists twisting and racking better than the corner lap; the glue faces are large and long-grain.
Fixing / glue
Glue; optional peg or screw; variant with a dovetail on the end for tension.
Effect on the cut list
No length allowance; volume removed T/2 x W_mating x W in each piece (for T: end half-lap on the ending piece).

Fabrication

  1. Layout: shoulders squared across at the width of the mating piece; centerline on the end and edge, found by scribing from both faces with one square setting and correcting to midway between the two marks.
  2. Set a depth stop on the saw so its cuts end just short of the centerline.
  3. Saw the two shoulders, then kerf the waste between them every 3–5 mm.
  4. Knock out the kerfed waste with a chisel and pare the floor flat down to the centerline, finishing with a chisel or a shoulder/rabbet plane.
  5. Machine options: a dado head on the table saw with the miter gauge, or a hand router running between two guides clamped on the shoulder lines.
  6. Dry-fit, then glue and clamp with a caul to spread the pressure.

Parameters

ParameterValueStatus
Depth1/2 of thickness on each pieceThe Joint Book p.40-41, p.49; Constantinescu & Cârstea (1959) p.118; Fairham (1921) p.22¶Source

T variantthe ending piece has an end half-lap, the other a center recessThe Joint Book p.45; Fairham (1921) p.12¶Source
"Full lap" variantthe thinner piece is not cut; it sits at full thickness in a recess of that depth in the face of the otherThe Joint Book p.50¶Source

Notes. T and X variants combined in one card (same elementary cuts); the dovetailed T-lap is only mentioned as a variant. Constantinescu & Cârstea (1959, p.118): „îmbinarea în cruce, prin chertare, la 1/2 din grosime”. Fairham (1921, p.23) checks the gauge setting by pricking from both faces: the two marks must coincide.

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Diagonal lattice work in windows, doors and outdoor structures; diagonal braces between table or chair legs. In frames and shelf brackets, a strut joined this way prevents racking (Fairham 1921, p.13).
When not to use
Check on each piece which way the angle leans before cutting; the mirror-image mistake is easy to make.
Strength
Strong and good-looking when laid out accurately; the angled shoulders carry the T piece. Narrowing the lap where it crosses leaves more wood in the through piece and so strengthens it. The straight end-grain shoulders of the angled lap give the joint torsional rigidity (Joinery Handbook 2020, p.75).
Fixing / glue
Glue; optional dowels or plugged screws.
Effect on the cut list
The T piece is cut with the oblique end (length allowance ≈ W/tan(angle) at cutting); volume removed T/2 over the oblique zone of each piece.

Fabrication

  1. Layout: take the angle from the full-size drawing with a sliding bevel; mark the angled shoulders on the face of each piece and carry them around to the back of the through piece.
  2. Cut the T piece to length at that angle (radial arm saw or miter gauge; on a sliding jig, the support block is tilted to the same angle).
  3. Through piece: with the blade raised to the centerline, kerf both angled shoulders, then clear the waste between them with closely spaced kerfs or a dado head.
  4. T piece cheek: on the radial arm saw with the blade horizontal, or on the table saw with a sliding-fence jig; the cut stops exactly at the shoulder line.
  5. Pare both cheeks flat with a chisel or shoulder plane and assemble, through piece face up.

Parameters

ParameterValueStatus

Width of the oblique recessW_mating / sin(angle) (e.g. 45/sin60° ≈ 52 mm)=Geometry
Optional reinforcementdowels or plugged screws driven through the jointThe Joint Book p.54¶Source
Chiselling directionwith the grain, which changes direction across an angled lap; the same applies to the bottom of the lapFairham (1921) p.25¶Source

Notes. The "angled cross lap" (oblique X, with pegs) and "narrow angled lap" (p.54) variants are described only as variants. Fairham (1921, p.13) notes that when the oblique piece runs through, its end grain shows at the top of the frame.

Frame miter

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Flat frames of all kinds: pictures, mirrors, borders around panels and solid edging around tabletops. Frames with 6 or 8 sides are also the starting point for oval or round frames. The 1939 Romanian manual uses it on frames whose moulding runs along the sides, so the profiles meet on the diagonal; unmoulded frames are joined square.
When not to use
Any loaded application unless reinforced, since both glue faces are end grain. Parts whose widths differ by more than 2:1: accuracy and strength both drop as the difference grows.
Strength
Low: both glue faces are end grain, there is no mechanical help, and the result depends on the adhesive alone. It is normally reinforced with biscuits, splines set in saw kerfs, a corner brace or frame connectors.
Fixing / glue
Glue (on end grain, insufficient alone); biscuits, loose spline, dowels, veneer splines, frame nails or the metal corner connectors used by picture framers.
Effect on the cut list
Each part has the outside length of its side (point to point); no tenon allowance. Waste: triangle of L = W at each end. Extra parts if reinforced (biscuits #10/#20, splines).

Fabrication

  1. Lay out 45° (or 180°/n) at each end; when sawing by hand, the saw runs against a guide block fixed on the layout line.
  2. Saw the miters by hand with the guide, on the table saw with a miter sled, or on the radial-arm saw, after testing the angle on scrap.
  3. Fine-tune the cut faces with a plane on a miter shooting board; to change the angle by a fraction, pack a thin shim between fence and part.
  4. End grain soaks up glue, so apply plenty; clamp in a frame clamp or jig that keeps the corners from sliding.
  5. Add the reinforcement: biscuit slots, kerfs for splines, or a brace glued to the back.

Parameters

ParameterValueStatus
miter angle (4 sides)45° to the square cut; blade perpendicular to the face of the part, cut line sloping across the widthThe Joint Book p.106-107, 112; Fairham (1921) p.177; Joinery Handbook (2020) p.78¶Source
angle for n sidesmiter angle = 360°/n; cutting angle = (360°/n)/2 (e.g. 6 sides → 30°, 8 sides → 22.5°)The Joint Book p.110; Fairham (1921) p.178-179 (bisecting the angle; 22.5° for an octagon)¶Source
machine settingcheck the machine scale: some read the cutting angle, others read 90° minus itThe Joint Book p.110¶Source
inside length, regular concentric shapel = 2r / tan θ (r = radius, θ = miter angle, per the formula in the book)The Joint Book p.110¶Source
outside length, regular concentric shapeL = 2r · cos θ (formula as given in the book)The Joint Book p.110¶Source
different widthsangle drawn on one part and copied to the other with a sliding bevel; avoid width ratios above 2:1The Joint Book p.117¶Source
reinforcementone or more hidden biscuits; alternatively a corner brace glued on the back or splines in kerfsThe Joint Book p.112-113; Wood Joinery p.24 (loose spline, biscuits, dowels); Joinery Handbook (2020) p.78 (dowels, biscuits, loose tongue, small blocks glued on the corner); Fairham (1921) p.157 (veneer keys on picture frames)¶Source
typical section20 x 50 mm frame≈Trade practice
marking 45° without a miter squarefrom a square-cut end, mark a square whose side equals the dimension being cut; its diagonal gives 45°Fairham (1921) p.182¶Source
sawing and truingrough cut in a miter box (beech or hornbeam) or a sawing block kerfed at 45°; the cut face is then planed true with the part held in a trimming jig or on a shooting boardBellu (1939) p.114-115; Fairham (1921) p.179-182¶Source
end-to-edge gluingthe miter is an end-to-edge-grain joint; without interlocking surfaces (dowels, tenons, rabbets) it carries little load, and it should be protected from moisture changesWood Handbook (2021) p.10-16 – 10-17; Joinery Handbook (2020) p.74¶Source

Notes. The formulas l = 2r/tan θ and L = 2r·cos θ are copied from the book (p.110); its angle symbol is not clearly defined, so check them before implementation. Miter cuts differ by where the cut runs and how the blade sits (p.106-107): across the face width with the blade square (frame miter, this card), across the end with the blade tilted (cross or end miter), along the edge with the blade tilted (length or edge miter), and a tilted blade combined with an angled path (compound miter). Wood Joinery p.24: a plain miter can be reinforced with loose spline, biscuits or dowels. The old Romanian manual term is 'încheietură unghiulară de ramă' (Bellu 1939, p.66). Fairham (1921, p.178) calls any fitting of a moulding round an angle a mitre, cut on its bisector.

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Corner reinforcement added to a frame (picture frame, border, box) once the miters are glued; splines in a contrasting species also act as decoration. Also used for repairs and before the box is veneered (Fairham 1921, p.157).
Strength
The splines add long-grain glue surface across the corner and greatly increase the strength of a plain miter.
Fixing / glue
Glue; splines or veneer. Nails, if used, go in through the frame sides and across the miter, so that the frame's own weight loads them sideways rather than pulling them out.
Effect on the cut list
No length allowance. Extra parts: triangular splines (e.g. 3 x 30 x 30 mm, from a 3 x 30 strip) — 1-3 per corner.

Fabrication

  1. Miter both ends; for the second cut, a stop on the fence fixes the final length.
  2. Glue the frame and let it cure.
  3. With the glued frame held on its corner in a jig (height table or carrier), saw 1-3 kerfs across the corner, parallel to the faces or at an angle.
  4. From a contrasting species, plane a strip until it slides snugly into the kerf; cut it into triangles and glue them in.
  5. Once dry, saw off the projecting spline material and sand it level with the frame.

Parameters

ParameterValueStatus
kerf depththe blade cuts about one third of the miter length (from the outside point inward)The Joint Book p.115¶Source
spline thicknessequal to the kerf width (plane a strip to the kerf thickness)The Joint Book p.115; Fairham (1921) p.157 (saw-cut veneer glued into the kerf)¶Source
number of kerfs (hand version)2-3 cuts with a hand saw, with contrasting veneer glued into themThe Joint Book p.114; Fairham (1921) p.157 (kerfs sawn after the glue has set)¶Source
materialcontrasting wood (light frame with dark splines, or the reverse)The Joint Book p.114¶Source
kerf width3 mm (table saw blade) / 0.6-1 mm (hand saw + veneer)≈Trade practice
spline grainspline grain perpendicular to the miter line (crosses the corner)=Geometry
part thicknessdescribed for boxes of ≈ 6–10 mm (1/4–3/8 in) stock, where other reinforcement does not fit; on picture frames it is preferred to nailingFairham (1921) p.157¶Source

Notes. Romanian has no established term for 'feathered miter'; a descriptive name was used there. Other options (p.113): kerf the corner on the table saw with a fence-riding jig, or cut away part of the back of the corner and glue a triangular brace into it. A bridle miter (p.115) gives twice the glue area of a lap miter — see lap-miter. Joinery Handbook (2020, p.78) mentions reinforcing the mitered corner with small pieces of strong timber glued in after assembly.

SheetF19

Lap miter (half-lap miter)

also: half-lap with miter face, miter with half-lap on the back

Îmbinare la jumătatea lemnului cu tăietură la 45° pe fațăGehrungsüberblattung

Used in: Frames (doors, windows, pictures)Visibility: half-hidden

TopologyLframe
Source
Joinery Handbook, ed. 2 (Swedish Wood / TMF, 2020), p. 74–75
All sources (3)Hide list
  1. Joinery Handbook, ed. 2 (Swedish Wood / TMF, 2020), p. 74–75
  2. The Joint Book, p. 115-117
  3. W. Fairham, Woodwork Joints: How They Are Set Out, How Made and Where Used (J. B. Lippincott, 1921), p. 13–14 — archive.org

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Frames and casings that should show a mitered corner on the front but need the strength of a half-lap behind it.
When not to use
Width ratio between rail and stile above 2:1. Only the front shows a miter; from the back the joint reads as a half-lap.
Strength
The half-lap at the back carries the load: it provides a large area of long-grain glue contact, which a plain miter lacks. Fairham (1921, p.13) nevertheless rates it a rather weak joint, chosen for the look of the face.
Fixing / glue
Glue; optional nails / pegs through the half-lap.
Effect on the cut list
No allowance: each part has the outside length of the frame. Volume removed: T/2 x W x W at each end (half rectangle, half triangle on the face).

Fabrication

  1. Cut everything to final length. Stiles: a 45° kerf, T/2 deep, across the corner of the front face marks where the miter starts.
  2. Still on the stiles, clear the front half of the thickness from that corner triangle with a sliding sled fitted with 45° stops; the shoulders stay untouched.
  3. Rails: form an ordinary square end half-lap first; the half that remains is then mitered so that it meets the stile shoulder.
  4. Pare to a close fit, glue and clamp.

Parameters

ParameterValueStatus
half-lap depthhalf the thickness (T/2)The Joint Book p.117¶Source
face angle45° on the face corner of the stiles and on the remaining portion of the railsThe Joint Book p.117¶Source
cutting tolerancesaw slightly outside the line and pare to it with a chisel for a close fitThe Joint Book p.116¶Source
care with the face cutthe 45° kerf across the face must not go deeper than T/2: a deeper kerf shows on the finished joint and weakens itThe Joint Book p.116¶Source
width ratiomaximum 2:1The Joint Book p.117¶Source

Notes. Variant on p.115 (bridle miter): the rail gets an open slot and a mitered face, the stile a tenon shouldered on both faces; the glue area is twice that of the lap miter, and rails and stiles of different thickness can be joined. Could become a separate card among the bridle joints.

SheetF20

Dovetail keys (keyed miter with dovetail keys)

also: dovetail splines, false (decorative) dovetails on a miter

Îmbinare la 45° armată cu pene în coadă de rândunică

Used in: Frames (doors, windows, pictures)Carcasses, boxes and drawersVisibility: exposed

TopologyLframecarcass
Source
Joinery Handbook, ed. 2 (Swedish Wood / TMF, 2020), p. 78
All sources (4)Hide list

  2. The Joint Book, p. 118, 132, 146-147
  3. W. Fairham, Woodwork Joints: How They Are Set Out, How Made and Where Used (J. B. Lippincott, 1921), p. 129–130, 168–169 — archive.org
  4. J. Hurst-Wajszczuk, Dovetail Joints Redux (Woodcraft Magazine, 2011), § Dovetail Keys — woodcraft.com

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Decorative reinforcement of mitered corners (frames, boxes, cross miters) with imitation dovetails of contrasting wood. Fairham (1921, p.168) describes it on the mitered corners of thin boxes that are veneered afterwards; Woodcraft (2011) on jewellery boxes, where every side shows.
Strength
Functional reinforcement of the weak end-grain glue line of the miter. The keys are cut with their grain running along their length, which is what makes them strong.
Fixing / glue
Glue; the dovetail keys.
Effect on the cut list
No allowance on the frame parts. Extra parts: dovetail profile strip (e.g. 16 x 12 mm) of contrasting wood, cut into pieces ≈ socket length + 3 mm, 1-3 per corner.

Fabrication

  1. Glue the miter and let it dry.
  2. Rout the sockets across the glued corner: the frame sits in a V-cradle on the router table (with a slot for the bit), one socket at a time, turning the frame for the next; alternatively use a sliding fence with 45° stops.
  3. Make the key stock: two table-saw cuts at the dovetail angle along the edge of a board, with the grain, then rip the profile free.
  4. Glue short lengths into the sockets, tapping them home; when dry, saw off the excess and sand flush.

Parameters

ParameterValueStatus
key grainalong the length of the key (with the grain)The Joint Book p.146¶Source
appearanceeven a key of the same species shows as a different tone, because its trimmed face is end grainThe Joint Book p.146¶Source
socketrouter table, frame held in a V-cradle with a slot for the bit; cut one socket, turn the frame, cut the nextThe Joint Book p.147¶Source
making the keytwo table-saw cuts with the blade tilted to the dovetail angle, along the grain in a board edge; the profile is then ripped offThe Joint Book p.147; Woodcraft (2011) § Dovetail Keys (same bit raised to full height, strip routed on both edges)¶Source
fittingshort lengths glued and tapped in, sawn off after drying and sandedThe Joint Book p.147; Fairham (1921) p.168 (short lengths glued into the trenches, levelled when dry); Woodcraft (2011)¶Source
jigsliding fence jig with two 45° stops; long frame parts are tied together temporarily with two battensThe Joint Book p.147¶Source

Notes. Interpretation of the socket orientation from the illustrations; the trapezoidal profile shows on the outside faces of the corner. On the cross miter with rabbet (p.118) the dovetail key replaces the butterfly key.

SheetF21

Doweled butt joint

also: dowel joint, round tenon joint, doweling

Used in: Carcasses, boxes and drawersFrames (doors, windows, pictures)Lengthening (mouldings, skirtings, rails)Visibility: hidden

All sources (8)Hide list

  7. CNDIPT, Curriculum cls. a IX-a, Fabricarea produselor din lemn (proiect în consultare, 2025), p. 18 — edu.ro
  8. Min. Educației – CNPEE, Olimpiada „Fabricarea produselor din lemn”, etapa județeană 2024, cls. a XII-a, barem, p. 2 — cdn.edupedu.ro

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Butt joints in carcasses, frames and lengthening joints. Nothing projects past the joint line, so every part is cut straight to its finished length. The dowels act in place of a tenon; fewer and shorter ones are enough where they only have to register the faces.
When not to use
Where the load pulls the parts apart along the dowel axis: the dowels then work in tension, their weak direction. Also in edge-to-edge glue-ups of solid wood, where long dowels across the joint resist the seasonal movement of the boards.
Strength
Load across the dowels (shear) is carried well, load along them (tension) poorly. All the holding power is in the glue line, and inside a round hole only a small part of the glued surface is long grain to long grain; how the dowel grain lines up with that of the part therefore decides much of the strength.
Fixing / glue
Glue (PVA) + fluted beech, maple or birch dowels; optional clamping screw.
Effect on the cut list
Adds no length to the parts (butt joint). Adds parts: dowels Ø6-12 × 30-50 mm (n pieces per joint). Removed volume: cylindrical holes.

Fabrication

  1. Cut the parts to final length, with square ends.
  2. Lay out the hole centres along the joint on one part and carry them over to the mating part with a square, or drill the first part and transfer the positions with dowel centres.
  3. Drill square to the face with a doweling jig or a drill press with a stop; reference both parts from the same face.
  4. Lightly countersink the hole mouths for the glue reservoir.
  5. Glue the holes, the dowels and the meeting edges; insert the dowels in the first part, assemble and clamp.

Parameters

ParameterValueStatus
dowel diameter1/3 ... 1/2 of the part thickness (e.g. Ø8 at 20-22 mm)The Joint Book p.152¶Source
commercial diameters6 ... 12 mm (1/4" ... 1/2"); common lengths 25 ... 50 mmThe Joint Book p.152; Joinery Handbook (2020) p.59; wolfcraft (2014) p.5 (Ø6, 8, 10)¶Source
hole depth in each partmin. 1.5 × diameterThe Joint Book p.152, p.154¶Source
glue reservoirhole ~1-2 mm (Joint Book) or 2-3 mm (wolfcraft) deeper than the dowel + chamfer (countersink) at the hole mouthThe Joint Book p.154, p.161; wolfcraft (2014) p.6; Fairham p.102 (countersinking)¶Source
dowel spacing (as tenons)min. 1 diameter between hole wallsThe Joint Book p.158¶Source
hole position accuracydeviation no more than ~0.2-0.3 mmThe Joint Book p.155; wolfcraft (2014) p.4 (mating holes must coincide exactly, hence a jig)¶Source
holes square to face90°, referenced from the same face on both partsThe Joint Book p.157; wolfcraft (2014) p.6 (drill held upright, no side pressure); Fairham p.96 (gauged from the face side)¶Source
typical dowel pitch32 ... 100 mm (carcasses: 32 mm system or ~100 mm)≈Trade practice
dowel length2 × effective depth − 2 mm (e.g. Ø8 × 35/40)≈Trade practice
fluted/spiral dowelsthe grooves vent trapped air and surplus glue, so the dowel does not build up pressure in the hole as it is drivenThe Joint Book p.152-153; Fairham p.95; wolfcraft (2014) p.4; Joinery Handbook (2020) p.59¶Source
dowel diameter (wolfcraft)2/5 ... 3/5 of thickness; stock 12-14 mm → Ø6, 15-18 mm → Ø8, 19-30 mm → Ø10wolfcraft (2014) p.6¶Source
depth in face / in edge (L and T)in the face of a board at most 2/3 of its thickness; in the edge the rest of the dowel + 2-3 mm (e.g. 18 mm board, 40 mm dowel: 12 mm in the face, 28 + 2 = 30 mm in the edge)wolfcraft (2014) p.6¶Source
pitch in the 32 mm system32 mm between centres, the spindle pitch of multi-spindle dowel drills, to be kept when designingJoinery Handbook (2020) p.59¶Source
dowels in edge-jointed tops (Fairham)230 ... 250 mm apart (9-10 in), two at each end, 22 ... 32 mm long; on 50-65 mm stock, two rowsFairham p.96-97¶Source
dowel speciesbeech (wolfcraft, Fairham); compressed birch with chamfered ends that swells in the glue (Joinery Handbook)wolfcraft (2014) p.4; Fairham p.93; Joinery Handbook (2020) p.59¶Source
glue on the meeting facesglue goes on the meeting edges too, not only in the holeswolfcraft (2014) p.6¶Source

Notes. Along a lengthening joint the dowel grain runs the same way as the parts, so dowels and parts shrink and swell together. Across an edge joint they do not; there the dowels are kept short, few and used only for alignment. Joint Selector (JB p.185): listed under 'Dowels and biscuits', the group of machine-age alternatives that spare the hand fitting of the parts. Wood-Joinery p.23: the dowel replaces the tenon, a doweling jig is used. Romanian manuals treat the dowel as a tenon: the school curriculum lists 'applied cylindrical tenons' among carcass corner joints (CNDIPT grade 9, p.18), and Hinescu (1989, p.44) calls it an 'applied round tenon', one of the forms of the mortise and tenon. The sources give different values: diameter 1/3-1/2 of the thickness (Joint Book) against 2/5-3/5 (wolfcraft), glue reservoir 1-2 mm against 2-3 mm. Fairham does dowel edge-jointed tops, but with short dowels far apart (230-250 mm), which agrees with the rule above.

Halving joints

SheetF22

Edge lap (jigged edge lap, egg-crate)

also: edge cross lap, honeycomb joint, egg-crate dividers, slotted edge joint

Încrucișare pe cant, la jumătatea lățimii (grilaj de despărțitoare)Kreuzverbindung (Eierkisten-Verbindung)

Used in: Carcasses, boxes and drawersVisibility: exposed

TopologyX
Source
Joinery Handbook, ed. 2 (Swedish Wood / TMF, 2020), p. 75 (§4.1.2)
All sources (3)Hide list
  1. Joinery Handbook, ed. 2 (Swedish Wood / TMF, 2020), p. 75 (§4.1.2)
  2. The Joint Book, p. 40-42, 44, 53-54
  3. W. Fairham, Woodwork Joints (J. B. Lippincott, 1921), p. 15–16, 20 — archive.org

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Interlocking divider grids for drawers and boxes, and other light grids and lattices; a light-duty joint, often cut in plywood. Fairham (1921, p.20) shows it in the partitions of a deep bottle drawer, with the ends housed in the drawer sides; for pigeon holes in bureaux and bookcases he sometimes prefers housing, or housing combined with halving. The Joinery Handbook (2020, p.75) recommends it for internal dividers in boxes, drawers and furniture frames.
When not to use
Splitting risk: the slots take out half of each part's width and leave little long-grain glue contact, so add reinforcement where loads are expected.
Strength
Glue does little here (the glue faces are mostly end grain); the joint holds by its shape. It can be stiffened against twisting by housing one piece's thickness in shallow secondary dadoes cut in the other, or with pegs.
Fixing / glue
Glue (small contribution); optional pegs or plugged screws; on plywood often unglued.
Effect on the cut list
No length allowance; volume removed T_mating x W/2 x T at each intersection. All dividers of the same width.

Fabrication

  1. Tooling: a router bit or dado head as wide as the stock is thick, and an auxiliary fence on the miter gauge.
  2. Notch the auxiliary fence half the stock width deep, fit an indexing key in that notch, then shift the fence by one pitch, cut its working notch and fasten it.
  3. Indexing: the first slot is cut with the stock against the key; every later slot is cut after dropping the previous one over the key.
  4. Against tear-out on the exit side, back the work with a sacrificial board, or cut the slots in oversize-thickness stock and plane the parts down afterwards until they fit.
  5. By hand: saw the two sides of each slot to half depth and chop out the waste with a chisel.
  6. Assemble one part slots up, the other slots down.

Parameters

ParameterValueStatus
Slot depth1/2 of width (W/2) on each pieceThe Joint Book p.40-41, p.53; Fairham (1921) p.15–16¶Source
Slot width= thickness of the mating piece (e.g. 12 mm)The Joint Book p.55¶Source
Backing boardagainst grain tear-out at the router exitThe Joint Book p.53¶Source
Spacing between slotsper the compartment layout (e.g. 80–100 mm)?To be decided

Notes. Slot width = thickness of the mating piece is the rule stated for the box joint/edge lap jig (p.53-55).

SheetF23

Through dovetail

also: open dovetail, through-cut dovetail, common dovetail

Îmbinare în coadă de rândunică cu dinți deschiși (străpunși)offene Zinkung

  2. The Joint Book, p. 130-137

  4. V. Constantinescu, I. Cârstea, Lucrări practice de tâmplărie (1959), p. 113–115 — archive.org

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Corners of boxes, chests, carcasses and drawers (drawer back to sides); in contemporary furniture it is often left exposed on purpose, as evidence of handwork. The 1959 Romanian manual lists chests, small boxes, door and window casings and shelving frames.
When not to use
When the ends must not show on the front face (then use half-blind or secret).
Strength
Very strong. The flared tails resist being pulled out of the pin board, and the cheeks between tails and pins give long-grain glue contact; of all dovetail corners it has the most glue area. Constantinescu & Cârstea (1959, p.113) call it the strongest corner joint and note that it also keeps the boards from cupping.
Fixing / glue
Glue; mechanical lock, no extra elements.
Effect on the cut list
Each part = outside dimension + ~1 mm (0.5 mm proud at each end for planing). No extra parts; the volume of the sockets is removed over a length = the thickness of the mating piece.

Fabrication

  1. Mark the baseline with the gauge (slightly over the thickness of the mating piece) on both faces and edges of both parts.
  2. Lay out the pins (slope 1:5…1:8 with a sliding bevel or a template), then transfer them to the tails (or vice versa).
  3. Saw on the waste side of the lines with a dovetail saw (or on the table/band saw with the blade tilted).
  4. Chop out the waste with a chisel from both faces to the baseline, with a slightly undercut bottom.
  5. Test fit with a block and mallet; glue.
  6. After drying, plane/file the protruding pins and tails flush.

Parameters

ParameterValueStatus
tail slopebetween 1:5 and 1:8 (≈ 11.3° … 7.1°); chosen according to the wood and the type of jointThe Joint Book p.135¶Source
usual slope1:6 softwood (≈ 9.5°), 1:8 hardwood (≈ 7.1°)≈Trade practice
pin width≈ half the wood thickness (or more) at the widest partThe Joint Book p.134¶Source
tail width≈ 2-3 times the pin width, tails evenly spacedThe Joint Book p.134; Joinery Handbook (2020) p.76 (some styles make the tails wider than the pins)¶Source
variable spacingoptional uneven layout: tails narrow toward the edges and widen in the middle, so pins cluster near the edges; this reinforces the edges and restrains cupping. Pin and tail sizes need not be in proportionThe Joint Book p.134¶Source
half pinsboth edges end with a half pinThe Joint Book p.134; Fairham (1921) p.135 (outer pin lines parallel to the edges); Constantinescu & Cârstea (1959) p.113 (pins left at the edges)¶Source

Notes. Wood Joinery p.13 describes it as a kind of straight-pin joint locked by diagonal cuts, the strongest for two parts with the grain in the same direction; uses: drawers, box corners, rail-to-leg connections. The 'mitered corner' variant (p.137) could become a separate option.

Half-blind dovetail (lapped dovetail)

also: stopped dovetail, half-concealed dovetail, drawer dovetail

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Drawer fronts: the sides are dovetailed into the back of the front, so the show face stays plain while the corner keeps dovetail strength. The 1934 Romanian course recommends it for table, desk and wardrobe drawers: the joint stops short of the front thickness, so the front stays plain.
Strength
Resists the pull on a drawer front very well, though with less glue area than a through dovetail. The tail length, set by the gauge line on the end of the front, governs both the glue area and the mechanical hold.
Fixing / glue
Glue; mechanical lock.
Effect on the cut list
The side is lengthened by the tail length (≈ 2/3 TA) over the inside dimension: side length = drawer depth − lap (TA/3). The front has the outside width of the drawer. No extra parts.

Fabrication

  1. With the drawer parts dressed and square, set the gauge to the side thickness and scribe it on the inside face of the front.
  2. Reset the gauge to ≈ 2/3 of the front thickness (the tail length); scribe it on the end of the front and around the end of each side.
  3. Lay out the tails on the outside face of the side (slope 1:5…1:8), square the lines over the end, then saw and chop them.
  4. Set the side in its assembled position with the tails on the front's end-grain line, and knife their outline onto the end.
  5. Saw each socket wall on a diagonal from the front's inside corner, stopping at both scribed lines; chop the rest from the end grain with the chisel against the pin face, then test-fit and glue.

Parameters

ParameterValueStatus
two gauge settingsalways two settings, whatever the thicknesses (a through dovetail between equal thicknesses needs only one)The Joint Book p.138; Fairham (1921) p.120¶Source
setting 1gauge = thickness of the side; marked on the inside face of the drawer frontThe Joint Book p.139¶Source
setting 2 (tail length)≈ 2/3 of the front thickness; marked on the end of the front and around the end of the side on both faces and edgesThe Joint Book p.139¶Source

Notes. The Romanian term used in joinery manuals is 'semiascunsă'. Hinescu (1989, p.46) classes the joints as open, half-blind and blind.

SheetF25

Blind mitered dovetail (secret mitered dovetail)

also: fully concealed mitered dovetail, secret dovetail

Îmbinare în coadă de rândunică ascunsă, la 45°verdeckte Gehrungszinkung

Used in: Carcasses, boxes and drawersVisibility: hidden

TopologyLcarcass
Source
W. Fairham, Woodwork Joints: How They Are Set Out, How Made and Where Used (J. B. Lippincott, 1921), p. 127–129 — archive.org
All sources (5)Hide list

  2. The Joint Book, p. 130-131, 140-141
  3. Curs de tehnologia lemnului. Diferite încheieturi aplicate la mobile, binale și construcții în lemn (autor ilizibil în scanare, cca 1934), p. 12 — archive.org
  4. Joinery Handbook, ed. 2 (Swedish Wood / TMF, 2020), p. 76

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Carcass and box corners that must look like a plain miter from every side, with the grain running unbroken around the corner, while dovetails inside provide the strength. Fairham (1921) gives it for better-class cabinet and box work; the 1934 Romanian course describes it on small cases and backgammon boxes: all pins shorter than the wall thickness, the solid edges mitered, so only the corner lines show.
Strength
Hidden dovetail strength; from the outside it looks like a plain miter.
Fixing / glue
Glue; hidden mechanical lock.
Effect on the cut list
Both parts have the outside dimension (point of the miter). No extra parts.

Fabrication

  1. On each part, gauge the exact thickness on the inside face and mark a 45° line from each edge.
  2. Rabbet the inside face: depth ≈ 2/3 T, width ≈ T/3; do not cut beyond the 45° line.
  3. Pin part: lay out the pins on the rabbet from a template, chop the sockets, then miter the edge shoulders and finally the lip.
  4. Tail part: set the finished pin part on it against the gauge lines, mark the tails from it, chop the sockets, then miter the shoulders and the lip; test and glue.

Parameters

ParameterValueStatus
initial layouttails and pins are laid out as for the half-blind; gauge at the exact thickness on the inside of each pieceThe Joint Book p.140-141¶Source
rabbet depthfrom the inside face ≈ 2/3 of the thickness toward the opposite face (a lap of ≈ 1/3 remains)The Joint Book p.140¶Source
rabbet width≈ 1/3 of the distance to the inside gauge line (≈ T/3 from the end)The Joint Book p.140¶Source
geometric conditionchoose depth and width so that the inner corner of the rabbet touches the 45° line drawn on the edgeThe Joint Book p.140¶Source
miter45° on the lap and on the shoulder at the edge (45° is marked from each edge)The Joint Book p.141; Fairham (1921) p.128 (mitre at the top and bottom edges)¶Source

fully blind (double-lapped) variantlap carried by the pins or by the tails; a load-bearing part should be the pin partThe Joint Book p.131, 141¶Source
tail slope1:5 … 1:8The Joint Book p.135¶Source
mitering the lipthe lip is mitered with a chisel and rebate plane guided by a block planed to 45° and clamped under the part, so the arris stays sharpFairham (1921) p.129¶Source
variant with covered edgesrabbet and miter on the show face only; the top and bottom edges are not mitered and are covered by the moulding or the lidFairham (1921) p.128-129¶Source

Notes. The 2/3 and 1/3 proportions are approximate in the book ('about'). The fully blind variant (full-blind / double-lapped, p.131, 141) could be a separate entry.

Box (finger) joints

SheetF26

Box joint (finger joint, comb joint)

also: finger joint, comb joint, multiple straight tenons, straight fingers

Îmbinare în dinți drepți (cutie)Fingerzinkung (gerade Zinkung)

Used in: Carcasses, boxes and drawersVisibility: exposed

Topologycorner
Source
W. Fairham, Woodwork Joints (J. B. Lippincott, 1921), p. 45 — archive.org
All sources (6)Hide list
  1. W. Fairham, Woodwork Joints (J. B. Lippincott, 1921), p. 45 — archive.org
  2. The Joint Book, p. 55-57
  3. 604877192-Wood-Joinery (slides), p. 15
  4. V. Constantinescu, I. Cârstea, Lucrări practice de tâmplărie (manual școlar, 1959), p. 112–113 — archive.org
  5. A. Hinescu, Cartea tâmplarului universal (Ed. Tehnică, București, 1989), p. 46 — archive.org
  6. Joinery Handbook, ed. 2 (Swedish Wood / TMF, 2020), p. 76 (§4.1.4)

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Corners of boxes, drawers and carcasses, common in factory-made furniture; with a pin through the fingers it also works as a wooden hinge for box lids. Fairham (1921, p.45) and the Joinery Handbook (2020, p.76) describe it as a box joint usually made by machine (circular saw or spindle moulder).
Strength
The fingers create many long-grain glue faces; that large glue area is what makes it very solid (Constantinescu & Cârstea 1959, p.112; Joinery Handbook 2020, p.76), with strength close to a dovetail. Unlike the dovetail it does not lock mechanically in one direction, and the fingers show on both faces of the corner (Hinescu 1989, p.46).
Fixing / glue
Glue; optional cross peg (wooden hinge).
Effect on the cut list
Length of each piece = outside dimension (the fingers cover the mating thickness) + ~1 mm for sanding. Volume removed: the gaps, depth T x pitch width, alternating.

Fabrication

  1. Jig: an auxiliary fence on the miter gauge with an indexing key; the key, the notch and the gap between them all equal the dado-head width.
  2. Before cutting, mark the outside faces and a reference edge on every part, and scribe a line across each end slightly beyond the stock thickness – it limits tear-out and sets the cut height.
  3. Cut the parts a little over final length and raise the dado head to the scribed line, so the fingers end up slightly proud for flush sanding.
  4. Sides: reference edge against the key, cut a gap, drop it over the key, cut the next, and so on across the width.
  5. Fronts and backs: turn a cut side around and hook its first gap over the key as a spacer; butt the front against it and cut its first gap, then index as before (several parts can be cut together).
  6. Trim the last finger to width, glue and clamp across the fingers so the long-grain faces close; sand the fingers flush.

Parameters

ParameterValueStatus
Width of fingers and gaps= thickness of the piece, 1/2 of thickness or the saw kerf width (e.g. 10 mm at T = 15); Constantinescu & Cârstea (1959): ≈ the board thicknessThe Joint Book p.55; Constantinescu & Cârstea (1959) p.113¶Source
Depth of the gapsslightly over the thickness of the mating piece (fingers stand proud ~0.5 mm, sanded flush)The Joint Book p.56¶Source
Fitfriction fitThe Joint Book p.55¶Source
Start of the seriesone piece starts with a finger, the other with a gap; both ends of a piece have the same layoutThe Joint Book p.56¶Source
Width of the piecesideally an odd multiple of the pitch; the last finger, wider/narrower, is adjusted to the widthThe Joint Book p.56¶Source

Notes. Variants p.56-57: fingers deeper than the thickness (stand proud as decoration), rounded corners, hinge by peg. Slides p.15 call it a "finger joint" and consider it weaker than the dovetail. Romanian manuals: „îmbinare cu cepuri drepte (dinți drepți)” (Constantinescu & Cârstea 1959, p.112) and „încheiere cu dinți drepți străpunși” (Hinescu 1989, p.46).

Carcass miters

SheetF27

Housed rabbet miter (end miter with rabbet and pegs)

also: shouldered miter, rabbeted box-corner miter

Încheiere la 45° cu falț, consolidată cu cuie de lemn

Used in: Carcasses, boxes and drawersVisibility: half-hidden

TopologyLcarcass
Source
A. Hinescu, Cartea tâmplarului universal (Ed. Tehnică, 1989), p. 45–47 — archive.org
All sources (3)Hide list
  1. A. Hinescu, Cartea tâmplarului universal (Ed. Tehnică, 1989), p. 45–47 — archive.org
  2. The Joint Book, p. 118-119
  3. W. Fairham, Woodwork Joints: How They Are Set Out, How Made and Where Used (J. B. Lippincott, 1921), p. 128–129, 168 — archive.org

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Box and drawer corners (front to side) that must hide all end grain. The joint comes from Japan; pegs of contrasting wood turn the reinforcement into a visible detail.
Strength
Strength comes chiefly from pegs driven from outside, through the side, into the front. Without them the joint is weak: the cross miter is end grain on end grain, and the small shoulder only slightly improves shear and racking resistance.
Fixing / glue
Glue + pegs of contrasting wood (Ø6-8) through the side.
Effect on the cut list
The front has the outside length; the side has the outside length (point of the bevel). Extra parts: pegs Ø6-8 x (side thickness + depth into the front).

Fabrication

  1. Side (same thickness as the front or thinner, as on a drawer): bevel its end at 45°, with the length set by a stop on the miter fence.
  2. Front: cut to length, then kerf its inside face at a distance from the end equal to the side thickness.
  3. With the blade tilted to 45°, cut away the waste on the inside of the front as far as the kerf; this leaves the miter and the shoulder.
  4. Glue; when dry, bore through the side into the front, glue the pegs in, then trim and sand flush.

Parameters

ParameterValueStatus
side thicknessequal to the front or thinner (e.g. drawer side)The Joint Book p.119¶Source
side bevel45° on the endThe Joint Book p.119¶Source
cut in the fronton the inside face, at the side thickness from the end; depth up to mid-height of the bevelThe Joint Book p.119¶Source
removing the rest45° blade tilt; clears the inside of the front up to the kerfThe Joint Book p.119¶Source
pegsshop-turned pegs, fitted after the glue has set, entering from the outer face of the sideThe Joint Book p.118-119¶Source
peg diameter6-8 mm, 2-3 per corner≈Trade practice
alternative reinforcementspline kerfs cut with the blade at 45°, limited to the outer 3/4 of the glued face; butterfly keys do not suit a cross miter, dovetail keys are used insteadThe Joint Book p.118-119; Fairham (1921) p.168 (dovetail keys on mitered box corners)¶Source
other anglesfor angles other than 45°: the beveled end lies flat on the table and a groove is cut into it with the blade (or bit) verticalThe Joint Book p.119¶Source
variant with hidden dovetailsthe rabbeted, mitered corner can take dovetails in the rabbet ('housed and mitred' or 'rebated and mitred' dovetail); top and bottom edges are not mitered and are covered by the moulding or the lidFairham (1921) p.128-129¶Source

Notes. The book defines the depth of the cut in the front only as reaching mid-height of the bevel; the model here (shoulder = difference in thicknesses) fits a side thinner than the front. For equal thicknesses the exact geometry still needs checking. The Romanian term is not established. Hinescu (1989, p.45-47) classes carcass corner joints as: rabbet and groove, loose tongue at 90° and 45°, and pins/dovetails; the rabbeted miter pegged with wooden pins does not appear as such in the Romanian sources checked.

SheetF28

Locked miter (lock miter)

also: interlocking miter, lock miter

Încheiere la 45° cu lambă și uluc (feder și nut)

Used in: Carcasses, boxes and drawersVisibility: hidden

TopologyLcarcass
Source
W. Fairham, Woodwork Joints: How They Are Set Out, How Made and Where Used (J. B. Lippincott, 1921), p. 46–47 — archive.org
All sources (3)Hide list
  1. W. Fairham, Woodwork Joints: How They Are Set Out, How Made and Where Used (J. B. Lippincott, 1921), p. 46–47 — archive.org
  2. The Joint Book, p. 120-121
  3. A. Hinescu, Cartea tâmplarului universal (Ed. Tehnică, 1989), p. 45–46, 205 — archive.org

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Drawer and box corners. The interlocking profile keeps the front from being pulled off, and both outer faces show only a miter line, with no end grain.
When not to use
Hard to cut accurately; the lock works in one direction only, so the joint must be oriented against the expected tension.
Strength
The interlocking tongues carry the load mechanically, so glue matters less than in other miters; the lock acts against pulling along the line of the front.
Fixing / glue
Glue; mechanical lock, no extra elements.
Effect on the cut list
Both parts have the outside length of the corner; no parts are added. Volume removed from the grooves and rabbets at each end.

Fabrication

  1. Groove in the side: on the inside face, one front-thickness from the end, 1/3 of the side thickness deep.
  2. Front: in the end grain, cut a slot about half the front thickness wide and as deep as the side is thick; the narrow strip left on the inside becomes the front's tongue.
  3. Side: with the cutter set to 2/3 of the thickness, rabbet the end so that the remaining tongue fits the slot in the front.
  4. Front: trim its narrow tongue to the depth of the groove in the side.
  5. With the blade at 45° and a stop for position, bevel the projecting outer tongues on both parts.
  6. Glue. Clamping pressure is needed in one direction only; a block over the miter spreads it.

Parameters

ParameterValueStatus
groove in the sideon the inside face of the side, one front-thickness from the end; depth ≈ 1/3 of the side thicknessThe Joint Book p.121¶Source
groove in the front endslot in the end: ≈ half the front thickness wide, as deep as the side is thick; the narrow inner tongue left beside it fits the groove of the sideThe Joint Book p.121¶Source
rabbet in the sidedepth 2/3 of the side thickness; the outer tongue it leaves fits the slot in the frontThe Joint Book p.121¶Source

special bitrouter bits with the complete lock-miter profile exist; each part is then shaped in a single passThe Joint Book p.120¶Source

Notes. The exact dimensions of the tongue/groove are approximate (the book gives proportions: 1/3, 1/2, 2/3); the model above is a coherent interpretation, to be verified in 3D. In practice a lock miter bit (45° angle) is used. The Romanian terms for rabbet-and-groove and loose-tongue corners at 45° are in Hinescu (1989, p.45-46).

SheetF29

Waterfall joint (length miter / edge bevel)

also: edge miter, 45° lengthwise bevel, waterfall joint

Încheiere la 45° pe lungime, cu fibra continuă

Used in: Carcasses, boxes and drawersVisibility: hidden

TopologyLcarcass
Source
Joinery Handbook, ed. 2 (Swedish Wood / TMF, 2020), p. 78
All sources (4)Hide list
  1. Joinery Handbook, ed. 2 (Swedish Wood / TMF, 2020), p. 78
  2. The Joint Book, p. 106-107, 122-123
  3. W. Fairham, Woodwork Joints: How They Are Set Out, How Made and Where Used (J. B. Lippincott, 1921), p. 182–183 — archive.org
  4. A. Hinescu, Cartea tâmplarului universal (Ed. Tehnică, 1989), p. 205 — archive.org

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Cabinets in veneered plywood or solid wood where the grain pattern should continue unbroken around the corner, e.g. back and ends cut from one sheet; also polygonal stave work (n-sided containers).
Strength
All glue contact is long grain, so the bond is strong, provided the parts are kept aligned while clamping: the bevels tend to slide under pressure.
Fixing / glue
Glue; optional loose spline or biscuits for alignment (see rabbet-miter).
Effect on the cut list
Each panel widens by the thickness T (the point of the bevel reaches the outside face); a triangular strip T x T is lost along the length. If continuity is required, the parts are cut consecutively from the same sheet.

Fabrication

  1. Rip a 45° bevel along the first edge. Which face goes up depends on the tilt: outside face up when the blade tilts toward the fence, inside face up when it tilts away.
  2. Mating edge: turn the fence-side piece end for end and make a second rip; this bevels it the opposite way and removes a triangular offcut.
  3. Return that piece to its original orientation and pair it with the first, so the grain continues around the corner.
  4. Glue segments two at a time, with clamps or tape. (When grooving the bevels, an angled featherboard holds the part upright against the fence.)

Parameters

ParameterValueStatus
angleblade tilted at 45°, cut along the length (rip)The Joint Book p.123; Fairham (1921) p.182 (square of side = thickness, diagonal at 45°)¶Source
grain continuitycut both parts from one board/sheet; turning one end for end keeps the figure almost continuousThe Joint Book p.122-123¶Source
tilt toward/away from the fenceoutside face up for tilt toward the fence, inside face up for tilt awayThe Joint Book p.123¶Source
angle for n segmentsbevel = 180°/n (e.g. 6 segments → 30°, 8 → 22.5°)=Geometry
typical materialveneered plywood 18 mm≈Trade practice
truing the bevelson wide stock mitered through the thickness, the bevel is trued with the plane on its side on a 45° shooting board ('donkey's ear')Fairham (1921) p.182¶Source
clampingin production, the carcass press has horizontal clamping heads that tilt 0…45° for carcasses with miter cornersHinescu (1989) p.205¶Source

Notes. Variants (p.123): segmented work is easier to glue two pieces at a time; in coopering, narrow staves with slightly beveled edges are joined into an arc and planed smooth once dry. The term 'waterfall' is an ad-hoc translation in Romanian. Joinery Handbook (2020, p.78) recommends reinforcing the miter with a loose tongue glued into a groove.

SheetF30

Rabbet miter (rabbeted miter)

also: stepped miter, miter with ledge

Încheiere la 45° cu falț

Used in: Carcasses, boxes and drawersVisibility: hidden

TopologyLcarcass
Source
W. Fairham, Woodwork Joints: How They Are Set Out, How Made and Where Used (J. B. Lippincott, 1921), p. 46–47 — archive.org
All sources (3)Hide list
  1. W. Fairham, Woodwork Joints: How They Are Set Out, How Made and Where Used (J. B. Lippincott, 1921), p. 46–47 — archive.org
  2. The Joint Book, p. 124-125
  3. A. Hinescu, Cartea tâmplarului universal (Ed. Tehnică, 1989), p. 47, 205 — archive.org

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Long-grain (edge) miters on boxes and square cases; the inner step locates the parts and keeps the miter closed while clamping.
Strength
Glued on long grain, so strong. Because the inner step registers the parts, the bevels cannot creep and the joint squares itself; corner blocks are still useful to close the outside point.
Fixing / glue
Glue; clamping blocks.
Effect on the cut list
Both parts have the outside width/length (point of the bevel at the outside face); no extra parts.

Fabrication

  1. Blade height T/2 for every cut. Part 1, inside face down: first kerf with the outside of the blade at T from the fence.
  2. Part 1: second kerf with the inside of the blade at T/2 from the fence; clear the strip between the kerfs (rabbet T wide, T/2 deep).
  3. Part 2, same blade height: one kerf in the inside face, with the outside of the blade at T/2 from the fence.
  4. Part 2: blade tilted to 45°, piece turned end for end with the inside face up; bevel the edge down to the kerf.
  5. Part 1: inside face up, bevel the lip at 45° down to the rabbet.
  6. Glue with corner blocks on the outside edge.

Parameters

ParameterValueStatus
blade heighthalf the thickness (T/2) for all cutsThe Joint Book p.125¶Source
part 1 – first cutdistance fence to outside of blade = thickness TThe Joint Book p.125¶Source
part 1 – second cutdistance fence to inside of blade = T/2; the waste between the cuts is removedThe Joint Book p.125¶Source
part 2one cut at distance fence to outside of blade = T/2, then bevel at 45° up to the cutThe Joint Book p.125¶Source
bevel45° on both parts, up to the groove/cut on the inside faceThe Joint Book p.125¶Source

Notes. Geometry reconstructed from the machine steps (p.125): part 1 = rabbet T x T/2 + beveled lip; part 2 = rabbet T/2 x T/2 + bevel. Checked on paper that the parts do not overlap. Hinescu (1989, p.47) lists rabbeted joints among the basic carcass joints.

SheetF31

Compound miter

also: double miter, compound cut

Tăietură dublu înclinatăSchiftergehrung

Used in: Carcasses, boxes and drawersVisibility: hidden

TopologyLcarcass
Source
A. Hinescu, Cartea tâmplarului universal (Ed. Tehnică, 1989), p. 94–95 — archive.org
All sources (4)Hide list
  1. A. Hinescu, Cartea tâmplarului universal (Ed. Tehnică, 1989), p. 94–95 — archive.org
  2. The Joint Book, p. 106-107, 111, 126-129
  3. W. Fairham, Woodwork Joints: How They Are Set Out, How Made and Where Used (J. B. Lippincott, 1921), p. 131–133, 178–179 — archive.org
  4. Curs de tehnologia lemnului. Diferite încheieturi aplicate la mobile, binale și construcții în lemn (autor ilizibil în scanare, cca 1934), p. 12 — archive.org

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Pieces whose walls slope outward or inward: boxes, trays, planters, stave work; in carpentry, the hips and valleys of hipped roofs.
Strength
Like the cross miter: glue surface mostly end grain; reinforced with spline or keys. Angle errors multiply with the number of sides.
Fixing / glue
Glue; beveled strips temporarily glued for clamping; optional spline or keys.
Effect on the cut list
True wall width = height / cos S; length on the long edge = outside side at the base (or top). Waste at each end: compound prism.

Fabrication

  1. Work out the angles first: from a full-size elevation at the chosen slope and the plan, find the true wall width, the edge bevel, the miter angle and the blade tilt (or compute them with the formulas below).
  2. Bevel the top and bottom edges to the slope angle so the piece sits flat.
  3. With blade and fence set, cut one end of every part; then reverse the fence angle, place the opposite edge against it and cut each part to length.
  4. Test on scrap. By hand: true the bevels with a plane on a shooting board, using a tapered fence block.
  5. For clamping, glue temporary beveled cleats to the parts (paper in the glue line makes them easy to knock off) so the pressure acts square to the joint; assemble in stages.

Parameters

ParameterValueStatus
definitiona blade tilt combined with an angled (miter) cut; the top and bottom edges are also beveled so the piece sits flatThe Joint Book p.107, 126-127¶Source
accuracythe slope angle itself is not critical, but all cuts must use identical settings; a 1° error per cut accumulates over all the sidesThe Joint Book p.126¶Source
graphic methodon a full-size drawing (elevation + plan): projecting the plan onto the sloped wall gives the true width and the edge bevel; distances A and B taken from the side view set out the miter angle, and a line parallel to it gives the blade tiltThe Joint Book p.111, 127; Fairham (1921) p.178-179 (graphic bisection of the angle)¶Source
fence angle (formula)M = arctan( sin S · tan(180°/n) ), S = wall tilt from vertical, n = number of sides (e.g. n=4, S=15° → 14.5°; S=30° → 26.6°; S=45° → 35.3°)≈Trade practice
blade tilt (formula)B = arcsin( cos S · sin(180°/n) ), from the vertical blade (n=4, S=15° → 43.1°; S=30° → 37.8°; S=45° → 30°)≈Trade practice
top/bottom edge bevel= S (slope angle), so the piece sits flat=Geometry
by handa guide block planed to the bevel angle is clamped on the inside face at the miter angle for sawing; the cut faces are trued on a shooting board, where a tapered block under the part brings the bevel square to the planeThe Joint Book p.128-129¶Source
dovetails on sloping wallson boxes with sloping sides, the ends are cut to the wall slope, and pins and tails marked on the outside face are shifted by the difference between the right angle and the sloping angle1934 Romanian course p.12; Fairham (1921) p.131-132 (bevelled dovetailing for hoppers, troughs, knife boxes)¶Source
machine settingsa table saw with a blade tilting 0…45° and an angle crosscut fixture on the table provide the two settings of the cutHinescu (1989) p.94-95¶Source

Notes. The formulas for M and B are standard (not in the documents), numerically verified for n=4. The chapter also deals with moldings (p.129): coping is an option only at inside corners, outside corners have to be mitered; crown molding is cut inverted, propped flat against the fence. None of the independent sources checked gives the M and B formulas; they remain checked numerically only.

SheetF32

Reinforced width miter (doweled miter)

also: doweled 45° corner, doweled miter

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Box/carcass corner from wide boards mitered at 45° across the full width, where the ends must not show; the dowels align and reinforce the miter.
When not to use
Dowels too close to the outer face (they end up short in the second part or break through the face).
Strength
The miter alone is weak (end grain to glue); the dowels add mechanical strength and alignment. Glue + dowels.
Fixing / glue
Glue + dowels.
Effect on the cut list
Length = outside length of the carcass (the miter adds nothing). Extra parts: dowels Ø6 × ~30 mm, n ≈ width/60.

Fabrication

  1. Cut both parts to their finished length with square ends; the miter comes later and must not shorten them.
  2. Fix a shop-made drilling block to the inner face at the joint line (small pins hold it) and set the depth stop on the bit.
  3. Bore part A, then bore part B through the other side of the same block, so the holes match.
  4. Saw the 45° miters on both parts so that the outside length of each part stays unchanged.
  5. Glue the holes and dowels and seat the dowels in one part. Bring the other part on and clamp across the dowels, with a shaped block on the outside so the miter closes at its edge.

Parameters

Joint Selector (JB p.185): listed under 'Dowels and biscuits'. Fairham (p.100) shows the frame version, with the dowels square to the joint line; in the carcass corner of this card the dowels run parallel to part B, so their length depends on the thickness of A. Joinery Handbook (p.77) and wolfcraft (p.4) confirm that miters are reinforced with dowels.

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Carcass corner (top or base over a side) where the overhanging part has a moulded (routed) edge; the joint is a butt joint with a row of dowels.
Strength
Closely pitched dowels restrain the top along the whole joint line, which helps keep it from cupping; glue + dowels.
Fixing / glue
Glue + dowels.
Effect on the cut list
Moulded part: length = carcass length + 2 × overhang. Extra parts: dowels Ø8 × 35 (e.g. 6 pcs at depth 300).

Fabrication

  1. Size the top (the part that carries the moulding) to length and width, and lay out on it the moulding and the line of the side.
  2. Make a drilling jig to that layout, with the holes at a smaller pitch near both ends.
  3. Bore the side and the top with the jig registered on the same reference face; for the mating part, turn the jig round and move its stop.
  4. Rout the moulding on the exposed edges, then glue up: dowels driven against the spacer block, parts assembled and clamped.

Parameters

Sliding dovetail drawer joint (side–back)

  2. The Joint Book, p. 144-145

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Drawer back to sides, with the sides running past the back (traditionally so the drawer cannot drop out when fully opened); also the drawer front, with solid wood left at each end.
Strength
Mechanically locks the sides to the back, so the drawer's contents or the movement of drying wood cannot push them apart; markedly stronger under load than a square housing.
Fixing / glue
Glue (partial); no extra elements.
Effect on the cut list
The back is lengthened by 2 x the socket depth (e.g. +2 x 6 mm) over the inside clear dimension between the sides. The sides are lengthened by the extension past the back (e.g. 20 mm).

Fabrication

  1. Router table with an auxiliary wooden fence: keep the side square to the fence with a plywood backer and remove most of the waste with a straight bit, ≈ T/2 deep.
  2. Change to a dovetail bit and cut the angled wall (single-shoulder version), keeping clear of the straight outer wall.
  3. Leave the bit height unchanged; reposition the fence so only part of the bit cuts, and shape the end of the back until it fits the housing.
  4. Check the slide, glue at the top edge/front, clamp.

Parameters

ParameterValueStatus
socket positionthe housing needs solid wood beyond it: too near the end of the side, weak short grain is left; the drawer front likewise keeps a lip at each endThe Joint Book p.144¶Source
operation 1router table, straight bit: roughing groove ≈ half the material thicknessThe Joint Book p.145; Woodcraft (2011) § Sliding Dovetail (straight bit narrower than the dovetail bit's neck, fence left in place)¶Source
operation 2dovetail bit: the sloped shoulder (single shoulder) without touching the straight outer shoulderThe Joint Book p.145; Joinery Handbook (2020) p.77 (single- or double-sided dovetail)¶Source
the tonguesame bit height; only part of the bit exposed beyond the fence, passes repeated on the end of the side/back until it fits the housingThe Joint Book p.145; Woodcraft (2011) § Sliding Dovetail (same bit height, creep up on the fit)¶Source

Notes. The single-shoulder tongue is the one from step 2; the two-shoulder version is made by routing both faces (p.145, pivoting fence). The independent sources found describe the sliding dovetail in general (Joinery Handbook 2020, p.77; Fairham 1921, p.145-148); the drawer application appears only in the Woodcraft (2011) article.

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Simple boxes and cabinets, temporary frames; usually reinforced with screws, dowels, biscuits or corner brackets.
When not to use
Unreinforced, with glue only, it is weak – it can be broken by hand (end-grain glue joint).
Strength
The weakest joint: the end grain soaks up the glue and does not bond well (Joinery Handbook 2020, p.74). The Wood Handbook (2021, p.10-17) states that a plain end-to-face joint cannot carry appreciable load and recommends interlocking shapes so that long-grain faces are glued; here the strength comes from the fasteners.
Fixing / glue
Glue + screws, dowels, biscuits or corner brackets.
Effect on the cut list
The piece that fits between the others is cut to the inside dimension (L_ext − 2T); no volume is removed. Extra parts: screws/dowels/biscuits.

Fabrication

  1. Cut the end of piece A perfectly square and to length.
  2. Mark the position on the face of piece B.
  3. Apply glue on the end (possibly a sizing coat) and on the face.
  4. Assemble and fasten with screws/dowels/biscuits; clamp square.

Parameters

ParameterValueStatus
Glue jointend grain to long grain – weakslides p.4; Joinery Handbook (2020) p.74; Wood Handbook (2021) p.10-17¶Source
Reinforcementbiscuits or spline, screws, dowels; in board carcases, round tenons or applied splines, and glued-on solid wood blocks to take the screwsslides p.4, p.7; Hinescu (1989) p.47¶Source
Recommended screws at T = 184 x 40, 2 per corner, with pilot hole and countersink≈Trade practice

Notes. Besides the slides, it appears in the Wood Handbook (2021, fig. 10-8 A) and the Joinery Handbook (2020, p.74); The Joint Book has no separate section on it. Possible overlap with the dowels/biscuits group (reinforced butt joints) – to be unified.

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Hanging heavy cabinets on a wall: one strip on the wall and one on the back of the cabinet, with 45° bevels that hook together.
Strength
The weight pulls the cabinet toward the wall; very good for heavy loads.
Fixing / glue
Screws + glue (on the cabinet); wall plugs (on the wall).
Effect on the cut list
Extra parts: 1 strip 19 x 90 x cabinet width, ripped in two; cabinet back set back 19 mm.

Fabrication

  1. Rip a strip at 45° along its length.
  2. Fix the wall half with the bevel facing up toward the wall, using wall plugs and screws.
  3. Glue and screw the other half on the back/rail of the cabinet with the bevel facing down.
  4. Hang the cabinet by lowering it onto the wall strip.

Full housing / through housing (through dado)

also: through dado, cross-grain groove joint, through housing, dado

Îmbinare în uluc străpuns (nut transversal)Durchgehende Quernut (Einnutung)

Used in: ShelvesCarcasses, boxes and drawersVisibility: half-hidden

All sources (5)Hide list

  3. 604877192-Wood-Joinery (slides), p. 11
  4. W. Fairham, Woodwork Joints (J. B. Lippincott, 1921), p. 166–167 — archive.org
  5. Wood Handbook, FPL-GTR-282 (USDA Forest Products Laboratory, 2021), cap. 10, p. 10-17 — research.fs.usda.gov

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Fixed shelves in bookcases and cabinets, partitions, drawer supports. Because the housing shows on the front edge, it is usually hidden behind an applied bead or a face frame. The Joinery Handbook (2020, p.77) also uses it for bookshelves slid into their housings.
When not to use
Poor at resisting pull-out and racking – stiffness must come from the back and other parts. Sanding the shelf after fitting quickly spoils the tight fit. Where the joint must resist tension, add a dovetail.
Strength
The glue faces are mostly end grain, so the glue contributes little; the housing carries shelf loads in shear very well, and a fixed back stiffens the case. As with any end-to-face glue joint, it should be protected from large moisture changes, which set up internal stresses (Wood Handbook 2021, p.10-17).
Fixing / glue
Glue; optional nails/screws through the upright hidden under plugs or the front bead.
Effect on the cut list
The shelf is cut to length = clear distance between uprights + 2 × housing depth (e.g. +12 mm). Volume removed from the upright: T_shelf x depth x upright width.

Fabrication

  1. Lay out both uprights together: for every housing draw one shoulder line only, keeping the waste on the same side each time, and copy the marks to the second upright.
  2. Saw guide: a block whose height plus the housing depth equals the saw's blade depth (teeth to back), so the back of the saw meets the block when the cut is deep enough. Clamp it square on the line, knife the line and chisel a small sloping notch on the waste side to start the saw.
  3. Saw the first shoulder against the block. Mark the second with the shelf itself as a gauge and saw it the same way.
  4. Chop out the waste and flatten the floor with a router plane or router.
  5. By machine: dado head on the table saw (miter gauge, spacer for equal spacing) or a router guided by a T-square fence.
  6. Test-fit, glue and clamp; on long shelves use slightly crowned cauls so the pressure reaches the middle.

Parameters

ParameterValueStatus
Housing width= thickness of the housed piece, light tap fit (e.g. 18 mm)The Joint Book p.60; Joinery Handbook (2020) p.77¶Source

Notes. Combined from "Full housing by hand" (p.60-61) and the dado head method (p.62-63, slides p.11). The full rabbet housing variant at the corner is reinforced with pegs. Fairham (1921, p.166) also calls it a trenched and housed joint.

Stopped housing (stopped dado)

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Fixed shelves where the joint must not show at the front (bookcases, cabinets without a face frame).
When not to use
Do not try to stop a cross-grain dado on the table saw: it is unsafe and the blade leaves a curved end. Rout it instead, or use the strip method.
Strength
As for the through housing. The uncut wood at the front of the upright hides the joint, and the notched shelf corner rests against it.
Fixing / glue
Glue; optional short dovetail at the front for tension.
Effect on the cut list
Shelf: length + 2 × housing depth, plus the corner notches. With the strip method the upright is cut slightly narrower and the ~6 mm strip is added (glued back).

Fabrication

  1. Mark the housings. For the table-saw method, first rip a thin strip off the front edge of each upright and keep it with its part.
  2. Cut all housings through with the dado head (miter gauge with auxiliary fence and spacing gauge), then glue the strips back on.
  3. Router method: a saddle jig with a stop block that ends the cut short of the front edge.
  4. By hand: at the front end of the housing, bore a flat-bottomed hole to full depth and square it with a chisel; it gives the saw room to run.
  5. Notch the front corners of the shelf to the stop distance; the remaining shoulder sits against the solid front of the upright.
  6. Test-fit and glue.

Parameters

ParameterValueStatus
Housing width and depthas for the through housing (T_shelf x ≈ T_upright/3)The Joint Book p.60, p.62¶Source
Stop distance from the front edge≈ 12 mm (1/2"); 10–15 mm in practiceFairham (1921) p.167¶Source
Notch at the front corner of the shelf= stop distance x housing depthThe Joint Book p.62=Geometry
Strip methoda thin strip is ripped off the front edge and kept, the housings are cut through, then the strip is glued backThe Joint Book p.62-63¶Source

Notes. The book treats the stopped housing within "Full housing on the table saw" (p.62-63); separated from the through housing because the geometry differs. The Joint Book gives no stop distance; Fairham (1921, p.167) stops the housing 1/2" (≈ 12 mm) short of the front edge.

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Shelves and other internal cabinet parts; cabinet bottoms at the corners and drawer backs/fronts, provided an applied face covers the joint later.
When not to use
Not for parts fixed with screws through slotted holes, such as solid-wood drawer runners: once rabbeted, the end is too thin for the slots, so use a full housing there.
Strength
The shoulder bears on the face of the upright, which stiffens the joint and reduces racking compared with a full housing – the better choice for shelves. One shoulder is enough (a second would only weaken the shelf end), and it hides the edge of the housing. The Wood Handbook (2021, p.10-17) recommends exactly this kind of interlocking shape for end-to-face glue joints, so that long-grain faces carry the load.
Fixing / glue
Glue; optional nails/pegs at cabinet corners.
Effect on the cut list
Shelf: length = clear distance + 2 × housing depth (e.g. +12 mm). Volume removed: housing 12 x 6 in the upright; rabbet 6 x 6 on each end of the shelf.

Fabrication

  1. Bit and layout: a straight bit about 2/3 of the shelf thickness. Clamp the two matching uprights side by side, flat and square, and lay out the housings across both at once.
  2. First housing: fix a fence parallel to the layout at a distance equal to the bit-to-base-edge offset, and rout about 1/3 of the thickness deep.
  3. Following housings: screw a fence strip to a runner that fits the routed housing exactly; the strip is as wide as the distance to the next housing minus the base offset.
  4. Shelf ends: a second gauge equal to base offset plus housing depth positions the fence for rabbeting.
  5. Rout the rabbets on both ends; check that the shoulder-to-shoulder length equals the clear distance between uprights and that the tongues are short enough for the shoulders to seat.
  6. Test-fit, glue and clamp.

Parameters

ParameterValueStatus
Housing width (bit diameter)≈ 2/3 of shelf thickness (e.g. 12 mm at 18 mm)The Joint Book p.65¶Source
Housing depth≈ 1/3 of upright thickness (e.g. 6 mm)The Joint Book p.65¶Source
Rabbet on the shelf end1/3 T_shelf deep, length = housing depth; a single shoulderThe Joint Book p.64-65; Joinery Handbook (2020) p.77=Geometry
Distance between shelf shoulders= desired clear distance between uprightsThe Joint Book p.65¶Source

Notes. The p.65 proportions (bit ≈ 2/3 of shelf thickness, depth ≈ 1/3 of upright thickness) are confirmed by the book's text. Variant with a half dovetail on one shoulder (p.65). The Joinery Handbook (2020, p.77) uses it to fit a top shelf between the sides (barefaced housing); Hinescu (1989, p.45) calls such carcase joints „încheieri cu falț și uluc”.

SheetF41

Stop-routed housed rabbet

also: blind shouldered housing, rabbet housed in stopped dado

Încheietură cu falț și uluc oprit

Used in: ShelvesCarcasses, boxes and drawersVisibility: hidden
