Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Shelves and cabinet bottoms where an invisible joint is needed at the front without a face frame; drawer assemblies (front/back into sides).
Strength
As strong as the housed rabbet and invisible from the front. A half-dovetail on the tongue adds resistance to loads that push the sides outward.
Fixing / glue
Glue; optional half dovetail on the tenon for tension.
Effect on the cut list
As for the housed rabbet (shelf + 2 × depth); in addition a corner notch on the tenon = stop distance.

Fabrication

  1. Position the saddle jig by matching its centerline to the housing's, and clamp a stop block that limits the router travel short of the front edge.
  2. Rout the stopped housings.
  3. Tongue fit: set the rabbeting bit's cutting depth equal to the housing depth, then lower the bit pass by pass until the tongue enters the housing snugly.
  4. Cut back the front of the tongue by the distance the housing stops short of the edge, and pare the new shoulder with a chisel.
  5. Dry-fit and confirm that the front edges are flush, then glue.

Parameters

ParameterValueStatus
Housing width and depthas for the housed rabbet (≈ 2/3 T_shelf x ≈ 1/3 T_upright)The Joint Book p.65, p.67¶Source
Rabbet depth = housing depthrabbeting bit set to the housing depthThe Joint Book p.67¶Source
Housing stopslightly before the front edge (e.g. 10–12 mm)The Joint Book p.67¶Source
Numeric stop distance≈ 12 mm (1/2")Fairham (1921) p.167 (la ulucul oprit)¶Source

Notes. The end of the routed housing is rounded (radius = bit radius) – either squared with a chisel or the tenon corner is rounded.

SheetF42

Stopped tapered sliding dovetail

also: sliding dovetail, dovetail housing, dovetail tongue

Îmbinare în șanț coadă de rândunică, oprită și conicăGratverbindung (gestemmter, konischer Grat)

Used in: ShelvesCarcasses, boxes and drawersVisibility: hidden

TopologyTcarcass
Source
V. Constantinescu, I. Cârstea, Lucrări practice de tâmplărie (1959), p. 213 — archive.org
All sources (4)Hide list
  1. V. Constantinescu, I. Cârstea, Lucrări practice de tâmplărie (1959), p. 213 — archive.org
  2. The Joint Book, p. 130, 133, 142-143
  3. W. Fairham, Woodwork Joints: How They Are Set Out, How Made and Where Used (J. B. Lippincott, 1921), p. 127, 145–148 — archive.org
  4. Joinery Handbook, ed. 2 (Swedish Wood / TMF, 2020), p. 77

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Shelves, dividers and bottoms set into carcass sides, with the housing stopped short of the front edge so it does not show. The same profile locks tenons or tongues loaded in tension (e.g. rails into legs).
When not to use
Long housings without taper: the joint binds over its whole length during assembly. Boards that are not flat make accurate cutting and assembly difficult.
Strength
Locks mechanically: the sides cannot spread away from the shelf. With a taper, the parts slide freely and only bind over the final few centimeters. Glue at the front edge is enough; the full length need not be glued.
Fixing / glue
Glue only on the last few centimeters (front edge); no extra elements.
Effect on the cut list
The shelf is lengthened by 2 x the groove depth (e.g. +2 x 7 mm) over the inside clear dimension; with a stopped groove, the shelf is shortened at the front by the stop (e.g. 10 mm) in the tail zone. No extra parts.

Fabrication

  1. Pick the dovetail angle to suit the saw and plane you will use, and a tail width that leaves a small shoulder within the shelf thickness.
  2. Side: on the back edge mark the housing (depth < T/2); square the lines across the face, the upper one converging toward the front to give the taper.
  3. Side: chop a small recess at the stopped end to give the saw room; saw the square wall to depth, then the angled wall with a dovetail saw; clear the bottom.
  4. Shelf: mark the depth across the face, draw the dovetail profile on the back edge and the matching taper across the end.
  5. Shelf: plane off the shoulder and the tapered tail with a dovetail plane and cut the tongue back at the stop. The fit should only tighten over the last part of the travel, where a clamp draws it home.

Parameters

ParameterValueStatus
groove depth (in the housing piece)less than half the thickness of the housing pieceThe Joint Book p.143¶Source
tail widthfits within the thickness of the tongued piece, leaving a small shoulder (one shoulder = tongue with one sloped face)The Joint Book p.142-143¶Source
taperthe top line of the socket narrows toward the front; the same taper is marked on the end of the tongueThe Joint Book p.143; Joinery Handbook (2020) p.77 (groove slightly tapered for easier assembly and a better fit); Fairham (1921) p.127 (slight bevel so the joint drives tight)¶Source
typical taper3-5 mm across the shelf width (≈ 1:50 … 1:80)≈Trade practice
tail anglesame angle on the saw and the dovetail plane (guide); for the router: 14° or 1:6 usual≈Trade practice

Notes. The taper dimensions and the 14° angle are current practice, not from the book. For the stop, the 1959 Romanian manual gives 2 cm from the front; Fairham (1921) keeps the dovetail parallel for three quarters of its width and tapers it only toward the front.

also: biscuited T, fixed shelf with biscuits

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Fixed shelves, dividers or sides joined to the face of another board (T), in solid-wood or panel carcasses.
Strength
Glue area, and with it strength, grows with the number and size of the biscuits; when they only locate the shelf, a few are enough.
Fixing / glue
Biscuits + water-based glue.
Effect on the cut list
Shelf = inside opening (no allowance). Biscuits: n ≈ depth/120.

Fabrication

  1. Clamp a straightedge across side A on the shelf line, so that it also locates shelf B; mark the biscuit positions on both parts.
  2. Slot the face of A with the fence off and the base plate standing against the straightedge.
  3. Clamp B flat on the bench and slot its end with the machine base riding on the bench.
  4. Glue, insert the biscuits, assemble and clamp.

Parameters

ParameterValueStatus

Another method (wolfcraft, p.16): square the shelf onto the side, mark it, then fold it over onto its back at the line and clamp it; the slots in its edge and in the face of the side are cut from that one set-up. Lamello asks for 13 mm thickness for a #20 slot in a face, slightly above the Joint Book rule 'thickness > biscuit width / 2'.

T-bridle joint (center leg bridle)

also: T-bridle, tee bridle joint, center leg bridle

Îmbinare cu cep deschis în T (peste traversă continuă)Schlitz und Zapfen (T-Verbindung)

All sources (6)Hide list

  2. The Joint Book, p. 71, 72, 75
  3. W. Fairham, Woodwork Joints (Lippincott, 1921), p. 27–28, 30 — archive.org
  4. G. Ellis, Modern Practical Joinery (Batsford, 1902), p. 86 — archive.org
  5. P. N. Hasluck (ed.), Cassell's Carpentry and Joinery (D. McKay, 1907), p. 55 (fig. 192) — archive.org

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Used where a rail must stay unbroken while a leg or post joins it from below: a centre table leg under a long apron, or the foot of a trestle table; also common on half-round (demilune) tables. Fairham (1921, p.27) recommends it for a leg joined to the frame of an occasional table: the grain of the leg runs right to the top, which looks neater than a tenon.
When not to use
The fork does not enclose the rail on top; if the load pulls the leg down off the rail, it is pegged.
Strength
Compared with a lap joint, the two fork cheeks give twice the gluing surface and a stiffer joint against racking (p.71); the rail is not cut through.
Fixing / glue
Glue; optionally transverse pegs.
Effect on the cut list
No lengthening of the rail (it stays continuous). The leg is not lengthened (the fork is in its own end). Volume removed: 2 seats on the rail + the slot in the leg.

Fabrication

  1. Set the thickness of the rail core = fork width (≈ T_leg/3).
  2. On the rail cut seats on both faces, across the leg width, down to the core thickness.
  3. In the end of the leg cut the fork (slot) with depth = rail height.
  4. Fit, glue, optionally peg.

Parameters

ParameterValueStatus
fork width≈ 1/3 of the leg thicknessThe Joint Book p.80 (general T/3 rule); Fairham (1921) p.30 (thickness divided into three)¶Source
seats on the railrecesses on both faces of the rail, width = leg width, depth = (T_rail − fork width)/2=Geometry
fork depth= rail height (the apron enters fully)=Geometry
fittingthe fork arms slightly tapered, so the joint tightens as it goes home; the rail shoulders slightly undercut, to hold the ends of the arms downEllis (1902) p.86¶Source

Notes. The dimensions are chosen for three equal divisions on the leg; The Joint Book gives no dimensions for the T variant; Fairham (1921) uses the same division into three, and the Joinery Handbook (2020, p.75) also allows it between members of different section, at 45–90°. Ellis (1902, p.86) describes the forked tenon, where both pieces stay continuous (wide doors, counter fronts). Straight variant: the rail is not thinned, and the fork width = T_rail.

SheetF45

Through wedged tenon

also: wedged through tenon, foxtail-wedged tenon, fox-wedged tenon

Cep străpuns împănat (cu pene în capăt)Verkeilter Zapfen

Used in: Tables, chairs and bedsFrames (doors, windows, pictures)Visibility: exposed

TopologyTL
Source
Joinery Handbook, ed. 2 (Swedish Wood / TMF, 2020), p. 75
All sources (8)Hide list
  1. Joinery Handbook, ed. 2 (Swedish Wood / TMF, 2020), p. 75
  2. The Joint Book, p. 72-74, 87-90
  3. Constantinescu, V., Cârstea, I., Lucrări practice de tâmplărie (1959), p. 107, 117 — archive.org
  4. Bellu, P., Manualul tâmplarului, vol. I (Ed. Uniunea Camerelor de Muncă, 1939), p. 69–71, 73, 105 — archive.org
  5. W. Fairham, Woodwork Joints (Lippincott, 1921), p. 56, 63 — archive.org
  6. G. Ellis, Modern Practical Joinery (Batsford, 1902), p. 49, 60 — archive.org
  7. P. N. Hasluck (ed.), Cassell's Carpentry and Joinery (D. McKay, 1907), p. 67 — archive.org
  8. C. H. Hayward, The Woodworker: The Charles H. Hayward Years, Vol. III — Joinery (Lost Art Press, 2016), p. 910, 913, 915 — blog.lostartpress.com

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Where the joint works in tension: leg stretchers, trestle tables, chairs, shelves with multiple tenons through the carcase sides (p.74).
When not to use
The wedges must be oriented to push toward the ends of the mortise (end grain), not toward the long walls, otherwise the piece splits (The Joint Book p.87; Constantinescu & Cârstea 1959, p.117).
Strength
Very high pull-out resistance: the wedges flare the tenon until it fills a mortise that widens toward the exit face, so the tenon is locked mechanically, not just held by glue (p.72, p.87).
Fixing / glue
Glue + 1–2 contrasting hardwood wedges; optionally a peg near the shoulder.
Effect on the cut list
Rail + thickness of the pierced piece + 2–3 mm at each end. Extra parts: 2 wedges per tenon (e.g. 8 × 4→0.5 × 40 mm), cut from a strip the thickness of the tenon.

Fabrication

  1. Cut the mortise through. On the exit face only, lengthen it by ≈1.6 mm at each end and bevel the end walls back toward the entry face, keeping a short straight section at the entry.
  2. Lay out the tenon. Before sawing, drill a small stop hole for each wedge kerf, about 1/4 of L from the shoulder; it keeps the split from running on.
  3. Saw the cheeks and shoulders; then saw each wedge kerf in from the tenon end until it reaches its stop hole.
  4. Make the wedges from a strip as thick as the tenon, with the grain running along the wedge (a notched plywood jig on the circular saw is enough).
  5. With glue applied and the shoulders clamped tight, drive both glued wedges in turns so that they finish at the same depth.
  6. When the glue has cured, bring the wedge and tenon ends level with the face (saw, then plane).

Parameters

ParameterValueStatus
mortise flare+≈1.6 mm (1/16") at each end, on the exit face only, tapering to nothing toward the entry face; a short straight section remains at the entry. Other values: ≈ 2 mm on the wedge side (Bellu 1939); ≈ 3 mm (1/8 in) … 5 mm (3/16 in) at each end (Hayward 2016)The Joint Book p.88 (step 1), p.73; Bellu (1939) p.71; Ellis (1902) p.49 (flare on the back edge); Hayward (2016) p.913, p.915¶Source
depth of the wedge cutsdown to a small hole drilled at ≈ 1/4 of the tenon length from the shoulder (cut = 3/4 of L, from the end)The Joint Book p.88 (steps 2-3)¶Source
end hole of the cutsmall hole (Ø 2–3 mm) against splitting of the tenonThe Joint Book p.88; Ø = trade practice¶Source
position of the cutspatterns: two wedges, one central, at the edges, diagonal; typically 2 cuts at ≈ 1/4–1/6 of the tenon width from the edges; on a fox-wedged blind tenon the cuts sit ≈ 5 mm (3/16 in) from the edges (Fairham 1921), longer wedges at the edges and shorter toward the middle (Ellis 1902)The Joint Book p.73 (patterns); numeric position = trade practice; Fairham (1921) p.63; Ellis (1902) p.60¶Source
wedge width≤ tenon thickness (wedges cut from stock as thick as the tenon); if a wedge has to be thicker, its kerf in the tenon is opened into a shallow V. Bellu (1939): wedges as thick and as long as the tenon, at most 15 mm wide, so they do not burst the railThe Joint Book p.87, p.88 (step 4); Bellu (1939) p.69, p.73, p.105¶Source
wedge grainrunning the length of the wedge (a cross-grain wedge breaks under the mallet); a contrasting, decorative species (The Joint Book) or the same wood as the work — never a fir wedge in oak (Bellu 1939); straight-grained hardwood (Ellis 1902)The Joint Book p.87-88; Bellu (1939) p.69; Ellis (1902) p.60¶Source
wedge taper≈ 1:8–1:10 (5–7°); thickness at the thick end ≈ 4 mm for 1.6 mm flare + 2 mm cut; Bellu (1939): under 10 mm at the thick endBellu (1939) p.73 (thickness at the thick end); taper = trade practice≈Trade practice
tenon length= thickness of the pierced piece + surplus cut off after dryingThe Joint Book p.88 (step 6)¶Source
orientation of the wedgesacross the pierced piece, so the wedges press toward the mortise ends, not toward the long wallsThe Joint Book p.87; Constantinescu & Cârstea (1959) p.117¶Source
variant — wedges beside the tenonglued wedges driven between the tenon and the flared mortise ends, one on each side (a third in the middle of the tenon if needed); the mortise is just long enough for one wedge at each end; the usual practice for doors and framesBellu (1939) p.69–71, p.105; Hasluck (1907) p.67; Hayward (2016) p.913, p.915¶Source

Notes. p.73 also shows the flared mortise for wedges with two tapers (knock-down tenon). Also used for shelving: a row of through tenons without face shoulders, each one wedged, passes through the carcase side (p.74). The Joint Book gives no wedge taper. In Romanian door and window joinery (Bellu 1939, p.69–73) the wedges go beside the tenon, in the flared mortise, and only after the frame has been cramped and checked for square; on thin frames the rail is first clamped next to the tenon so it does not split. The wedges are driven alternately so the rail does not shift (Hayward 2016, p.915).

SheetF46

Angled tenon and shoulder

also: skewed tenon, angled shoulder tenon, tenon at a raked leg

Cep înclinat cu umăr înclinat

Used in: Tables, chairs and bedsVisibility: hidden

TopologyT≠ 90°
Source
G. Ellis, Modern Practical Joinery (Batsford, 1902), p. 80 — archive.org
All sources (4)Hide list
  1. G. Ellis, Modern Practical Joinery (Batsford, 1902), p. 80 — archive.org
  2. The Joint Book, p. 75, 91-92
  3. Hinescu, A., Cartea tâmplarului universal (Ed. Tehnică, 1989), p. 97 — archive.org
  4. W. Fairham, Woodwork Joints (Lippincott, 1921), p. 66 — archive.org

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Chairs and tables with splayed or tapered legs, where rails and stretchers meet the leg at an angle other than 90°. The shoulder is cut to that angle and the tenon follows it, so the mortise can stay square to the leg.
When not to use
Works only while the tenon still has continuous long grain; at steeper angles the alternative is to angle the mortise (p.75).
Strength
Good if the tenon keeps continuous grain; a tenon skewed to the grain is weaker than a straight one.
Fixing / glue
Glue; optionally a peg.
Effect on the cut list
Rail: +L at each end plus the extension due to the angled shoulder (W_B·tan θ on the long edge); cut longer and trim to the drawing.

Fabrication

  1. Set the mitre gauge to the shoulder angle read off the full-size drawing, and mark the shoulder position on the rail, already cut to its final length.
  2. With the dado cutters set to the shoulder depth, waste two cheeks, flipping the rail between passes; move the gauge to the other side of the blade, reset the angle and waste the remaining two.
  3. Saw the edge shoulders at the same angle and rip the tenon to width so the waste falls away.
  4. Make the mortise normally, square to the leg.
  5. Fit and glue.

Parameters

ParameterValueStatus
shoulder anglefrom the 1:1 drawing; typically 3–15° off 90° on chairs and tables with raked legsThe Joint Book p.91; typical values = trade practice; Hinescu (1989) p.97 (angled shoulders cut on the tenoning machine)¶Source
tenon orientationlaid out perpendicular to the angled shoulder → mortise square to the leg; the tenon ends up oblique to the grain of the railThe Joint Book p.91¶Source
continuous grainsome fibres must run unbroken from the shoulder to the tenon end: tenon width ≤ W_B − L·tan(θ)The Joint Book p.91 (rule); formula = geometry¶Source
tenon thickness≈ T/3The Joint Book p.76¶Source

Notes. Difference from 'mortise-tenon-angled': here the mortise is square to the leg and the tenon is skewed to the grain of the rail. The book also shows the variant with angled face shoulders. The extra sources consulted (Hinescu 1989, Fairham 1921, Ellis 1902) cover oblique frame joints, not splayed legs as such; the continuous-grain rule is still the one from The Joint Book. At large angles Ellis (1902, p.80) switches to inserted tenons.

SheetF47

Twin tenon

also: double tenon, two parallel tenons, twin mortise and tenon

Cep dubluDoppelzapfen

Source
Rivington's Notes on Building Construction, Part I (1891), p. 241–242 — archive.org
All sources (8)Hide list
  1. Rivington's Notes on Building Construction, Part I (1891), p. 241–242 — archive.org
  2. The Joint Book, p. 73, 97, 99
  3. Wood Joinery (604877192), p. 17
  4. Constantinescu, V., Cârstea, I., Lucrări practice de tâmplărie (1959), p. 110–111 — archive.org
  5. Curs de tehnologia lemnului — Diferite încheieturi (Școala Superioară de Arte și Meserii, București, cca 1934), p. 8 (fig. 9) — archive.org
  6. W. Fairham, Woodwork Joints (Lippincott, 1921), p. 60, 64–65 — archive.org
  7. G. Ellis, Modern Practical Joinery (Batsford, 1902), p. 78 — archive.org

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Thick pieces or pieces nearly square in section (leg stretchers, drawers, pieces working in torsion): two parallel tenons instead of one thick one. Romanian manuals give it for cabinet plinth frames, clamps and presses, and frames subject to strong vibration (Constantinescu & Cârstea 1959, p.110; Curs de tehnologia lemnului, c. 1934, p.8); in door joinery, for the middle rail of thick doors (Hasluck 1907, p.67; Rivington 1891, p.242).
When not to use
The sources disagree on strength: Constantinescu & Cârstea (1959, p.110) rate it more solid than a single 1/3 tenon, while Ellis (1902, p.78) calls it a necessary evil, since two thin tenons do not hold like one thick tenon of the same total thickness; Rivington (1891, p.242) prefers, where possible, a single tenon with cross-tongued shoulders.
Strength
Doubles the gluing surface and gives a broad base against twisting; combined with an edge shoulder it is also stiffer in racking (p.73, p.97).
Fixing / glue
Glue.
Effect on the cut list
Rail +L at each end; volume removed: 2 mortises in the stile, 3 strips on the end of the rail.

Fabrication

  1. Divide the rail thickness into 5 equal parts and mark the two tenons.
  2. Make two parallel mortises in the stile.
  3. Cut the shoulders and outer cheeks, then remove the core between the tenons (saw + chisel or router).
  4. Fit and glue.

Watch the terms: English usage varies — Hasluck (1907) calls the pair of tenons side by side across the width 'double', while Ellis (1902) uses 'double tenon' for tenons across the thickness of very thick framing. SheetF48

Keyed (tusk) tenon

also: through tenon with key, tusk tenon, wedged knock-down tenon, keyed through tenon

Cep alungit cu pană

Used in: Tables, chairs and bedsVisibility: exposed

TopologyT
Source
Constantinescu, V., Cârstea, I., Lucrări practice de tâmplărie (1959), p. 115, 118 — archive.org
All sources (6)Hide list
  1. Constantinescu, V., Cârstea, I., Lucrări practice de tâmplărie (1959), p. 115, 118 — archive.org
  2. The Joint Book, p. 72, 75, 90, 178-179, 181
  3. Curs de tehnologia lemnului — Diferite încheieturi (Școala Superioară de Arte și Meserii, București, cca 1934), p. 13 (fig. 26) — archive.org
  4. W. Fairham, Woodwork Joints (Lippincott, 1921), p. 61–62 — archive.org

  6. Joinery Handbook, ed. 2 (Swedish Wood / TMF, 2020), p. 75–76

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Furniture meant to be taken apart (trestle and refectory tables, travelling furniture, shelving): a through tenon projects past the stile and is locked by a tapered key passed through a hole in the projecting part. Constantinescu & Cârstea (1959, p.118) give it for workbench legs, embroidery frames and the legs of tables and benches; the course of c. 1934 (p.13) recommends it for heavier loads, on cupboards, tables, benches and workbench stands that must come apart.
When not to use
The key is always on show, so the design has to account for it (p.178). If too little wood is left beyond the key hole, the short grain there breaks out.
Strength
Rigid against racking and strong without glue; driving the key draws the shoulders tight, and pulling it out lets the joint come apart (p.178). For a stronger joint the rail is made wider (Constantinescu & Cârstea 1959, p.118).
Fixing / glue
No glue; removable hardwood key.
Effect on the cut list
Rail + thickness of the stile + extension (≈ 50–60 mm) at each keyed end. Extra part: 1 key per joint (e.g. 22 × 20→12 × 100 mm).

Fabrication

  1. Leave the through tenon long enough to project well past the stile. With the joint dry-assembled, mark the exit line on the tenon face.
  2. Lay out the key hole with its inner edge slightly inside the exit line, so the key bears on the stile, and leave a generous length of tenon beyond it against short grain.
  3. Chop the key slot through the tenon, with the outer wall sloped to suit the key.
  4. Taper the outer face of the key slightly; as it is driven, its inner face presses on the stile and the taper draws the shoulders tight.

Parameters

ParameterValueStatus

key slot positionstarts slightly inside the line where the tenon exits the mortise (≈ 1–3 mm into the stile thickness), so that the key presses on the stileThe Joint Book p.179 (step 2); value = trade practice; Constantinescu & Cârstea (1959) p.118 (the key bears on one edge of the leg)¶Source

tenon thicknessT/3 … T/2 (keyed tenons are usually thicker)The Joint Book p.76 (T/3 general)≈Trade practice

Notes. The numeric proportions appear neither in The Joint Book nor in the extra sources consulted; they are typical values. The Romanian name 'cep alungit cu pană' (elongated tenon with a key) is the one used by Constantinescu & Cârstea (1959, p.115, p.118), where the joint is knock-down and not glued. The book's image shows the key passing through the thickness of the tenon (perpendicular to its face).

Half-dovetail tenon (wedged, knock-down)

also: half-dovetailed tenon with wedge, dovetail tenon, knock-down, sliding half-dovetail tenon

Cep cu o latură în coadă de rândunică, blocat cu pană

All sources (4)Hide list

  3. Curs de tehnologia lemnului — Diferite încheieturi (Școala Superioară de Arte și Meserii, București, cca 1934), p. 13 (fig. 27) — archive.org

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Furniture meant to be dismantled and reassembled repeatedly (beds, tables, shelves). The underside of the tenon is cut as a half dovetail; once inserted, the tenon drops onto the matching slope in the mortise and a tapered wedge driven in above it holds it there. Fairham (1921, p.62) gives it for the cross rail and leg of a carpenter's bench; the course of c. 1934 (p.13) chooses it when the face must stay free of visible wedges.
When not to use
Narrow stock, or a tenon that is loose in thickness, leaves the joint without side-to-side support (p.180).
Strength
Very stiff when wedged; the wedge is the only part to remove for disassembly, and until then the tenon cannot lift off the slope (p.180).
Fixing / glue
Tapered hardwood wedge, no glue.
Effect on the cut list
Rail + thickness of the stile at each end (through tenon, flush). Extra part: 1 wedge per joint (e.g. 10 wide × 50 long, height 8 → 6 mm).

Fabrication

  1. First make a normal tenon, but shoulder it on the faces only; the half dovetail is then laid out and cut on its lower edge.
  2. Through mortise: top end straight, bottom end sloped to match the dovetail, with extra height on the exit side to receive the wedge.
  3. Check the clearance: held with its top edge against the top of the mortise, the tenon must slide in.
  4. Push the tenon through, let it drop onto the slope, then drive the tapered wedge into the gap above; plane the wedge down until, fully home, it ends flush with the tenon end.

Parameters

ParameterValueStatus
shouldersside (face) shoulders only, no edge shouldersThe Joint Book p.180¶Source
dovetailalways on the lower edge of the tenonThe Joint Book p.180¶Source
dovetail angle≈ 1:6–1:8 (8–10°)≈Trade practice
mortisethrough; full tenon width at entry; bottom end sloped at the dovetail angle, widening toward the exit; extra height on the exit side for the wedgeThe Joint Book p.180-181 (step 1)¶Source
entryinserted with the top edge against the top of the mortise, then lowered onto the slopeThe Joint Book p.181 (steps 2-3)¶Source
wedgetapered; goes above the tenon; thinned as needed so that it finishes flush with the tenon end; a hardwood wedge driven in above the tenon (Fairham 1921)The Joint Book p.181 (step 3); Fairham (1921) p.62¶Source
wedge taper≈ 1:15–1:20≈Trade practice
variantsblind tenon with removable pegs; tenon with vertical wedge (tusk); wedges hidden beside the tenon, so the face stays free of wedges (course, c. 1934); a pair of folding wedges driven over the tenons (Ellis 1902)The Joint Book p.181; Curs de tehnologia lemnului (c. 1934) p.13; Ellis (1902) p.80¶Source

Notes. The book does not give the dovetail angle, the wedge taper or the mortise dimensions; the values are constructed geometrically and must be verified when modeling (the mortise height at entry must let the wide end of the tenon pass). The Romanian description in the woodworking course of c. 1934 (p.13): a tenon cut as half a dovetail, with the wedges hidden beside it.

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Parts of different thicknesses with offset faces (e.g. rail/apron on a thick leg, set back from the leg face).
Strength
Biscuit centered on the thin part; glue + biscuits.
Fixing / glue
Biscuits + glue.
Effect on the cut list
No added length. Biscuits #10 (e.g. 3 pcs over 200 mm width).

Fabrication

  1. Mark the biscuit positions. Lay a spacer as thick as the offset on the thin part and set the fence, resting on the spacer, so the blade is centred in the thin part.
  2. Slot the thin part with the spacer between fence and face.
  3. Leave the blade height alone and slot the thick part at the same marks, with the fence directly on its face.
  4. Glue, insert the biscuits, assemble and clamp.

minimum part widthgreater than the slot at the surface: ~54 mm (#0), ~60 mm (#10), ~66 mm (#20)Lamello catalogue 26/27 p.114¶Source

Notes. A spacer between the fence and the work lets the slot be set at any height, which is what makes joints between parts of unequal thickness possible. When A is narrower than the slot length, a small biscuit (#0/#10) is required. Joint Selector (JB p.185): listed under 'Dowels and biscuits'. The same principle in wolfcraft (p.16): for boards thinner than 18 mm, a thin plywood strip under the edge brings the slot to mid-thickness.

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Making parts thicker than the available lumber by gluing two or more boards face to face: table legs, thick tops, workbench tops, turning blanks. The 1959 Romanian manual recommends it when a part must be thicker and resist deformation better.
When not to use
Not used with layers at different or unequalized moisture content, or with faces that cannot be planed flat over their whole area. PVA glue does not suit permanently loaded parts (high creep) or parts exposed to damp. Load-bearing glued laminated beams follow their own manufacturing and testing rules (in North America they are made only in approved plants, Wood Handbook 2021 p.11-18) → structural design.
Strength
The joint is a long-grain glue line, face to face. A well-made joint of this kind can be as strong as the wood in shear along the grain and in tension across it (Wood Handbook 2021, p.10-16). The main risk is shrinkage: with growth rings placed wrongly or layers at different moisture content, drying sets up stresses that open the glue lines at the ends and along the edges (Constantinescu & Cârstea 1959, p.125; Wood Handbook 2021, p.10-14). Too little pressure or faces that are not flat give thick, weak glue lines (Wood Handbook 2021, p.10-16). For load-bearing parts → structural design.
Fixing / glue
Glue only: PVA indoors; water-resistant adhesives (phenol-resorcinol, melamine, polyurethane, emulsion polymer isocyanate) for damp or outdoor use. No mechanical fasteners.
Effect on the cut list
Each layer is cut and planed separately, with a machining allowance: ≈ +2–3 mm in thickness for flattening and thicknessing, ≈ +5 mm in width (the layers slide on the glue when clamped) and +20–30 mm in length. The final size of the blank is reached only after gluing and conditioning, by planing the outer faces and edges and trimming the ends; for a 75 mm finished blank the outer layers are planed to ≈ 26–27 mm (otherwise the blank comes out thinner). No extra parts: the list holds the 3 layers.

Fabrication

  1. Cut the layers with a machining allowance and leave them in the shop until their moisture content has evened out; measure it before gluing.
  2. Flatten one face and one edge on the jointer or with a jointer plane, then plane to thickness. Plane the glue faces on the day of the glue-up.
  3. Dry-fit the layers with the grain running the same way and the inner face of each one on the outer face of the one below; mark the order with a cabinetmaker's triangle and check with a straightedge that the faces touch everywhere.
  4. Spread the glue evenly on one face (on both for hardwood) and close the stack within the assembly time on the adhesive's data sheet; the layers slide on the glue, so align the ends and edges before clamping.
  5. Clamp at ≈ 150 mm, alternating from the two edges, over heavy cross cauls, working from the middle toward the ends; retighten the clamps after 15–30 min and clean off the squeeze-out.
  6. After the press time, let the blank condition, then flatten one face and one edge, plane to width and thickness and square the ends.

Parameters

ParameterValueStatus
Number and thickness of layers (model)3 × 25 mm → 75 mm blank=Geometry

Hinescu asks for at most 8–10 % when gluing framesWood Handbook (2021) p.10-13, p.10-14; Joinery Handbook p.90; Hinescu (1989) p.118¶Source
Moisture content difference between layersbelow ≈ 5 percentage points for low-density species, below ≈ 2 for dense onesWood Handbook (2021) p.10-14¶Source

Notes. The name „înnădire în grosime (suprapunerea pieselor)” comes from Constantinescu and Cârstea (1959, p.119, p.125). Their ring rule (all layers the same way) is the opposite of edge gluing, where rings alternate; no other source consulted gives a rule for face lamination, so it is still to be confirmed with a cabinetmaker. The pressures in the sources (0.6–1.7 MPa) mean ≈ 36–100 kN on the face of this blank, hard to reach with hand clamps; the Wood Handbook (p.10-15) allows lower pressure on small, flat, well-planed surfaces. The 50 mm maximum per layer comes from North American rules for structural glulam, not from furniture. The assembly times are for one PVA glue; for another adhesive, take them from its data sheet.

When to use
Fastening a solid-wood top to the table aprons, allowing the wood to move across the width.
Strength
Keeps the top flat and pulled down; not glued, it slides in the groove with the movement of the top. A solid top fixed rigidly splits or opens at its glue lines as it dries.
Fixing / glue
Wooden (or metal) buttons + 4 x 30 screws.
Effect on the cut list
Extra parts: wooden buttons ~25 x 30 x 40 (e.g. 8-10 pcs). Apron: groove.

Fabrication

  1. Rout the groove on the inside face of the aprons before assembling the table.
  2. Make the buttons (rabbeted strip, cut into pieces), drill them for the screw.
  3. Place the top face down, insert the button tongue in the groove and screw it into the top.

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Gluing several narrow boards edge to edge to make wide panels: tops, shelves, sides, door panels.
When not to use
Not used when the edges cannot be planed perfectly straight and square; a rubbed joint (no clamps) only for lengths under ~0.9 m.
Strength
Long-grain-to-long-grain glue line. A well-fitted edge joint can match the wood in shear along the grain and in tension across it, and under test the wood usually fails before the glue line (Wood Handbook 2021, p.10-16; Fairham 1921, p.2). Nothing locks the boards mechanically, so alignment depends on clamping. A sprung joint (a slight hollow at mid-length) keeps the ends closed when they lose moisture faster than the middle; Bellu (1939, p.60) keeps the gap very small on short boards and a little larger on long ones, since otherwise the ends stay open and spoil the glue-up.
Fixing / glue
Glue only (PVA, hide glue for a rubbed joint). Optional reinforcement with biscuits, tongue or spline (see related joints).
Effect on the cut list
Each board +6 mm in width for planing and +20–50 mm in length for final trimming; final panel = sum of net widths. No extra parts.

Fabrication

  1. Mark the order and grain direction of the boards with a cabinetmaker's triangle; rip each one ~6 mm wider than its final size and keep a length allowance for trimming after glue-up.
  2. Joint the edges on the jointer, or with a long plane on a shooting board. Present mating boards with opposite faces to the fence so that any error in squareness is mirrored and cancels out.
  3. If the joint is to be sprung, take a few extra passes from the middle of the edge until a ~0.8 mm gap remains there while the ends still touch.
  4. Lay a straightedge across the dry-fitted boards: it must sit flat, with no rocking.
  5. For a clamped glue-up, alternate clamps above and below the panel and protect the edges with battens. Short pieces can instead be glued without clamps, rubbing them together with a fast-tacking glue (hide glue or PVA) until they grip.
  6. Once the glue has cured, square the ends and bring the panel to thickness.

Parameters

ParameterValueStatus
Ripping allowance over final width≈ 6 mm (1/4")The Joint Book p.27¶Source
Center gap for sprung joint≈ 0.8 mm (1/32") at mid-length, ends in contactThe Joint Book p.24, p.27; Bellu (1939) p.60¶Source
Maximum length for rubbed joint (no clamps)< 0.9 m (3')The Joint Book p.26¶Source
Growth ring orientationalternating (heart side up / heart side down) to limit cupping; Fairham (1921) notes the panel then tends to go slightly wavy, while quartersawn stock stays nearly flatThe Joint Book p.24, p.26; slides p.4; Constantinescu & Cârstea (1959) p.120–121; Fairham (1921) p.5¶Source
Width of component boards60–120 mm≈Trade practice
Clamp spacing (alternating top/bottom)250–300 mm≈Trade practice

Notes. The "machined locking edge" variant (profiled joint cutter) is mentioned only as a variant (p.27). Slides p.4 also describe the end-to-face butt joint (see butt-joint-end-to-face). Romanian manuals call it „înnădire pe cant prin îndreptare simplă și încleiere” (Constantinescu & Cârstea 1959, p.120) or „îmbinare netedă” (Tehnologia meseriei, p.75).

SheetF54

Splined edge joint (loose tongue)

also: loose spline joint, loose tongue joint, double groove with spline

Înnădire cu lambă aplicată și ulucFremdfeder-Verbindung

Used in: Panels and topsVisibility: half-hidden

Topologyedge
Source
W. Fairham, Woodwork Joints (J. B. Lippincott, 1921), p. 42–43, 49–50 — archive.org
All sources (7)Hide list
  1. W. Fairham, Woodwork Joints (J. B. Lippincott, 1921), p. 42–43, 49–50 — archive.org
  2. The Joint Book, p. 29-30
  3. 604877192-Wood-Joinery (slides), p. 6
  4. A. Hinescu, Cartea tâmplarului universal (Ed. Tehnică, București, 1989), p. 45–46 — archive.org
  5. Tehnologia meseriei, suport de curs dulgher-tâmplar-parchetar (după C. Roșoga, I. Davidescu, Cartea dulgherului), p. 76 — pdfcoffee.com
  6. Joinery Handbook, ed. 2 (Swedish Wood / TMF, 2020), p. 78 (§4.1.9)
  7. Revista din Lemn, „Îmbinarea nut și feder: la ce se folosește și cum se realizează” (13.12.2018) — revistadinlemn.ro

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Edge-gluing where the faces must come out flush: tops, panels, frames. A spline in a contrasting species turns the joint line into a visible accent.
When not to use
Size the spline carefully: if it is wider than the two grooves are deep together, the joint cannot close; if it is tight in thickness, moisture from the glue swells it and can crack the groove walls.
Strength
More glue surface than a plain edge joint, and the spline keeps the faces from shifting while the clamps are tightened; stronger than the plain joint. Hinescu (1989, p.45) rates it the most economical of the edge joints.
Fixing / glue
Glue; separate spline of plywood, HDF or solid wood.
Effect on the cut list
Extra part: spline T/3 x (2·depth − 0.5) x joint length (from continuous plywood or several solid pieces). Board width does not increase. Volume removed: groove T/3 x T/2 on each edge.

Fabrication

  1. Prepare the edges straight and square as for the plain joint.
  2. With the marked face always against the fence or bearing, cut a groove ≈ T/2 deep in the middle of each edge (slot cutter or circular saw).
  3. Make the spline as thick as the groove is wide (~T/3) and slightly narrower than twice the groove depth; solid-wood splines are ripped so that the grain runs across them.
  4. Try the spline in an offcut grooved with the same setting and correct its thickness if needed.
  5. Spread glue on the edges and into the grooves, seat the spline in one board, close the joint with the other and clamp. Alternatively, glue the spline into one board first and close the joint once that glue has set.
  6. Variants: a stopped spline, whose groove ends short of the board ends so nothing shows; or a spline whose visible end is closed with a piece of matching wood.

Parameters

ParameterValueStatus
Groove positioncentered on thickness, referenced from the marked faceThe Joint Book p.29, p.30¶Source
Groove depth (in each piece)≈ 1/2 of the wood thickness (e.g. 10 mm at T = 20)The Joint Book p.30¶Source
Spline thickness = groove width≈ 1/3 of the piece thickness (e.g. 6–7 mm at T = 20)The Joint Book p.30¶Source
Spline widthslightly under twice the groove depth (e.g. 19.5 mm)The Joint Book p.30; Revista din Lemn (2018)¶Source
Spline materialplywood/HDF (grain direction irrelevant, continuous length) or solid wood with cross grain; a cross-grain solid spline is the stronger and can be thinner, while one cut diagonally to the grain comes out in longer piecesThe Joint Book p.29-30; Fairham (1921) p.42; Hinescu (1989) p.46 (lambe din placaj)¶Source
Spline clearance in groove0.1–0.2 mm on thickness≈Trade practice
Stopped groove (hidden spline)the groove stops ≈ 38 mm (1 1/2") short of each end, where the edge of the top is mouldedFairham (1921) p.43¶Source

Notes. The Romanian term „lambă aplicată” comes from the joinery manuals (Hinescu 1989, p.45; Tehnologia meseriei, p.76); in the shop it is also called „feder”. Fairham (1921, p.42) distinguishes the cross tongue (grain across the spline) from the feather tongue (cut diagonally).

SheetF55

Shiplap joint

also: rabbeted edge joint, lapped rabbet joint, shiplap cladding

Înnădire cu falț (falțuri suprapuse)Falzverbindung (Stülpfalz)

Used in: Panels and topsVisibility: half-hidden

All sources (3)Hide list

  2. The Joint Book, p. 27, 30
  3. Tehnologia meseriei, suport de curs dulgher-tâmplar-parchetar (după C. Roșoga, I. Davidescu, Cartea dulgherului), p. 76 — pdfcoffee.com

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Panels, cladding, cabinet backs and floorboards. Each board carries a rabbet on one edge; the overlapping rabbets register the faces and add glue area, or they can be left dry so the boards can move. Romanian manuals use it for nailed wall boarding and for the second layer of entrance-door panels: when the wood shrinks, the overlap keeps the joint from opening into a visible gap (Constantinescu & Cârstea 1959, p.122; Tehnologia meseriei, p.76).
When not to use
With bowed boards the rabbets no longer bring the faces flush on their own; each board would need pressure at its middle, which is impractical on a wide glued panel.
Strength
The floor of each rabbet is an extra long-grain glue surface; the overlap gives moderate alignment, but nothing resists the boards being pulled apart.
Fixing / glue
Glue, or hidden nails/screws for cladding; no extra parts.
Effect on the cut list
Each board + rabbet width (e.g. +12 mm). Volume removed: T/2 x rabbet width on each edge.

Fabrication

  1. Cut the boards to final width + rabbet width.
  2. Cut (rabbet cutter, dado blade or rabbet plane) a T/2 rabbet on the top face of one edge.
  3. On the mating edge cut the rabbet on the opposite face.
  4. Test the overlap: the faces must come out in the same plane.
  5. Glue and clamp, adding a hold-down at mid-width where a board is bowed; for cladding, fix the boards without glue.

Parameters

ParameterValueStatus
Rabbet depth1/2 of thickness (e.g. 10 mm at T = 20)The Joint Book p.30; Constantinescu & Cârstea (1959) p.122¶Source
Rabbet width10–12 mm≈Trade practice
Extra width at cuttingadd the rabbet width to each board's net widthThe Joint Book p.30¶Source

Notes. In The Joint Book it appears only as a variant of the splined joint (p.30) and as an alternative on p.27; Romanian manuals treat it as a joint in its own right (Constantinescu & Cârstea 1959, p.122; Tehnologia meseriei, p.76). Possibly duplicated by a group covering rabbets – to be unified at consolidation.

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Flooring, paneling, panels and furniture backs; glued for tops or loose to allow wood movement.
When not to use
Bowed boards must be held flat against table and fence (hold-downs, feather boards) while machining; otherwise the groove wanders and the tongue comes out uneven.
Strength
The tongue is milled from the board itself, so it registers the faces during clamping without a separate part. Slides p.22 call it stronger than the plain joint, and Constantinescu & Cârstea (1959, p.122) call it very solid because of the larger glue area. The Wood Handbook (2021, p.10-16), however, finds that in practice the profile gives no more strength than a straight joint, because the mating faces cannot be machined accurately enough for even pressure. The sure gain is alignment.
Fixing / glue
Glue (tops) or no glue, with hidden nails/staples (paneling, flooring).
Effect on the cut list
Board with tongue +10 mm in width; volume removed: groove 7 x 10 on one edge, two shoulders 6.5 x 10 on the other. No extra parts.

Fabrication

  1. Cut the boards to final width plus tongue length.
  2. Groove (table saw, flat-top raker blade raised to T/2): with the fence 1/3 T from the blade, run the board once, then turn it to the other face and run it again so the groove ends up centered. A slot cutter or dado head does the same job.
  3. Tongue cheeks: with the board on edge and the blade set a touch lower than for the groove (the tongue must come out slightly shorter than the groove is deep), cut each face so the tongue is left just over the groove width.
  4. Check the fit and adjust the fence if needed; then, with the board flat and the blade at shoulder depth, cut off the two waste strips.
  5. For bowed stock, keep the board pressed to table and fence with hold-downs and feather boards. Assemble glued or dry.
  6. Variants: tongue and bead, or V-groove (chamfered edges).

Parameters

ParameterValueStatus
Groove width = tongue thickness≈ 1/3 of thickness, centered (e.g. 7 mm at T = 20)The Joint Book p.32; Constantinescu & Cârstea (1959) p.122¶Source
Groove depth≈ 1/2 of thickness (e.g. 10 mm), per The Joint Book; the Wood Handbook (2021) notes that a shallower groove aligns just as well and wastes less woodThe Joint Book p.32; Wood Handbook (2021) p.10-16¶Source
Tongue lengthslightly less than the groove depth (e.g. 9.5 mm)The Joint Book p.32; Revista din Lemn (2018)¶Source
Extra width at cutting+ tongue length on the board with the tongueThe Joint Book p.31¶Source
Side clearance of tongue in groove0.1–0.2 mm≈Trade practice

Notes. The groove width of ≈ 1/3 of thickness is stated by Constantinescu & Cârstea (1959, p.122); the 1/2 T depth is deduced from the machining steps on p.32 of The Joint Book. The tongue must not bottom in the groove, so that the joint closes on the faces (Revista din Lemn, 2018).

Butterfly key (bow-tie key, double dovetail key)

also: bow-tie key, double dovetail key, butterfly

Pană în dublă coadă de rândunică (încastrată)

Used in: Panels and topsFrames (doors, windows, pictures)Visibility: exposed

TopologyIL
Source
A. Christiana, Butterfly keys made easy (Popular Woodworking, 3 mai 2020), online — popularwoodworking.com
All sources (3)Hide list

  2. The Joint Book, p. 132, 148-149
  3. W. Fairham, Woodwork Joints: How They Are Set Out, How Made and Where Used (J. B. Lippincott, 1921), p. 164 — archive.org

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Reinforcement and decoration for frame miters, butt joints, edge joints (tabletop boards) and for stabilizing cracks; strongly associated with certain craft-furniture traditions. Fairham (1921, p.164) shows it on counter tops butt-jointed end to end when timber long enough cannot be had.
Strength
Adds visible strength across a miter or butt joint. The key's grain runs along its length, i.e. across the grain of the boards, so key and boards move differently; take this into account when choosing the key length.
Fixing / glue
Glue; the inlaid key.
Effect on the cut list
No change to the parts. Extra parts: butterfly keys (e.g. 60 x 25 x 8 mm rough), 1-3 per joint/corner, of contrasting wood.

Fabrication

  1. Shape a long strip to the double-dovetail profile and cut slices from it, each ≈ T/3 thick plus an allowance.
  2. Position the key across the joint and knife its outline, with the blade leaning in under the key edge.
  3. Deepen the outline and remove the waste with a chisel (or rout with a template) to ≈ T/3.
  4. Glue in the key (a slight chamfer on its lower edge helps it enter) and plane flush after drying.

When to use
Holds glued-up tabletops and doors flat while leaving the boards free to expand and shrink across their width. Fairham (1921, p.129) also gives it for signboards and wide pediments, to keep them from casting.
Strength
Flattening only: a wide dovetail batten slid into its housing without glue, so the panel can still move.
Fixing / glue
No glue (or a single fixing point).
Effect on the cut list
Extra part: batten (e.g. 25 x 50 mm) with length ≈ top width minus 20-30 mm.

Fabrication

  1. Rout a dovetail socket on the back of the top, across the grain (roughing + dovetail bit).
  2. Profile the batten with a dovetail tongue on one face.
  3. Slide the batten in without glue; optionally fix at a single point.

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Edge-gluing boards for wide panels and aligning faces; the reinforced version of the butt joint. Also works in plywood/particleboard.
Strength
In an edge joint the biscuits mainly register the faces, so a few per joint are enough. They are pressed beech with the grain on the diagonal and expand when a water-based glue wets them, which locks them in the slot.
Fixing / glue
Compressed-beech biscuits + water-based glue.
Effect on the cut list
Does not change dimensions; adds biscuits (n ≈ length/200 per joint).

Fabrication

  1. Arrange the boards in glue-up order and draw a short pencil line across each joint at every biscuit position.
  2. Set the machine fence at mid-thickness and the depth for the biscuit size.
  3. Cut the slots in both edges at the marks, referencing from the same face.
  4. Glue the slots and edges, insert the biscuits, clamp.

Notes. Merged with the 'Biscuit joint' entry in Wood-Joinery p.7 (reinforced butt; oval compressed-wood biscuit in slots). Wood-Joinery p.24: a miter can be reinforced with biscuits. Besides 90° slots (edge, T and L joints), the machine fence also gives 45° slots for miters. Joint Selector (JB p.185): listed under 'Dowels and biscuits', the group of machine-age alternatives that spare the hand fitting of the parts. The Romanian wolfcraft booklet calls them 'flat dowels': 4 mm oval plates set in a milled slot; the system was invented in 1955 by Hermann Steiner (p.14). To join two lengths of kitchen worktop it gives 4-5 slots along the edge (p.17). Lamello: the diagonal grain makes them hard to break, and they swell where glued, tightening the joint.

End-to-end scarf joint (plain glued scarf)

also: plain scarf, long-bevel splice, glued scarf splice

Înnădire cu tăietură oblică (teșitură 1:8)Schäftung

Used in: Lengthening (mouldings, skirtings, rails)Visibility: hidden

TopologyI
Source
Wood Handbook, FPL-GTR-282 (USDA Forest Products Laboratory, 2021), cap. 10, p. 10-16 – 10-17 — research.fs.usda.gov
All sources (3)Hide list
  1. Wood Handbook, FPL-GTR-282 (USDA Forest Products Laboratory, 2021), cap. 10, p. 10-16 – 10-17 — research.fs.usda.gov
  2. The Joint Book, p. 33-35
  3. Tehnologia meseriei, suport de curs dulgher-tâmplar-parchetar (după C. Roșoga, I. Davidescu, Cartea dulgherului), p. 73 — pdfcoffee.com

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Extending trim and moldings by gluing two lengths end to end (baseboards, sills, rails, casings); the same cut, glued at an angle, sets back a guitar headstock.
When not to use
In load-bearing work, place the joint over a support or close to one; the thin feather edges at the tips of the bevels break easily.
Strength
The long, shallow bevel turns an end-grain glue line into one running almost along the grain, over a large area. The Joint Book holds that at 1:8 the joint is, in theory, no weaker than solid wood; the Wood Handbook (2021) gives slopes of 1:12 or flatter as the strongest and reports that a well-made scarf reaches about 90% of the tensile strength of clear wood, against about 25% for a square end-to-end butt. It needs a good glue – epoxy over a priming coat for the highest strength.
Fixing / glue
Glue (epoxy recommended); no mechanical elements.
Effect on the cut list
Total length = L1 + L2 − 8T; each piece is cut with the overlap included (e.g. +160 mm on the assembly at T = 20) plus trimming allowance. Volume removed: triangular prism T x W x 8T from each end.

Fabrication

  1. Layout: on each piece square a line across the face at 8 × T from the end, then draw the 1:8 slope on both edges with a sliding bevel.
  2. Bring the bevel to the lines: saw off the waste if the width allows, otherwise plane the whole slope, starting from the upper corner; hold the plane skewed so the thin edge does not tear.
  3. Coat both faces with a priming layer of epoxy, then apply the bonding coat.
  4. Clamping: the bevels tend to slide under pressure, so pin or block them first; waxed paper under the joint catches squeeze-out; on wide stock a crowned batten across the center carries pressure to the middle.
  5. When dry, plane the faces and edges flush.

Parameters

ParameterValueStatus
Bevel slope1:8 (bevel length = 8 × thickness; e.g. 160 mm at T = 20; ≈ 7.1°)The Joint Book p.33, p.35¶Source
Glueepoxy in two coats: a priming coat absorbed by the wood, then the bonding coatThe Joint Book p.34¶Source
Angled glue facesoptional; make the joint stiffer in bending and shearThe Joint Book p.35¶Source
Slope for maximum strength1:12 or flatter; to approach the tensile strength of the wood, the glue area must be at least ~10 times the cross-section; 1:8 is the usual slope in structural plywoodWood Handbook (2021) p.10-16 – 10-17¶Source

Notes. Ending the bevels with a short square butt instead of a feather edge removes the fragile tips. p.35: where a light-duty scarf lengthens a table rail, the joint line can sit inside the leg, which both supports and hides it. The Romanian name „înnădire cu tăietură oblică” follows the course notes Tehnologia meseriei (p.73), where it is given for carpentry.

SheetF61

Edge-to-edge scarf

also: diagonal-rip extension, wide scarf splice

Înnădire cu tăietură oblică obținută prin spintecare în diagonală

Used in: Lengthening (mouldings, skirtings, rails)Visibility: hidden

TopologyI
Source
Wood Handbook, FPL-GTR-282 (USDA Forest Products Laboratory, 2021), cap. 10, p. 10-16 – 10-17 — research.fs.usda.gov
All sources (2)Hide list
  1. Wood Handbook, FPL-GTR-282 (USDA Forest Products Laboratory, 2021), cap. 10, p. 10-16 – 10-17 — research.fs.usda.gov
  2. The Joint Book, p. 36-37

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Gaining length from a single board that is slightly too short: a long diagonal rip splits it into two tapered halves, which are shifted along the cut, glued back together and ripped to a constant width.
When not to use
For load-bearing timbers do not rely on glue alone: add nails, screws or fixing plates.
Strength
The glue line runs at a shallow angle to the grain. With glue alone the taper must be very long; a spline or cross key adds a second glue surface and mechanical locking, so a steeper cut becomes acceptable.
Fixing / glue
Glue; optional spline, cross key, biscuit or headless anti-slip nail; for structural use nails/screws/plates.
Effect on the cut list
Final length = L + offset; final width = W − width lost to the offset (W − offset/8 at a 1:8 slope). One triangle is lost at each end; optional key piece.

Fabrication

  1. Rip the board along a diagonal with a taper jig (table saw or band saw): 8:1 for a load-bearing joint, or any angle under 20° for non-structural work.
  2. Shift the two halves along the cut until the assembly reaches the required length.
  3. Size the faces with glue, then glue up. One way to clamp: fix one half to the fence of a sled with a non-stick surface and press the other half against it, holding both there until the glue sets.
  4. Another way: keep the notched offcuts from the rip and clamp them to the outer edges, so the clamps bear on parallel faces; a biscuit or a headless nail stops the halves from sliding.
  5. After curing, rip to final width; a cross key can be added at this stage.

Parameters

ParameterValueStatus
Cut slope (structural)taper of 8 × board width (e.g. 720 mm at W = 90)The Joint Book p.37; principiul pantei: Wood Handbook (2021) p.10-16 – 10-17¶Source
Angle for non-structural workany angle under 20°, for species that glue easilyThe Joint Book p.37¶Source
Longitudinal offset of the halvesper the desired length (e.g. 200 mm)=Geometry
Cross key (optional)key in two aligned grooves, cut across the jointThe Joint Book p.37¶Source
Glue sizingrecommended to avoid a "starved" jointThe Joint Book p.36¶Source

Notes. The width loss is calculated geometrically (offset / slope); the book gives no value. Topology I (extension in length). No other source describing this method was found; the Wood Handbook (2021) only confirms the general principle of scarf joints: the smaller the angle between glue line and grain, the stronger the bond (usual slopes 1:8 – 1:12).

SheetF62

Squint-butted scarf

also: halved scarf with angled butts, lengthwise half-lap with squint ends

Înnădire la jumătatea lemnului, cu capete oblice (70°)

Used in: Lengthening (mouldings, skirtings, rails)Visibility: exposed

TopologyI

All sources (4)Hide list

  2. The Joint Book, p. 33, 38-39
  3. Tehnologia meseriei, suport de curs dulgher-tâmplar-parchetar (după C. Roșoga, I. Davidescu, Cartea dulgherului), p. 74–75 — pdfcoffee.com
  4. W. Fairham, Woodwork Joints (J. B. Lippincott, 1921), p. 89–90 — archive.org

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Lengthening members that work in bending (rails, light beams, decorative pieces); a cross key can be added for strength and appearance.
When not to use
Only where precise work is possible: every line is knifed and the faces are fitted by hand.
Strength
The lap faces glue long grain to long grain, and the 70° butts interlock the two pieces; it bends less and carries more than a plain bevel scarf.
Fixing / glue
Glue; optional cross key (wedge) of wood.
Effect on the cut list
Total length = L1 + L2 − 4T (e.g. −80 mm). Volume removed: half the thickness over the lap length on each piece, with a shoulder at 70°.

Fabrication

  1. Layout with a knife: a centerline on the edge, at least 4 × T long; from its two ends, lines at 70° running out to each face, parallel to one another.
  2. Angled cuts first: tilt the blade to 70°, clamp the two pieces together on the miter gauge and trim both ends at once; at the same tilt, lower the blade so the shoulder kerfs stop at the centerline.
  3. Saw out the waste along the centerline (by hand, band saw or table saw); a chisel held flat against the shoulder cleans up the inside corner.
  4. Fit with a shoulder plane down to the knife lines; test.
  5. Glue and clamp; optionally cut a cross groove for a key.

Parameters

ParameterValueStatus
Lap length≥ 4 × thickness (e.g. 80 mm at T = 20); the length is chosen, not given by a formulaThe Joint Book p.38-39¶Source
Cut depth1/2 of thickness (centerline)The Joint Book p.39; Constantinescu & Cârstea (1959) p.119; Fairham (1921) p.89¶Source
Angle of the ends (squint butts)70° to the facesThe Joint Book p.39¶Source
Cross keyoptional, for reinforcement and decorationThe Joint Book p.38¶Source

Notes. The Romanian name follows the course notes „Tehnologia meseriei” (carpenter-joiner-floorer), p.74–75, where the half-lap splice is shown with square or oblique ends. The square-ended version also appears as „înnădire prin chertare dreaptă” (Constantinescu & Cârstea 1959, p.119–120, nailed) and as the half lap scarf (Fairham 1921, p.89–90, screwed); neither of these two shows the squint butts.

Drawings generated by CutVisor from a 3D model (Blender); not to scale. Dashed lines are hidden edges.

When to use
Joining boards end to end (a mechanical connection where end-grain to end-grain glue would fail) and edge joints; non-structural lengthening joints.
Strength
Mechanical tie between the parts. Grain orientation: across the width of the spline, the usual rule for splines.
Fixing / glue
Glue; the double dovetail spline.
Effect on the cut list
No length allowance on the pieces. Extra part: double dovetail spline along the full length of the joint (e.g. 24 x 12 mm section), grain across the width.

Fabrication

  1. Rout a dovetail socket in each piece (roughing with a straight bit, then the dovetail bit).
  2. Mark the double profile on the edge of a board with cross grain and cut it on the table saw in four passes.
  3. Clean out the central V; test and fit the spline.
  4. Glue, tap together or clamp.

Parameters

ParameterValueStatus
spline grainacross the width of the spline (transverse to the joint line)The Joint Book p.150; Fairham (1921) p.42 (cross tongues are stronger than feather tongues)¶Source
difficultythe housings are easy to cut; the work lies in fitting the spline, which takes trial cuts on scrap, about the same effort as a routed sliding dovetailThe Joint Book p.150¶Source
cut on the table sawa table-sawn spline is left with a V in the middle, cleaned out with a chisel or rabbet planeThe Joint Book p.150¶Source
socketon the router table or table saw: straight groove for roughing, then the dovetail bitThe Joint Book p.151¶Source
spline on the table sawmark the profile on the edge of the board, set the blade angle and height; first two angles, then turn end for end for the othersThe Joint Book p.151¶Source
fittingslightly thinned with a rabbet plane or sanding block if too tight; pieces are tapped together or clampedThe Joint Book p.151¶Source
typical dimensionsin 20 mm board: socket 10-12 mm deep in each piece, 8 mm wide at the mouth, 12 mm at the bottom (14°)≈Trade practice

Notes. The 'dovetail batten' variant is treated separately (dovetail-batten). Fairham (1921, p.41) rates the double-dovetailed tongue edge joint the best constructionally but hard to make without machinery; Hinescu (1989, p.45) gives the loose-tongue edge joint as the most economical panel joint.
